Three columns carry the story. `%CPU` is a share of one core, so 96.4 is one core saturated. `ELAPSED` at 03:12 says this worker started three minutes ago, which is after the 09:12 alert, so something respawns it and the CPU is a symptom of a restart loop rather than a runaway calculation. `PPID` 3098 is the gunicorn master, so the worker belongs to the portal stack and not to the monitoring agent.

`pgrep -af portal` is faster when you only need to know a process exists. `ps -ef | grep portal` also works, but it matches its own `grep` line.

sections.h: top tells you busy from waiting
sections.body:
`top` in batch mode prints one snapshot and exits, which is what a ticket needs:

```
$ top -b -n1 | head -8
top - 09:41:12 up 21 days,  3:14,  2 users,  load average: 8.42, 6.90, 4.11
Tasks: 214 total,   2 running, 211 sleeping,   0 stopped,   1 zombie
%Cpu(s): 94.3 us,  2.1 sy,  0.0 ni,  2.9 id,  0.6 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.1 si,  0.0 st
MiB Mem :  16045.2 total,    512.4 free,   9210.7 used,   6322.1 buff/cache
MiB Swap:   4096.0 total,     12.0 used,   4084.0 avail Mem

    PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES  S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
   3122 app       20   0 2841304 341220  R  391.2   2.1  62:38.11 python3
```

A load average of 8.42 on a 4-vCPU host means about twice as many runnable tasks as cores. The CPU line says where the time went: `us` 94.3 is user-space compute and `wa` 0.6 is disk wait. A host at 94 `us` is working; a host at 60 `wa` is waiting on storage and the process list is not the problem.

The 391.2 in the process row is not a bug: a multithreaded process can use several cores and `top` sums them against one. Divide by the vCPU count before calling it abnormal.

Decision rule: if `wa` is above 20 while `us` is low, the host is waiting on disk, and killing the top process will not fix the call. Check `df -h` and the volume latency instead.

sections.h: ss -tulnp: the port, the PID and the address
sections.body:
`ss` replaces `netstat`, which is deprecated on current distributions. The flag string is worth memorizing: `-t` TCP, `-u` UDP, `-l` listening only, `-n` numeric ports, `-p` process.

```
$ sudo ss -tulnp
Netid State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
udp   UNCONN 0      0        127.0.0.53:53       0.0.0.0:*     users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=812,fd=13))
tcp   LISTEN 0      128          0.0.0.0:22       0.0.0.0:*     users:(("sshd",pid=914,fd=3))
tcp   LISTEN 0      128          0.0.0.0:80       0.0.0.0:*     users:(("nginx",pid=1204,fd=6))
tcp   LISTEN 0      511      127.0.0.1:8080     0.0.0.0:*     users:(("java",pid=4412,fd=128))
```

Read the `Local Address` column first. Port 80 sits on `0.0.0.0`, so any interface accepts it. Port 8080 sits on `127.0.0.1`, so only a process on this host can reach it: nginx proxies to java over loopback and no client on the network can call 8080 directly. That column explains a large share of tickets that read as "the service is down but the process is running".

`-p` needs root or `CAP_NET_ADMIN`; without it the Process column is empty, which is not the same as nobody owning the socket.

On a `LISTEN` socket, `Recv-Q` is the number of connections waiting to be accepted and `Send-Q` is the backlog limit. When `Recv-Q` reaches `Send-Q`, clients time out in the kernel before the application sees them.

Decision rule: if the socket is listed, the address matches what the client uses, and `Recv-Q` is at the `Send-Q` limit, this is an application capacity problem, not a network one. Send it to the app owner with the PID and both numbers.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Write the note in the order the next person reads it: host, process, port, decision.

- `web01`, `portal-worker@1` (PID 3122), respawned 09:38, 96 percent of one core
- `ss`: java on `127.0.0.1:8080`, nginx on `0.0.0.0:80`, `Recv-Q` 0 of 128
- `top`: load 8.42 on 4 vCPU, `wa` 0.6, so CPU-bound and not disk

Closing note: "Worker respawn loop on web01 since 09:12. One core saturated, no disk wait, java loopback-only behind nginx. Worker dies after the save queue drains. Restart holds ten minutes. Handing to the portal app owner with `journalctl -u portal-worker@1` attached."

Escalation criterion: escalate when the process is the customer's application and the evidence points inside it, which means a crash loop, an accept queue at its limit, or a bind address that contradicts the design. Fix and close when the cause is a unit you restarted or a second process holding the port.

diagram.title: From a slow portal to an owned port
diagram.caption: Each step produces one line of evidence. The bind address is the step L1 most often skips.

data.footer: Stop at the first step that produces a contradiction with the ticket.

video.title: How to Use the ss Command (Linux Crash Course Series)
video.why: Shows the real ss output columns and how the state filter changes them, which the text can only describe.

commands.what: Processes ranked by CPU, with parent PID and how long each has been running
One batch snapshot of load average, CPU breakdown and top processes, safe to paste in a ticket
Every listening TCP and UDP socket with the owning PID and bind address
Live sessions to the box, which shows whether clients are actually connecting
Confirms a named process exists without matching your own grep line

pitfalls: Restarting the service to clear the CPU alert destroys the process list, the thread state and the last log line; capture ps and journalctl output first or you have nothing to escalate with.
Treating the 391.2 percent CPU in top as an error; it is nearly four cores busy on a multithreaded process, and quoting 391 percent to the app team gets the ticket sent back.
Running ss -tulnp without sudo and reporting that no process owns the port; the Process column stays empty without root or CAP_NET_ADMIN.
takeaways: ps with --sort produces a ticket-ready snapshot, and %CPU above 100 means several cores, not a bad number.
ss -tulnp ties a port to a PID, and the Local Address column decides who can reach it.
A listening socket is not a working service; the accept queue and the application log decide that.

drill.prompt: On your lab VM, start a throwaway listener, prove which PID owns it, and capture one top snapshot while it runs.
checklist: python3 -m http.server 8080 runs in one terminal and ss -tulnp shows python3 on port 8080
You can say which hosts could reach the port given its Local Address value
ps -eo pid,ppid,pcpu,etime,args --sort=-pcpu names the same PID
top -b -n1 output pasted into a note with the load average and wa value read out

l2-5.title: Networking from Linux: addresses, routes and DNS checks
l2-5.subtitle: Prove the interface, the route and the resolver before you escalate.
objectives: Read interface, address and link state with ip addr and ip -br addr
Use ip route get to prove the interface, source and gateway for one destination
Separate resolver failure from lookup-path failure with getent hosts and dig
Hand over the failing hop instead of the phrase network down

ticket.subject: app02 cannot reach the billing API since this morning
ticket.body: The app team reports that app02 cannot reach the billing API at 10.20.5.11 port 8443 and that invoice jobs have failed since 06:00. Ping from app02 to its gateway 10.20.4.1 answers. Ping from app02 to 10.20.5.11 fails. No firewall change is recorded for this window.
ticket.impact: The morning invoice batch is halted; nothing else on app02 is affected.

sections.h: Ping by IP works, ping by name does not, and the ticket says network
sections.body:
Two different failures hide inside the phrase "the network is down". One is reachability: the packet never arrives. The other is resolution: the name never becomes an address. They look identical to the caller and share nothing on the wire.

A third one is more common on servers. The host reaches its gateway and cannot reach a host in another subnet, which means the local stack is fine and something in the middle drops the traffic. All three separate in about two minutes.

Three commands, run on the affected host and not on your laptop, tell you which one you have: `ip -br addr` for the local address and link state, `ip route get <destination>` for the path the kernel chooses, and `getent hosts <name>` for resolution through the same lookup path applications use.

sections.h: The interface says UP and the address is still wrong
sections.body:
Interface names are not portable. `eth0` is a habit from older images; current systems use predictable names such as `ens192` or `enp0s3`, and typing the old one returns `Device "eth0" does not exist` and costs a minute.

```
$ ip -br addr
lo               UNKNOWN        127.0.0.1/8 ::1/128
ens192           UP             10.20.4.31/24 fe80::250:56ff:fe8c:1a2b/64
docker0          DOWN           172.17.0.1/16
```

`-br` is the brief format, one line per interface, and it needs iproute2 4.x or newer. `ip addr show ens192` prints the full detail, including MTU, MAC address and the byte counters on each address, when the brief form is not enough. The state word matters. `UP` means the link is up and the interface is enabled. `DOWN` means it is administratively disabled. `NO-CARRIER` means there is no link at all. A `DOWN` docker0 bridge is normal on a host with no containers running, and calling that a fault is a fast way to lose the app team's attention.

Decision rule: if `ip -br addr` shows `NO-CARRIER` or an address in the wrong subnet, stop. Nothing above layer 2 can work, and routing or DNS checks will not change the finding.

sections.h: ip route get: the one line to quote
sections.body:
`ip route` prints the table. `ip route get` answers the question you actually have: for this destination, which interface, which source address, which gateway.

```
$ ip route
default via 10.20.4.1 dev ens192 proto static metric 100
10.20.4.0/24 dev ens192 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.4.31
172.17.0.0/16 dev docker0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.1 linkdown

$ ip route get 10.20.5.11
10.20.5.11 via 10.20.4.1 dev ens192 src 10.20.4.31 uid 0
```

The second output is the evidence line for the ticket. Traffic to 10.20.5.11 leaves `ens192`, sourced from 10.20.4.31, through 10.20.4.1. If the destination were inside 10.20.4.0/24, the same command would print `dev ens192 src 10.20.4.31` with no `via`, because the host would resolve the MAC address directly.

Two `default` lines with the same metric are a finding worth recording, not a formatting quirk: the kernel can use either, and the return path can come back through the other one, which breaks stateful firewalls. `ip neigh` shows which layer 2 neighbors answered and in what state, such as `REACHABLE`, `STALE` or `FAILED`.

sections.h: Three DNS tools, three different questions
sections.body:
`getent hosts` asks the same question an application asks. It reads `/etc/nsswitch.conf` and follows that order: `files` for `/etc/hosts`, then `dns`, and on some fleets `sss` for the directory. If `getent` resolves, the application can resolve.

`dig +short` sends a query straight to the resolver and ignores nsswitch and `/etc/hosts`. It answers "is the DNS server working", not "can this host resolve". `resolvectl status` shows which resolver systemd-resolved is using when it is in the path; on minimal images the same information is in `/etc/resolv.conf`.

```
$ getent hosts intranet.example
10.20.9.14      intranet.example
$ dig +short intranet.example
10.20.9.14
$ resolvectl status ens192
Link 2 (ens192)
    Current DNS Server: 10.20.0.10
       DNS Servers: 10.20.0.10 10.20.0.11
         DNS Domain: corp.example
```

Decision rule: when `dig` resolves and `getent hosts` does not, the DNS server is healthy and the lookup path on this host is broken. Check `/etc/nsswitch.conf` and `/etc/hosts` before opening a DNS ticket.

Decision rule: when both fail and the resolver is `127.0.0.53`, the local stub is the one not answering. Check `systemctl status systemd-resolved` before blaming the upstream servers.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Attach the outputs. They are the difference between a ticket the network team can act on and one they send back.

- `ip -br addr` from the affected host, pasted whole
- `ip route get` with the real destination address, not the name
- `getent hosts` and `dig +short` for the same name when the two disagree
- the source host and the destination host, because a one-sided test proves little

Closing note: "app02 10.20.4.31 routes to 10.20.5.11 via 10.20.4.1 on ens192 and the gateway answers ping. 10.20.5.11 does not answer from app02 and does answer from a host inside 10.20.5.0/24. Local interface, address and route are correct. Requesting a check of the inter-subnet rule between 10.20.4.0/24 and 10.20.5.0/24."

Escalation criterion: escalate to the network team when the interface, the source address and the route are correct and the far side does not answer, with those four outputs attached. Escalate to identity or DNS when `getent` fails for the name while `dig` against every configured resolver succeeds.

diagram.title: What app02's route actually says
diagram.caption: The box knows the way to the gateway. Everything past the core gateway is outside its routing table.

video.title: How to Use the ip Command in Linux: A Beginner’s Guide
video.why: Shows ip addr and ip route on a live host, including what the output looks like when an interface goes down.

commands.what: One line per interface: name, state, IPv4 and IPv6 address
Interface, source address and gateway this host would use for one destination
Resolves the name through nsswitch, the same path applications use
Asks the configured resolver directly, bypassing nsswitch and /etc/hosts
Layer 2 neighbors that answered, with MAC address and state

pitfalls: Running the checks on the jump host or your laptop instead of the affected server; different routes and different resolvers produce a confident, wrong answer.

Restarting NetworkManager or systemd-networkd over SSH to fix an address; the session dies with the interface and the box may not come back reachable. Use nmcli connection up only when console or out-of-band access exists.
Reading a successful dig as proof that applications can resolve names; applications go through nsswitch, and /etc/hosts or a directory module can still break them.
takeaways: Interface state, address and route are three separate facts, and ip -br addr plus ip route get gives all three.
getent hosts and dig answer different questions, and the disagreement between them is the diagnosis.
A correct route with no answer from the far side is a middle-of-path finding, not a local one.

drill.prompt: Prove three facts about your own machine's path and write the three lines a ticket would need.
checklist: ip -br addr output pasted, with the state word for the active interface explained
ip route get for a public address shows interface, source and gateway
getent hosts and dig +short agree for one name, and you can state what a disagreement would mean
You can name the first check you would run if the default route were missing

l2-6.title: The Linux triage runbook: disk, service, port, permission
l2-6.subtitle: A repeatable order for the four calls that look different and are not.
objectives: Run four checks in an order where each one rules out the next
Separate real disk use from deleted open files and inode exhaustion
Read a systemd exit code and map it to a failing layer
Test file access as the account that actually runs the service

ticket.subject: Nightly report service has failed three nights in a row
ticket.body: The report service on report01 fails around 02:10 and a manual restart makes it work until the next night. The app team says nothing changed and points at the server. Disk on / was 78 percent when the alert was raised. The 02:00 compliance report has not been delivered since Monday.
ticket.impact: The compliance team has not received the daily report for three days.

sections.h: The service fails at 02:10 and the restart buys one day
sections.body:
The alert names a failed unit. The app team says nothing changed and points at the server. A restart works until the next night: something on a schedule fills something up, and the unit dies when the next write fails.

Four checks cover almost every Linux ticket at this desk, and the order matters more than the commands. Disk first, because a full filesystem makes units fail and logs disappear. Then the unit, because systemd records an exit code that names the failing layer. Then the port, because a healthy unit nobody can reach is usually a bind or backlog problem. Then permission, tested as the account that runs the service, not as you.

The sequence is short enough to run on every call, and it stops you from restarting things and calling that a diagnosis.

sections.h: Check one: disk, and the space df cannot see
sections.body:
```
$ df -h /
Filesystem                       Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/vg_root-lv_root       40G   39G  1.0G  98% /

$ sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -3
12G     /var/log
3.1G    /var/lib
780M    /var/cache
```

`df` reports 39G used and `du` accounts for 15G. The difference is a deleted file a process still holds open: the blocks return only when the descriptor closes. `lsof +L1` lists them, because `+L1` selects link counts below one.

```
$ sudo lsof +L1 | head -2
COMMAND  PID USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE  SIZE/OFF NLINK    NODE NAME
java    4412 app    47w   REG  253,1 8589934592     0 1048657 /var/log/portal/app.log (deleted)
```

Restarting that process frees the space. Growing the volume does not, and hides the cause until it happens again.

Decision rule: if `df -h` shows usage that `du` cannot find, look for deleted open files before adding storage.

`df -i` is the other half: a filesystem can have gigabytes free and no inodes left, and the application still gets `No space left on device`. At 100 percent inodes the fix is deleting many small files, not resizing.

sections.h: Check two: the unit and the exit code it recorded
sections.body:
```
$ systemctl status report.service --no-pager
report.service - Nightly compliance report
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/report.service; enabled; preset: disabled)
     Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Wed 2025-11-19 02:10:44 UTC; 6h ago
    Process: 28841 ExecStart=/opt/report/bin/run.sh (code=exited, status=203/EXEC)
   Main PID: 28841 (code=exited, status=203/EXEC)
```

The `status=` value is a layer name, not a number to memorize:

| code | meaning | first check |
|---|---|---|
| 203/EXEC | ExecStart binary missing or not executable | `ls -l /opt/report/bin/run.sh` |
| 209/STDOUT | process could not write to stdout or stderr | `df -h` and the log target |
| 217/USER | the `User=` account does not exist | `id <account>` |

`journalctl -u report.service --since today --no-pager` gives the last lines the unit wrote, and that text is what the owner needs. A `203/EXEC` after a package update is a path change, not an application bug.

Decision rule: read the exit code before the log, because the code tells you which log matters.

sections.h: Check three: the port and its queue
sections.body:
When the unit is `active (running)` and the caller still gets nothing, the port is the next question.

```
$ sudo ss -tlnp 'sport = :8443'
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port Process
LISTEN 129    128          0.0.0.0:8443      0.0.0.0:*     users:(("java",pid=5510,fd=91))
```

Three facts come out of one line: the socket exists, it binds all addresses, and the accept queue is full. `Recv-Q` 129 against a `Send-Q` limit of 128 means connections wait in the kernel and clients time out before the application reads them. A restart clears the queue for a minute and adds no capacity.

Decision rule: if `ss` shows `LISTEN` on the address the client uses and `Recv-Q` sits at the `Send-Q` limit, stop checking the host and give the numbers to the application owner.

If the port is not listed, check the unit's configuration for a different port or a loopback bind before opening a firewall ticket.

sections.h: Check four: permission, as the account that runs it
sections.body:
`ls -l` on the file is not enough, because every directory in the path must also be traversable by the service account. `namei -l` walks the whole path and prints each component:

```
$ namei -l /var/report/out/nightly.csv
f: /var/report/out/nightly.csv
drwxr-xr-x root   root   /
drwxr-xr-x root   root   var
drwxr-x--- root   report report
drwxr-x--- root   report out
-rw-r----- report report nightly.csv
```

The first component without `x` for the service account is where the failure is. Test as that account instead of reading mode strings: `sudo -u report test -r /var/report/out/nightly.csv; echo $?` returns 1 when the account cannot read it, whatever the modes suggest.

On an SELinux host, a correct mode can still be denied by a label: `ls -Z` shows the context and `ausearch -m AVC -ts recent` shows recent denials. `setenforce 0` is not an L1 test; it changes the host's security state.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note has four lines, one per check, each with the output that proves it, so a reader sees which checks passed without rerunning them.

- `df -h`, `df -i`, and `lsof +L1` when the two disk numbers disagree
- `systemctl status` with the `status=` code and last journal lines
- `ss -tlnp` for the port, with `Recv-Q` and `Send-Q`
- `namei -l` on the path the service writes, plus the `sudo -u` result

Closing note: "report.service fails nightly at 02:10 with 203/EXEC. /opt/report/bin/run.sh is missing after the 11-17 package update, so the unit cannot start. Disk at 78 percent, no deleted open files, port 8443 listening on the right address. Handing to the report application owner to restore the binary path."

Escalation criterion: escalate when the four checks are clean and the failure is inside the application's own logic or data, and escalate immediately when the cause is disk exhaustion or an ownership decision outside your change authority. Close when the unit starts, the port answers, and the scheduled run writes the expected output file.

diagram.title: Four checks, in the order that saves time
diagram.caption: Each branch is a check with the finding it can produce. The disk branch explains most of the tickets that look like application faults.

video.title: Troubleshooting Linux Disk Space Issues at 2 AM?
video.why: Walks a disk-full call the way a support engineer actually takes it, which reinforces the first check in the runbook.

commands.what: Blocks used and inodes used, which fail with the same application error
Deleted files still held open by a process, which df counts and du cannot see
Unit state plus the numeric exit code that names the failing layer
One port only: bind address, accept queue size and owning PID
Permissions on every path component, not only the file

pitfalls: Matching df to du and assuming the volume is genuinely full; the gap is usually a deleted file still open, and growing the volume hides the cause for one more night.
Reading the exit code only after scrolling the journal; 203/EXEC points at the executable path, and chasing the application log for that code wastes the call.
Testing file access as your own account, which owns sudo and often the file; the service account is the one that gets denied, so the test must run as that account.
takeaways: Order is the runbook: disk, unit, port, permission, because each check removes a layer of the next.
df and du disagree only when a deleted file is still open, and lsof +L1 names it.
systemd exit codes name the layer: 203 is exec, 209 is stdout, 217 is the account.

drill.prompt: Run the four checks against your lab VM in order and record one line of evidence for each, including the checks that pass.
checklist: df -h and df -i both recorded with the use percentage visible
systemctl status on one unit quoted with its status= code or active (running)
ss -tlnp line for one listening port with the PID that owns it
namei -l on a file the service writes, plus the sudo -u test exit code

l3-1.title: ipconfig, ping, whoami: the first three commands on any Windows box
l3-1.subtitle: Establish identity, address and reachability before changing anything.
objectives: Prove which account and which privilege level you are working under with whoami and whoami /groups
Read ipconfig /all for address, gateway, DNS servers and DHCP state, and spot an APIPA address
Tell Request timed out, Destination host unreachable and could not find host apart, and say what each one rules out
Decide in one line whether the ticket is DNS, DHCP, link or application before you escalate

ticket.subject: Laptop shows full Wi-Fi but no browser page loads
ticket.body: The user opened the laptop at 08:55, the Wi-Fi icon shows five bars, and the browser says "This site can't be reached" for the invoice portal. Teams on the same laptop still receives messages. The user restarted once and tried the wired dock with the same result. Nothing was changed on the machine since yesterday.
ticket.impact: One accounts payable user cannot reach the invoice portal since 09:05; month-end invoices are waiting.

sections.h: Five bars of Wi-Fi and the user still cannot reach the portal
sections.body:
Five bars of Wi-Fi and the user still cannot reach the invoice portal. The tray icon measures the radio link between the laptop and the access point. It says nothing about the address the laptop received, whether the gateway answers, or whether the name in the browser became an address at all.

Tickets that start from that icon end in a reboot, a second call, and an escalation that names no failing layer. Three commands in the right order produce a ticket that names one: `whoami` says which account is asking, `ipconfig /all` says what the machine believes about its own addressing, and `ping` says whether one specific host answers right now. Under a minute of typing, and the next engineer does not repeat it.

sections.h: whoami: which account is asking, and with which rights
sections.body:
`whoami` prints the account as `domain\user`. Run it first when two people on the same machine get different results, because Group Policy, mapped drives, per-user VPN profiles and proxy settings all follow the account, not the computer.

`whoami /groups` lists every group in the current token, including the integrity level line that tells you whether the window is elevated. `whoami /priv` lists the privileges the token holds; a standard user has far fewer than an administrator. `whoami /upn` prints the user principal name, the `jdoe@corp.example` form that the mail and VPN teams will ask for.

```
C:\> whoami
corp\jdoe

C:\> whoami /groups | findstr /i "mandatory"
Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level  Label  S-1-16-8192
```

`Medium` means the window is not elevated. A fix that needs administrator rights will fail from that window even when the account is a local administrator, and the failure looks like a permissions bug rather than the User Account Control prompt the user dismissed.

sections.h: ipconfig /all: the machine's account of itself
sections.body:
`ipconfig /all` prints one block per adapter. Read four lines before any other: the IPv4 address, the default gateway, the DNS servers, and whether DHCP is enabled. An address starting with `169.254.` is an APIPA address, which means the machine asked for a lease and nothing answered; there is no point testing the internet until DHCP replies. `Media State . . . . . . . : Media disconnected` means the link is down at the network card, so the cable, the dock or the switch port is the finding.

```
C:\> ipconfig /all

Windows IP Configuration

   Host Name . . . . . . . . . . . . : ws-4412
   Primary Dns Suffix  . . . . . . . : corp.example

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   Description . . . . . . . . . . . : Intel(R) Ethernet Connection I219-LM
   DHCP Enabled. . . . . . . . . . . : Yes
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.20.14.87(Preferred)
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 10.20.14.1
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 10.20.0.10
                                       10.20.0.11
   Lease Obtained. . . . . . . . . . : Monday, November 24, 2025 8:41:12 AM
```

The DNS server line is the one people leave out of the ticket. A machine pointed at `10.20.0.10` while the rest of the floor uses `10.20.0.11` is a finding, not noise. `ipconfig /displaydns` shows the local cache and `ipconfig /flushdns` clears it, which is worth trying when one name fails and every other name works.

sections.h: ping: whether anything answers, and which failure you got
sections.body:
`ping` sends ICMP echo requests. On Windows, bare `ping` sends four and stops, so `-n 2` only shortens the wait; `-t` is the one that runs until you press Ctrl+C. Ping the address first, then the name.

```
C:\> ping -n 2 10.20.0.10

Pinging 10.20.0.10 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 10.20.0.10: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=128
Reply from 10.20.0.10: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=128

C:\> ping intranet.corp.example
Ping request could not find host intranet.corp.example. Please check the name and try again.

C:\> ping -n 2 10.20.14.77
Reply from 10.20.14.1: Destination host unreachable.
```

The three messages are three diagnoses. `Request timed out` means the request left and nothing came back. `Destination host unreachable` comes from a router or gateway that has no route, and it names the device that gave up. `could not find host` means the name never became an address, so the finding is DNS and more ping testing will not move it.

**Decision rule:** if ping by address succeeds and ping by name fails, stop testing reachability and run `nslookup intranet.corp.example 10.20.0.10`. A failed ping misleads in the same way: Windows Firewall drops inbound ICMP echo by default, so a server that ignores ping can still serve its application. Test the port the application uses before you write the word down.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Four lines close this ticket: the account from `whoami`, the address, gateway and DNS server from `ipconfig /all`, the exact ping command with its first reply or error, and the name that failed with its `nslookup` result. Then one sentence to the user that states what works and what does not.

> From ws-4412 as corp\jdoe: address 10.20.14.87/24, gateway 10.20.14.1 replies in 1 ms, DNS server is 10.20.0.10. `ping intranet.corp.example` returns "could not find host". The network path is up; name resolution for the intranet zone is not.

Escalate when the address is `169.254.x.x` and `ipconfig /renew` returns the same address, because that is a DHCP scope, relay or VLAN problem on the network side. Escalate also when ping by address and by name both succeed but a single application fails: that is not a network ticket, and it belongs to the application owner with the port test attached.

diagram.title: Configuration versus reachability
diagram.caption: The two halves of a network ticket. ipconfig /all reports what the machine was given; ping reports what answers now. Neither one alone closes the call.

data.verdict: Run ipconfig /all to see what the machine was configured with, then ping to see what answers. Quote both lines in the ticket.

video.title: Basic Networking Commands (Part 1)
video.why: Works through ping and ipconfig from a real command prompt, so the output fields in this lesson appear in the order you will see them on a call.

commands.what: Prints domain\user for the session; the identity half of every permissions ticket
Shows group membership and the integrity level, which tells you whether the window is elevated
Address, gateway, DNS servers, DHCP state and lease time for every adapter
Clears the local resolver cache when one name is stale and the rest work
Sends four echo requests, so the result is a number of replies, not a guess
Asks one named server, which separates a name failure from a resolver failure

pitfalls: Reading the Wi-Fi bars as connectivity. The icon reports radio signal only; a laptop with five bars and an APIPA address has no usable network at all.
Treating a failed ping as a dead host. Windows Firewall drops inbound ICMP echo by default, so test the application port before you tell anyone the server is down.
Quoting ipconfig without the DNS Servers line. A machine pointed at the wrong resolver explains a name-only failure, and that line is the evidence.
Running ipconfig /flushdns in a user session that is not elevated. It fails with a permission error and the cache stays as it was.
takeaways: Identity, address, reachability: three commands, three answers, in that order.
Request timed out, Destination host unreachable and could not find host are three different diagnoses, not one.
The DNS Servers line in ipconfig /all is part of the diagnosis, not trivia.

drill.prompt: On your own Windows machine, run whoami, whoami /groups and ipconfig /all, and write the four deciding lines into a scratch note. Then ping your default gateway, ping a name that you know exists, and ping a name that does not. Save the exact error text for the failing name.
checklist: The note holds the domain\user string and the integrity level from whoami /groups
The note holds IPv4 address, default gateway and one DNS server address
You have the exact text of the "could not find host" error next to the working gateway ping
You can say which of the three results would change if the cable were unplugged

l3-2.title: Processes and services: tasklist, Get-Process, Get-Service
l3-2.subtitle: What is running, under which account, and what starts at boot.
objectives: Name the process holding a port or a file with tasklist and Get-Process, including its PID and owner
Read State, StartMode and StartName from Get-Service and Win32_Service, and say what each value rules out
Separate a service from a scheduled task or a startup entry when a user asks what starts at boot
Decide whether a restart is your action or a change that needs approval

ticket.subject: Report engine will not start, says port 8080 is in use on fs01
ticket.body: The reporting service failed at 02:00 and the operator restarted the server. The service still stops a few seconds after it starts, and the application log says the port is already in use. The operator rebooted twice and reports that nothing changed. The nightly report has not run since the restart.
ticket.impact: Nightly reporting has not produced output for one cycle; three analysts are waiting on the 08:00 report.

sections.h: Port 8080 is in use and nobody can name the process
sections.body:
"The application will not start, it says port 8080 is already in use." The same shape arrives as a stuck print queue, a backup agent that dies at 02:00, or a file share that answers for one user and not another. All of them are one question: what is running, under which account, and what starts it at boot.

The expensive answer is a reboot. It clears the symptom and destroys the evidence, so the next call is identical. The cheap answer is a process list and a service query: a few seconds of typing that tells you whether the thing is a user application, a Windows service or a scheduled task. Those three escalate to three different teams.

sections.h: tasklist: the fastest read on what is running
sections.body:
`tasklist` prints image name, process ID (PID), session name, session number and memory use. `tasklist /v` adds the user name, CPU time and window title, which is how you separate a user's own `chrome.exe` from something running as `SYSTEM`. `tasklist /svc` maps each process to the services hosted inside it, which matters because one `svchost.exe` can carry a dozen services.

```
C:\> tasklist /svc /fi "imagename eq svchost.exe" | findstr /i spooler
svchost.exe                  1428   Spooler

C:\> tasklist /fi "imagename eq excel.exe"
Image Name                     PID Session Name        Session#    Mem Usage
========================= ======== ================ =========== ============
EXCEL.EXE                     8844 Console                    1    214,336 K
```

The filter syntax is narrow: it takes `eq`, not `=`, and the quotes are required because the expression contains a space. `tasklist` cannot show the executable path or the command line, so it names a process but not where it came from; that is the job of `Get-Process`.

sections.h: Get-Process: the same list, as objects you can sort
sections.body:
`Get-Process` returns process objects rather than text, so you select, sort and filter before anything prints. `Get-Process -Name excel` accepts wildcards. Sorting by working set answers "what is eating this machine" with a number instead of an impression.

```
PS C:\> Get-Process | Sort-Object WS -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 -Property Name, Id, WS, CPU

Name       Id        WS    CPU
----       --        --    ---
chrome   9184 1482752000 812.44
Teams    7620  964689920 341.02
OUTLOOK  4412  612368384  87.19
explorer 6120  198754304  41.88
svchost  1428  132120576   9.31
```

`WS` is the working set in bytes; Task Manager shows the same value in megabytes. `CPU` is total processor seconds since the process started, not a percentage, so a long-running process can outrank a busy one. Add `-IncludeUserName` to see the owner, and note that it needs an elevated session; without elevation `Path` is often empty for processes you do not own.

**Decision rule:** if `tasklist` shows the process but `Get-Service` has no service by that name, restarting services will never fix it. You are dealing with a user application or a scheduled task, and the escalation goes to the application owner.

sections.h: Get-Service: state, start type and the account behind it
sections.body:
`Get-Service` answers a different question: is this thing registered, is it running, and will Windows start it at boot. `Get-Service -Name Spooler` returns status, name and display name. `Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped'` lists what is not running, which is noise on a healthy workstation and a lead on a server that lost a dependency.

The columns that belong in a ticket come from the service configuration, not from the runtime state.

```
PS C:\> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object Name -eq 'Spooler' |
>> Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName

Name    State   StartMode StartName    PathName
----    -----   --------- ---------    --------
Spooler Running Auto      LocalSystem  C:\WINDOWS\System32\spoolsv.exe
```

`StartMode` is `Auto`, `Manual` or `Disabled`. A service that is `Auto` and `Stopped` after a reboot failed to start, and the reason is in the System event log, not in the service list. `StartName` is the account: `LocalSystem` has broad rights on that machine, `NT AUTHORITY\NetworkService` has few local rights, and a domain account such as `CORP\svc-print` depends on its password and on the policy that applies to it. Nearly every problem with a domain-account service is a password, lockout or logon-rights ticket.

`sc.exe qc Spooler` prints the same configuration when PowerShell is not available. `Restart-Service -Name Spooler` restarts it, and on a print or file server that is a change: confirm the approval before you run it, and say in the ticket that you did.

sections.h: What starts at boot is not always a service
sections.body:
Three mechanisms start software without anyone logging in, and they are not interchangeable. Services start under the service control manager before any user logs on. Scheduled tasks start on a trigger, under the account stored in the task. Startup entries in the Run key or the Startup folder start only when that particular user logs on.

```
PS C:\> Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select-Object Name, Location

Name      Location
----      --------
Teams     Startup
OneDrive  HKU\S-1-5-21-8823...\Run
```

When a user says "it starts by itself and I cannot stop it", that list plus `Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Report-Engine"` names the mechanism and the account. Turning an entry off changes someone's workflow: record it and hand it over rather than disabling it on the call.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Four facts, then one sentence: the process name and PID, the account it runs under, whether it is a service and its `StartMode`, and what you changed or deliberately did not change.

> On fs01: port 8080 is held by PID 8844. `Get-Process -Id 8844` shows java.exe at D:\apps\report\jre\bin\java.exe, started by scheduled task Report-Engine under CORP\svc-report. Spooler is Running, StartMode Auto, StartName LocalSystem. No restart performed.

Escalate when the process runs as a domain service account and the service starts then stops within a minute, because the cause is that account's password, lockout or logon rights and the fix belongs to the identity team. Escalate also when a service is `Auto`, `Stopped`, and the System log shows event 7000 or 7009, since dependency chains are an application-owner decision and not something to guess at with a restart.

diagram.caption: Six steps, cheapest first. Only the last one changes anything, and it is the one that needs approval on a server.

data.footer: A process is what runs now; a service is what Windows starts for you.

l3-3.title: Accounts and lockouts: net user and the local admin problem
l3-3.subtitle: Find a locked, disabled or over-privileged account without guessing.
objectives: Read Account active, Password expires and group membership from net user without changing anything
Distinguish a lockout from a disabled account and an expired password, and name the evidence for each
Choose between waiting, unlocking and escalating a repeat lockout, and justify the choice in the ticket
Explain why adding a user to the local Administrators group is an approval, not a fix

ticket.subject: Locked out again, third time today
ticket.body: The user was unlocked at 09:40 and says the password prompt now rejects the same password that worked this morning. A colleague reset the password yesterday afternoon. Two other people on the same floor sign in normally. The user has a personal phone with mail and a mapped drive to the finance share.
ticket.impact: One finance user cannot sign in to any workstation since 09:52; the 10:00 payment run is blocked.

sections.h: It says my password is wrong, and it is not the password
sections.body:
"It says my password is wrong." That one message covers a locked account, a disabled account, an expired password, a mistyped domain, and a genuinely wrong password. A reset fixes exactly one of those five and makes the other four harder to tell apart, because the reset destroys the timestamp that would have shown which one you had.

The repeat case is the expensive one. The user is unlocked at 09:40, locked again at 09:52, and the ticket now has two resets and no diagnosis. The order that works is read first, act second: read the account state, name the condition, then decide whether the fix is yours to make.

sections.h: net user: read the account before touching it
sections.body:
`net user` with no arguments lists the local accounts on the machine. `net user jdoe` prints one account's state. The fields that decide the ticket are `Account active`, `Account expires`, `Password last set`, `Password expires`, `Last logon` and the group lines.

```
C:\> net user jdoe
User name                    jdoe
Full Name                    J. Doe
Account active               Yes
Account expires              Never
Password last set            11/03/2025 9:14:02 AM
Password expires             02/01/2026 9:14:02 AM
Last logon                   11/24/2025 8:37:11 AM
Local Group Memberships      *Users
Global Group memberships     *None
The command completed successfully.
```

`Account active  No` means the account is disabled, and no password reset changes that. A `Password expires` date in the past means the password expired. A `Last logon` older than the ticket time means this machine has not seen the account today, so you may be reading the wrong account entirely: on a domain-joined workstation, `net user` reads the local account unless you add `/domain`, and if the local account does not exist the answer is "The user name could not be found." `net user jdoe /domain` needs a reachable domain controller and shows the domain account instead.

sections.h: Locked, disabled and expired are three different states
sections.body:
`net accounts` prints the local lockout policy: `Lockout threshold`, `Lockout duration` and `Lockout observation window`. With a threshold of 5 and a duration of 15 minutes, the account unlocks itself a quarter of an hour after the last bad attempt, and the correct action for a single lockout is often to wait and to find the source. `net accounts /domain` reads the domain policy and needs a domain controller.

On the domain side, a lockout appears on a domain controller as event 4740, and the failed attempts behind it as 4625. When a user locks out again minutes after an unlock, the 4740 `Caller Computer Name` field names the machine that keeps trying. In practice that is a phone with a stale mail profile, a mapped drive holding old credentials, or a scheduled job running as the user.

There is no `net user /unlock`. `net user jdoe /active:yes` enables a disabled account; it does not clear a lockout, and the two are frequently confused. A domain account is unlocked in Active Directory, with `Unlock-ADAccount -Identity jdoe` from a machine that has the RSAT Active Directory module, or in the account properties in Active Directory Users and Computers. That right is delegated to specific groups, so a failure here is a permission answer, not a broken cmdlet.

**Decision rule:** if `Account active` reads `No`, stop resetting the password. If the account locks again within minutes of an unlock, stop unlocking and escalate with the caller computer name, because the source is still presenting the old password somewhere on the network.

sections.h: The local admin problem
sections.body:
`net localgroup administrators` lists who is a local administrator on the machine in front of you. `Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators` gives the same answer as objects, and needs Windows 10 or Server 2016 with the LocalAccounts module. Both are read-only and both belong in the ticket, because "the user cannot install the software" and "the user is a local administrator and UAC is still blocking the installer" are different answers to different teams.

The shortcut to avoid is adding the user to that group to unblock a ticket. It grants full control of the machine, it survives long after the ticket closes, and in most organizations it is a change that needs approval from the endpoint team, not a helpdesk action. Where local administrator passwords are managed, they are per-machine and not shared: Windows LAPS stores them in Active Directory in the `msLAPS-Password` attribute, and the older LAPS client uses `ms-Mcs-AdmPwd`. Reading either one is restricted to a delegated group. L1 uses the retrieval process it was given, or escalates, and never writes that password into a ticket note.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Write the account exactly as `net user` prints it, say whether you read the local or the domain account, give the four fields that decided the case, and add the policy values from `net accounts`. If you unlocked, disabled or enabled anything, state it with the time.

> Read corp\jdoe on ws-4412: Account active Yes, Password expires 02/01/2026, last logon 08:37 today. Two 4740 events on dc01 at 09:41 and 09:52, caller computer ws-3310. Password not reset, account not unlocked.

Escalate when the lockout returns after an unlock, with the caller computer name attached, because clearing a stored credential is a workstation cleanup and not a helpdesk action. Escalate when the fix needs the LAPS password, since retrieval is a delegated right, and escalate any request to add an account to the local administrators group for a reason the ticket does not record.

diagram.title: Five states, five different actions
diagram.caption: Read down the branches in order. Each result is a fact you can quote, and only one of them is fixed by a password reset.

Trying net user jdoe /unlock. No such switch exists; enabling an account with /active:yes does not clear a lockout either.
Adding the user to the local Administrators group to unblock an installer. It grants permanent control of the machine and is a change, not a fix.

A repeat lockout is a source problem, and the 4740 caller computer name is the evidence to escalate with.
Local administrator membership is an approval path; LAPS passwords are delegated and never go in a ticket note.

l3-4.title: Event logs: Get-EventLog, Get-WinEvent and six IDs that matter
l3-4.subtitle: Turn a vague 'it logged me out' into a timestamp you can defend.
objectives: Read the System, Application and Security logs and say which one answers the caller's question.
Choose Get-EventLog or Get-WinEvent from the shell version in front of you.
Build a FilterHashtable query that returns one time window instead of the whole log.
Recognize six event IDs and state what each one lets you claim in a ticket.

ticket.subject: It signs me out every morning around nine
ticket.body: Since Monday the user is signed out of webmail and Outlook between 08:55 and 09:10, then signs back in and works the rest of the day. They rebooted twice and changed their password yesterday with no change. Two colleagues on the same floor are unaffected.
ticket.impact: An accounts-payable clerk loses 15 to 20 minutes each morning; the Monday close is at risk.

sections.h: The user says they were logged out, and the ticket has no time in it
sections.body:
"Logged out" covers four different failures: the screen locked, the session ended, the account locked, or the password stopped working. The caller cannot tell them apart and will usually offer a guess, often "the network dropped," which is the least likely of the four. Write that guess into the ticket and the next engineer inherits it as fact.

The evidence already exists on the machine and on the domain controller. Windows writes a record for each of those four events with a timestamp, an account name, and, for logons, a source machine. Your job on the call is to convert the sentence into an event ID plus a time. That pair is what every later decision uses.

Three logs matter here: **System** for drivers, services and reboots; **Application** for programs that crashed; **Security** for logons and lockouts. Security is the one you cannot read from a standard shell. Without elevation you get an access error or an empty result, and an empty result reads exactly like "no such event."

sections.h: Get-EventLog is the old name, and it is not on the new shell
sections.body:
Windows ships two shells that look identical. Windows PowerShell 5.1 has `Get-EventLog`. PowerShell 7 does not: the cmdlet was left behind when the shell moved off the .NET Framework, so a command that works on your colleague's console fails on yours. Check the version before you debug anything else.

```
PS C:\> $PSVersionTable.PSVersion

Major  Minor  Build  Revision
-----  -----  -----  --------
5      1      19041  3803
```

`Get-EventLog` is fine for a quick read because it returns entry types that match what the Event Viewer console shows. Use it on 5.1 when you want the last twenty entries in front of a human.

Use `Get-WinEvent` for anything that goes into a ticket or into another command. It exists in both shells, it reads the modern `Microsoft-Windows-*` channels, and its filter is applied by the event log service before events travel to your console. That last point is why a filtered query returns in a second while an unfiltered one takes a minute on a busy server.

sections.h: Ask for a window, not the whole log
sections.body:
`Get-WinEvent -LogName System` pulls what it can and sorts it after the fact. `-FilterHashtable` takes the same fields the Event Viewer filter dialog offers and hands the work to the service:

```
PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=41,1074,6008; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-3)}

   ProviderName: Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Power

TimeCreated                Id LevelDisplayName Message
-----------                -- ---------------- -------
11/24/2025 7:52:41 AM      41 Critical         The system has rebooted without cleanly shutting down first.
```

The keys you will use are `LogName`, `Id` (one value or a comma list), `StartTime`, `EndTime`, `ProviderName`, `Level` and `UserID`. `StartTime` takes a `[datetime]`, so `(Get-Date).AddHours(-12)` is valid and is easier to defend than a bare date someone has to interpret.

Results come back newest first. `-MaxEvents` caps them, which matters because one lockout on a busy controller can produce hundreds of records inside an hour.

A query with no matches is not silent. `Get-WinEvent` writes `No events were found that match the specified selection criteria` to the error stream, so a zero result reads like a broken command until you know the wording. Add `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` only after you have decided that zero is a valid answer.

sections.h: Six IDs, and what each one lets you claim
sections.body:
| ID | Log | What the record says | What you do with it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4625 | Security | A logon failed. Sub-status `0xC000006A` is a bad password, `0xC0000234` is a locked account | Count them and note the source workstation |
| 4740 | Security, on a DC | An account was locked out, with the caller's computer name | Find the stale credential on that machine |
| 41 | System | The machine rebooted without a clean shutdown | Pair it with 6008, which carries the actual shutdown time |
| 1074 | System | A process or user started a shutdown, with a reason string | Confirms a planned patch window |
| 7036 | System | A named service entered the running or stopped state | Tells you what stopped and when |
| 1000 | Application | A program crashed, with the faulting module | Names the component, not the fix |

Two rules cover most calls built on that table. If 4740 appears, the PC in front of you is not the fault: something on some machine is still sending the old password, and an unlock alone buys one day. If 41 appears without a matching 1074, the machine went down hard, which points at power, the hypervisor, or a bugcheck, and not at anything the user did.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Write the note as evidence, not narrative: log name, event ID, timestamp, account, source, and how many times it repeated. One line per finding.

Decision rule: same ID, same clock time, three days running, means it is scheduled. Look for a task, a policy refresh or a reboot window, and stop asking the user what they did. Irregular timestamps with 4625 dominating means a credential source, so ask which device still holds the old password.

Closing note to paste: "System log shows 41 at 07:52 on 11/24 and 6008 for a shutdown at 07:41; no 1074 in the window. Security shows four 4625 from PC-0412 at 08:47 and 4740 at 08:49. Account unlocked at 08:58; 4740 returned at 09:06. Suspected stale credential on PC-0412."

Escalate to L2 when 4740 returns after two unlocks in one shift, or when 41 appears more than once in 24 hours on a server. At that point the question is power or platform, and it is no longer an account ticket.

diagram.title: Four logon records, one clock
diagram.caption: The lockout at 08:49 trails the failed logons at 08:47 by two minutes. The account was not broken; one machine kept sending a stale credential, and the second lockout after the unlock says so.

l3-5.title: PowerShell for L1: objects, pipes and safe one-liners
l3-5.subtitle: Stop parsing text; select, sort and filter real objects.
objectives: Explain why a cmdlet's output has named properties and not columns of text.
Use Get-Member to find a property name before writing a filter.
Build a one-liner that filters, selects and exports without formatting first.
Test a state-changing command with -WhatIf before it runs.

ticket.subject: The stopped-services report is 40 lines of System.ServiceProcess.ServiceController
ticket.body: The weekly patching check pipes stopped services into Set-Content and attaches the file to the change record. Since a colleague rewrote it, the file holds one repeated type name per line and no service names, so the change record is unreadable. The same pipeline still shows a correct table on screen.
ticket.impact: Friday's patch report for 60 servers has no service list, and the change record cannot be approved without it.

sections.h: The one-liner that handed back a type name
sections.body:
Someone on the desk built a weekly check for stopped services. It piped the output into `Set-Content`, and the attached file held forty lines of `System.ServiceProcess.ServiceController` with no service names anywhere. The pipeline looked correct on screen, because the console renders objects as a table and the file does not.

The mistake is treating objects as text. PowerShell does not hand you lines. It hands you objects with named properties, and the table you see is a rendering decision made at the very end. Once you know the property names, you select them instead of scraping them, and the file, the CSV and the screen all agree.

sections.h: Ask the object what it has
sections.body:
`Get-Member` ends the guessing. Pipe anything into it and it prints the type name and every property and method:

```
PS C:\> Get-Service -Name Spooler | Get-Member

   TypeName: System.ServiceProcess.ServiceController

Name       MemberType  Definition
----       ----------  ----------
Name       Property    string Name {get;set;}
Status     Property    System.ServiceProcess.ServiceControllerStatus Status {get;set;}
StartType  Property    System.ServiceProcess.ServiceStartMode StartType {get;}
Stop       Method      void Stop()
```

The `TypeName` line tells you what you are holding. The property list gives you the exact spelling to type later: `Status`, not `State`. That thirty seconds replaces most of the trial and error in a one-liner.

sections.h: Filter the object, not the line
sections.body:
`Where-Object` keeps the objects that satisfy a condition on a property. From PowerShell 3.0 onward you can drop the braces and `$_` for a simple comparison:

```
PS C:\> Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped' | Select-Object -First 4 Name, Status, StartType

Name          Status   StartType
----          ------   ---------
BITS          Stopped  Manual
MapsBroker    Stopped  Automatic
RemoteAccess  Stopped  Disabled
wuauserv      Stopped  Manual
```

`-eq`, `-ne`, `-gt`, `-lt`, `-like` and `-match` are the operators you need, combined with `-and`, `-or` and `-not`. Two differences from other languages catch people out: comparisons are case-insensitive by default, and `-eq` against a collection returns the matching members instead of a single true or false.

`StartType` matters as much as `Status`. A service set to `Automatic` that sits stopped after a clean boot is a finding. A service set to `Manual` that is stopped may be exactly right, and restarting it is a change you did not need to make.

sections.h: Select, sort, then format last
sections.body:
`Select-Object` chooses properties, `Sort-Object` orders by one, and `Format-Table` decides how the console prints them. Order matters, because `Format-*` turns your objects into formatting instructions and everything downstream then sees the formatting rather than the data.

```
PS C:\> Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk -Filter "DriveType=3" |
>>   Select-Object DeviceID, @{n='FreeGB';e={[math]::Round($_.FreeSpace/1GB,1)}}

DeviceID FreeGB
-------- ------
C:         41.2
D:        310.8
```

That `@{n=...;e=...}` block is a calculated property. It adds a column that does not exist on the object, which is how a raw byte count becomes a number a change board will read. Learn the form once and every report becomes one command.

sections.h: Before you press Enter
sections.body:
Read `Get-Help <cmdlet> -Examples` before using an unfamiliar parameter. It costs ten seconds and has caught more mistakes at this desk than any checklist.

Test a state-changing command with `-WhatIf` first. It prints the actions without taking them, and it works on `Restart-Service`, `Stop-Process`, `Remove-Item` and other cmdlets that support `ShouldProcess`. Keep `-Confirm` on when one command will touch more than one object.

Put `-ErrorAction Stop` inside `try/catch` whenever the result decides the next step. Without it a failed lookup returns nothing, the pipeline continues, and the script reports success with empty output, which is worse than an error.

Do not paste `Invoke-Expression` or a download-and-run block from a chat window. An L1 account can read logs and restart a spooler. It should not be executing code of unknown origin on a production host.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note carries the command, the property the decision rests on, and the count. "Three services set to Automatic are stopped, including Spooler, since the 06:12 boot" is a finding. "Services look wrong" is not.

Decision rule: `Automatic` and stopped means restart it once and watch the status for five minutes, then capture the 7036 and 7000 records if it stops again. `Manual` and stopped means change nothing and say so in the note.

Closing note to paste: "Get-Service filtered on Status -eq 'Stopped' returns 12 objects. Three are StartType Automatic: Spooler, PrintNotify, Fax. Spooler stopped at 06:12 per 7036 in the System log and did not restart. No 7000 in the window."

Escalate to L2 when the fix needs a startup-type change or an account change, since both are change records rather than desk actions, or when the cmdlet you need is blocked: no `Get-ADUser`, no remote `Get-CimInstance`, no rights to read the log you need.

diagram.title: One object, five honest steps
diagram.caption: Each step works on objects until the last one, which is the only step allowed to care about column widths. Formatting early is what puts type names in a file.

data.footer: If the output leaves PowerShell, stop before step five.

pitfalls: Piping into findstr or Select-String to pull out a field: the field is already a property, and text matching breaks on any value containing a space.
Format-Table before Export-Csv: the CSV receives formatting objects, so the next tool sees column widths instead of data.
Leaving -ErrorAction at Continue inside a chain: a failed lookup returns nothing, the pipe carries on, and the script reports success with empty output.
takeaways: Cmdlets return objects; the table on screen is a rendering choice made at the end.
Get-Member before Where-Object, because the property name is most of the problem.
Format-* is for humans; Select-Object is for files and for the next command.

drill.prompt: Rewrite one text-scraping command from your desk as an object pipeline that ends in Export-Csv.
checklist: Get-Member output pasted with the TypeName line identified
Where-Object uses a property name, not a text match
A calculated property produces a numeric column with one decimal
The CSV opens with the expected headers and no formatting artifacts

l3-6.title: The Windows triage runbook: slow PC, no RDP, locked account
l3-6.subtitle: Three common calls, one order of checks, evidence in the ticket.
objectives: Order the checks for a slow PC, an RDP failure and a lockout without guessing.
Read TcpTestSucceeded, fDenyTSConnections and event 4740 as evidence rather than symptoms.
Write a handover that names the check, the result and the timestamp.
Decide within two minutes whether a call stays at L1 or goes to L2.

ticket.subject: Nobody can remote into app01 since the reboot
ticket.body: app01 was rebooted in the 06:00 window and Remote Desktop now fails for three admins with 'An internal error has occurred'. Ping to 10.20.6.14 answers and file shares on the same host work. The hypervisor console session still works and the reboot itself was scheduled.
ticket.impact: Three admins are working through the console; a vendor session at 11:00 needs RDP.

sections.h: The 08:55 call that says nothing works
sections.body:
Three calls arrive before nine: a laptop that has become slow, a server nobody can reach over Remote Desktop, and a user who cannot sign in at all. The caller describes all three as "nothing works," and the first engineer to write a theory into the ticket usually routes it to the wrong team.

The three share one opening move: get three facts before any command. Is it one user or many. Is it one machine or any machine. When did it start. One user on one machine is a desk ticket. Many users, or the same fault on a second machine, is not, and saying so early is most of the value L1 adds.

sections.h: Slow PC: CPU, disk, startup, in that order
sections.body:
"Slow" has four usual causes: a process burning CPU, a disk that cannot keep up, too much starting at logon, or too little memory. Separate them with numbers, not with the colors in Task Manager.

```
PS C:\> Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending |
>>   Select-Object -First 5 Name, Id, CPU, @{n='MB';e={[math]::Round($_.WorkingSet64/1MB)}}

Name       Id     CPU     MB
----       --     ---     --
MsMpEng   3184  912.44  402.1
OUTLOOK   6712  288.10  611.7
chrome    9044  141.02  988.3
```

High `CPU` means a process is doing work. Read the name before you call it a problem, because the antivirus engine and the update service are both supposed to work. Then check the disk:

```
PS C:\> Get-Counter '\PhysicalDisk(_Total)\Current Disk Queue Length' -SampleInterval 2 -MaxSamples 3

Timestamp               CounterSamples
---------               --------------
11/24/2025 9:02:11 AM   \\pc-0412\physicaldisk(_total)\current disk queue length : 0.04
```

A sustained queue above 2 on one spindle, or above 4 on a small SSD set, makes the disk the bottleneck, and every other number is downstream of it. Startup load comes from `Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select-Object Name, Location, User`. Report those entries; do not disable them for the user.

sections.h: No RDP: test the port before the password
sections.body:
Remote Desktop fails in three places: the service is stopped, the listener is disabled in the registry, or a firewall drops 3389. The password is the fourth possibility and the one callers blame first.

```
PS C:\> Test-NetConnection -ComputerName app01 -Port 3389 -InformationLevel Detailed

ComputerName           : app01
RemoteAddress          : 10.20.6.14
RemotePort             : 3389
InterfaceAlias         : Ethernet
SourceAddress          : 10.20.4.55
TcpTestSucceeded       : True
```

`TcpTestSucceeded : True` means a packet reached a listening socket, which rules out the firewall and the service in one line and sends you to authentication. `False` sends you to the host:

```
PS C:\> Get-Service TermService | Select-Object Name, Status

Name        Status
----        ------
TermService Running

PS C:\> Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server' -Name fDenyTSConnections |
>>   Select-Object fDenyTSConnections

fDenyTSConnections
------------------
0
```

`0` allows connections and `1` refuses them in the registry, which overrides a healthy service. On the host itself, `qwinsta` shows a session named `rdp-tcp` in `Listen` state when the listener is up, and `Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup 'Remote Desktop'` shows whether the inbound rule is enabled and on which profile.

sections.h: Locked account: prove it away from the PC
sections.body:
A lockout is a domain event, not a desktop event. The record is 4740 on the controller that handled it, and the caller-computer field names the machine that kept sending the wrong password. If that machine is not the one the user sits at, the user is telling the truth, and the fix lives on a phone, a mapped drive or a scheduled task still running as that account.

```
PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4740; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-12)} -MaxEvents 3 |
>>   Select-Object TimeCreated, @{n='Account';e={$_.Properties[0].Value}}

TimeCreated            Account
-----------            -------
11/24/2025 8:49:26 AM  ap.clerk
```

On a workstation with a local account, `Get-LocalUser -Name ap.clerk | Select-Object Name, Enabled, LockedOut` answers the same question. For a domain account, `Get-ADUser -Identity ap.clerk -Properties LockedOut, LastBadPasswordAttempt` needs RSAT installed, and `Search-ADAccount -LockedOut` lists every locked account at once.

Two rules. If `LockedOut` is `False` and the user still cannot sign in, you have a password problem, not a lockout, and further unlocks waste the call. If the lockout returns within minutes of an unlock, a device is still retrying, so find it before the next unlock or you will be unlocking all shift.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The handover carries three lines: what the caller reported, which check confirmed or contradicted it, and the event ID with a timestamp. That is enough for L2 to start where you stopped instead of starting over.

Decision rule: one user, one machine, evidence in the logs, and you own it. Many users, or a second machine with the same symptom, or an event ID pointing at a service or the hypervisor, and you escalate now with the reason attached.

Closing note to paste: "app01 RDP fails for three admins since the 06:00 reboot. Ping 10.20.6.14 answers, SMB to the same host works. Test-NetConnection port 3389 from desk subnet returns TcpTestSucceeded False. TermService Running, fDenyTSConnections 0. No 3389 listener in qwinsta. Not an account fault."

Escalate to L2 when `TcpTestSucceeded` is `False` from two source networks after the service and the firewall rule are confirmed, when disk queue stays above 4 after a reboot, or when 4740 returns after two unlocks in one shift.

diagram.title: Which check owns the call
diagram.caption: Each branch is one command with one possible answer. The last branch is a decision, not a failure: no evidence at L1 is itself a finding worth escalating.

video.title: Troubleshooting Windows - CompTIA A+ 220-1102 - 3.1
video.why: Walks the establish, test, verify and document order against Windows symptoms, which is the sequence this runbook enforces and the text can only assert.

commands.cmd: Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, Id, CPU
commands.what: Whether a process is consuming the machine or something else is
Three samples of disk pressure, which separates a slow disk from a busy CPU

commands.cmd: Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select-Object Name, Command, Location, User
commands.what: What launches at logon, as evidence rather than something to disable
Whether a packet reaches a listening RDP socket from where you sit
0 allows Remote Desktop, 1 refuses it regardless of the service state
Sessions and the rdp-tcp listener in Listen state on the host itself
Lockouts with the caller computer name, read with an elevated shell

pitfalls: Unlocking the account without reading the caller computer: the lockout returns within minutes and the user stops trusting the fix.
Testing RDP only from your own desk: a firewall rule can allow your subnet and drop the user's, so a good test proves less than it seems.
Trusting guest CPU on a virtual machine: host contention shows as low CPU inside the guest with high disk latency, and the process list looks innocent.
takeaways: Ask three questions first: one user or many, one machine or any, since when.
TcpTestSucceeded separates a listening socket from an authentication failure in one line.
A lockout that returns after an unlock is a device still retrying, not a user forgetting.

drill.prompt: Run the three opening checks against one lab Windows host and time yourself from first command to written handover.
checklist: Test-NetConnection to port 3389 returns a value with the address shown
fDenyTSConnections read and its value explained in one sentence
Get-WinEvent returns the most recent 41 or 1074 with a timestamp
A three-line handover written that a stranger could act on

l4-1.title: The CIA triad and thinking like an attacker, within the rules
l4-1.subtitle: Confidentiality, integrity and availability as three different tickets.
objectives: Sort a security ticket into confidentiality, integrity or availability before assigning a queue.
Read file timestamps, hashes and session lists as evidence for the property that broke.
Ask the three attacker questions on a normal call without touching the system under suspicion.
State the authorization boundary that separates lab practice from unauthorized access.

ticket.subject: All our finance files have weird names and there is a note in the folder
ticket.body: Since this morning nobody in the department can open the finance share. Every spreadsheet now ends in .locked and a file called READ-ME.txt is sitting in the root. The on-call engineer restored the folder from last night's backup, but the same files were renamed again an hour later. Users can still log in and their other drives work.
ticket.impact: Six finance users blocked from the quarter forecast since 08:10; a second rename happened after the restore.

sections.h: The .locked share that landed in the wrong queue
sections.body:
At 02:14 the finance share stops behaving. The morning shift takes three calls from one department: nobody can open the quarter's forecast, every spreadsheet now ends in `.locked`, and a file called `READ-ME.txt` appeared in the root. The first ticket goes to the file server team, because the symptom is a file server symptom. Hours later the drive is restored, and the account that did it still holds an open session to the server.

One command shows the shape:

```powershell
PS C:\> Get-ChildItem \\fs01\finance -Recurse -Filter *.locked |
>>   Select-Object -First 4 Name, Length, LastWriteTime

Name                       Length LastWriteTime
----                       ------ -------------
Q3-forecast.xlsx.locked     20480 11/18/2025 02:14:07
AP-ledger-2025.xlsx.locked  18432 11/18/2025 02:14:07
READ-ME.txt                  1024 11/18/2025 02:14:08
```

Two facts settle it. Every file was renamed inside the same second, which nobody does by hand. And a note was written one second after the renames. This is not a permissions fault, not a sync client, not a failing disk. Three properties broke at once: the files cannot be used (availability), the contents were replaced (integrity), and the process had to read each file before it could encrypt it (confidentiality). That combination is an incident: the restore waits until someone captures the session and the timestamps.

sections.h: Three properties, three different queues
sections.body:
**Confidentiality** means only the people you intended can read the data. The ticket sounds like: a folder shared as "anyone with the link", a mailbox rule forwarding invoices to a personal address, a database export posted to a forum. The closing question is who could have seen it, and for how long.

**Integrity** means the data is still what was written. The ticket sounds like: a price list edited overnight, a contract with an amount nobody approved. The closing question is what changed, when, and under whose account.

**Availability** means the people who need it can use it. The ticket sounds like: a login loop, a share that times out, a service that restarts every 40 minutes.

| Property | What the caller loses | Typical L1 symptom | First artifact to grab |
|---|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | privacy of the data | a file shared too widely | mail trace, share audit log |
| Integrity | trust in the data | values changed overnight | file hash, previous version |
| Availability | use of the data | share or app unusable | timestamps, session list |

Real incidents break more than one: ransomware breaks all three, a misfired email only confidentiality. Name the property the caller lost first, because that naming decides the queue, the urgency, and whether anyone may repair the system before evidence is captured.

sections.h: What an attacker wants, and why the symptom tells you
sections.body:
Thinking like an attacker needs no tooling. It needs the three questions an attacker asks before touching anything: what here is worth reading, what here is trusted without being checked, and what here would stop the business if it vanished. Those map onto confidentiality, integrity and availability in that order.

The value of the loop on a normal ticket is evidence, because the motive predicts the artifact. An attacker after data leaves traces in access logs, mail flow and authentication history, not in file timestamps. An attacker after integrity leaves traces in changed files and version history; an attacker after availability, in services, sessions and bandwidth. If the symptom and the evidence disagree, the call is misclassified and the ticket is heading for the wrong team.

**Decision rule:** if a change is mass, timestamped within a few minutes, and accompanied by a note or a new file extension, treat it as a security incident, preserve first, restore second. If one file differs and nothing else shares that timestamp, treat it as user error or a sync conflict and fix it normally.

sections.h: The line you do not cross to think like an attacker
sections.body:
Everything above is reasoning. Action against a system you do not own is a different category.

Written authorization is required before any test, scan, credential attempt or payload touches a host. Authorization means a signed scope document naming the hosts and ranges, the testing window, the techniques allowed, an emergency contact, and who signs it. Permission in a chat message is not authorization. A ticket assigned to you is not authorization. A customer asking "can you check whether we are vulnerable" is a request to route to the security team, not a license to scan.

Inside an authorized test: stay in the lab or on the exact hosts in scope, log every command with a timestamp, stop when you find what looks like real customer data, and report it the same day. Outside one: do not scan, do not try credentials found in a file, do not open a suspicious attachment, and do not test a firewall rule from a customer host.

Unauthorized access is a criminal offense in most jurisdictions regardless of intent, and "I was only checking" is not a defense. A scan you run on a customer range also breaks the evidence chain and can take a production service down.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note is short, and it is written before anything changes:

```text
fs01 finance share: every file under \\fs01\finance renamed to *.locked
between 02:14:07 and 02:14:08 on 11/18. READ-ME.txt written 02:14:08.
Restore NOT started. Open SMB session from 10.20.30.44 captured with
Get-SmbOpenFile. No other share affected so far. Callers: finance team,
6 users, quarter forecast due today.
```

Then close or escalate on one line each:

- Close when the property is restored from a known good source, the account that caused it is disabled, and the ticket records both timestamps.
- **Escalate to the security team immediately when** data was readable by someone who should not have had it, when files were changed under an account nobody can explain, or when a machine is still talking to the share after the damage.

An availability ticket you can fix. A confidentiality ticket you cannot un-read, so treat it as an incident from the first minute.

diagram.title: Five questions that decide the queue
