diagram.caption: The first three questions separate a security incident from a broken share. The last two decide whether you are allowed to repair it yet.

steps.label: When did it change?
steps.detail: one timestamp or a slow drift

data.footer: Reasoning about an attacker is free. Acting like one needs a signed scope.

video.title: CIA Triad - N10-008 CompTIA Network+ : 4.1
video.why: Walks the three properties with concrete breach examples, which makes the classification habit stick faster than the table alone.

commands.what: Shows whether hundreds of files share one rename timestamp, which separates an attack from a user mistake.
Lists who still holds an open handle on the share, so the session can be captured before the restore kills it.
Produces a comparison value for the integrity question: is this the same file that was approved?
Lists what the endpoint protection already caught, with the time and the file it acted on.
Object-access events for the change window, only on servers where file auditing is enabled.

pitfalls: Restoring from backup before capturing the open session list and file timestamps. The restore overwrites the rename times, and the account that did it keeps working.
Reading one "access denied" on the share as a permissions problem. When every file moved in the same second, permissions are the symptom, not the cause.
Testing the suspected weakness on a customer host because the ticket was already open. That is unauthorized access, it contaminates the evidence, and it can take the service down.
takeaways: Confidentiality, integrity and availability fail in different ways and land in different queues.
A mass change within one minute, plus a note, means incident: preserve before you repair.
Thinking like an attacker is analysis; acting like one requires written scope and stays in the lab.

drill.prompt: Take the last three security-flagged tickets in your own queue, or three incidents from the news, and write one line each: the property that broke, the artifact that would prove it, and the team that owns the fix. Use only tickets you are cleared to read, and redact names and addresses.
checklist: Each of the three rows names exactly one property as the first casualty.
Each row names a concrete artifact, such as a hash, a timestamp or an audit log entry.
You can state the decision rule from memory: mass change plus a note means preserve first.
You wrote down which of the three would have been escalated to security on the first call.
No customer name or real address appears in what you wrote.

l4-2.title: Identity: authentication, authorisation, MFA and least privilege
l4-2.subtitle: Who you are, what you may do, and why both checks exist.
objectives: Tell an authentication failure from an authorization failure using the status code and the sign-in log.
Check group membership and token age before requesting any access change.
Explain why two passwords are not MFA, and which factor is easiest to phish.
Route an access request through the role owner instead of granting it on the call.

ticket.subject: Portal says I do not have access to the finance report
ticket.body: The user moved from sales to finance last week. They can sign in to the finance portal and see the dashboard, but every report returns a page saying they do not have access. The password was reset twice this morning and they tried Edge and Chrome. Their manager says they should already have the right group.
ticket.impact: One finance analyst cannot produce the weekly report since 08:30; the manager is asking for an ETA.

sections.h: The access-denied call that a password reset could not fix
sections.body:
On Monday a.singh moved from sales to finance. The ticket says the portal will not let them in. The login works, the dashboard loads, and the report returns "You do not have access to this report." L1 has already reset the password twice and tried a second browser. Neither can work, because the sign-in already succeeded.

Two checks on the user's own machine:

```powershell
PS C:\> whoami /groups | Select-String -Pattern "Finance"

CORP\Finance-Read    Group    S-1-5-21-882134762-1149273812-2017342081-4112
                     Mandatory group, Enabled by default, Enabled group

PS C:\> Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership a.singh | Select-Object Name, GroupCategory

Name           GroupCategory
----           -------------
Domain Users   Security
Finance-Read   Security
VPN-Users      Security
```

The group is present and it is a security group, which is what an application checks. The account is right, the permission is right, and the report still refuses, so the problem is the claim the portal is reading. Group membership is copied into a token at sign-in, and the app trusts that token until it expires. a.singh was added to Finance-Read at 09:10 and signed in at 08:41, so the token predates the group. Sign out and back in, and the report opens.

That is the whole ticket, and it was never a password.

sections.h: Four words people use as one
sections.body:
**Identification** is the claim: a username or an employee number. It is not proof.

**Authentication** is the proof that the claim is true: a password, a key, a fingerprint. It answers "are you who you say you are".

**Authorization** is the decision about what that proven identity may do: read the finance report, approve a payment, restart the service. It answers "is this allowed".

**Accounting** is the record that lets you rebuild both later: sign-in logs, audit trails, change history.

| Question | Control | Fails as | Evidence to look at |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who are you? | authentication | 401, bad password, MFA prompt | sign-in log |
| What may you do? | authorization | 403, access denied, hidden menu | group, role, token claims |
| What did you do? | accounting | nothing visible until audit | audit log, timestamps |

That distinction makes the first ticket a five-minute call instead of five. A 401 is an authentication problem. A 403 after a successful sign-in is an authorization problem: different owner, different fix, different queue.

sections.h: MFA is a second proof, not a second password
sections.body:
**MFA** means two different kinds of evidence, not two items from the same kind. The kinds are something you know (password, PIN), something you have (authenticator app, hardware key, smart card), and something you are (fingerprint, face). Two passwords are not MFA. A password plus a security question is not MFA either, because both are knowledge.

The reason to combine kinds is that they fail differently. A password leaks from a reused site or a phishing page without the attacker touching the device. A hardware key cannot be phished into a fake site, because it verifies the site before it signs anything. A push notification is convenient and it is the weakest link: it asks a tired person to approve something at 02:00.

**Decision rule:** if a user says they got an MFA prompt they did not start and approved it to make it stop, stop treating the call as a login problem. Someone else knows the password. Escalate as a suspected account compromise, revoke the sessions, reset the credential, and pull the sign-in log with the source address.

```powershell
PS C:\> Get-MgAuditLogSignIn -Filter "userPrincipalName eq 'a.singh@corp.example'" -Top 3 |
>>   Select-Object CreatedDateTime, AppDisplayName, @{n='Error';e={$_.Status.ErrorCode}}

CreatedDateTime      AppDisplayName              Error
---------------      --------------              -----
11/18/2025 02:11:44  Office 365 Exchange Online  0
11/18/2025 02:11:57  Office 365 Exchange Online  50126
```

Two attempts, twelve seconds apart, from an application the user does not open at night: that is the finding, not the noise.

sections.h: Least privilege is a process, not a favor
sections.body:
Least privilege means an account holds the access its job needs, for as long as it needs it, and nothing more. On the desk it arrives as small requests: add me to this folder, give me local admin, let me approve invoices while my manager is away.

The rule: access is granted by the resource owner, through the documented request, with an end date. Not by whoever answered the phone. A shared admin account is worse than a delay: the audit log cannot say who did what, and every action under it belongs to everyone.

Three moves that close most access tickets without escalating:

1. Check the role catalog or the group description first. Many requests are for a group the user is already in.
2. If the request matches a documented role, route it through the request form and quote the role name in the ticket.
3. If it does not, say no in writing, name the role that would cover the need, and copy the resource owner. "No" with a path forward closes the ticket.

**Decision rule:** never grant permanent access to solve a temporary problem. Ask for an end date; if the requester cannot name one, the request is not ready.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
```text
a.singh (CORP): signs in to the finance portal, report returns "no access".
MFA satisfied 08:41. Finance-Read group added 09:10, after the sign-in, so
the token does not carry it. Sign out and in at 09:26 issued a new token;
report opens. No password reset needed.
```

- Close when the user has opened the resource, and the ticket records the time of that attempt.
- **Escalate to the identity team when** the group, the role and the token are all correct and access still fails, when the account shows a sign-in from an address or country the user cannot explain, or when an MFA prompt was approved that the user did not start.

A permissions ticket that ends with "should work now" is not closed. It ends when the user has done the thing, and you wrote down when.

diagram.title: One sign-in, two different decisions
diagram.caption: Steps 3 and 4 are authentication. Step 7 is authorization, and it fails even though the user proved who they are.

video.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 1.2
video.why: Shows the three checks as separate controls with the failure each one produces, which is the split this lesson asks you to make on the phone.

commands.what: Every group and SID the current token carries, which is what the local machine and many apps actually check.
Group membership on the account, and whether each group is a security group or only a distribution list.
Distinguishes a disabled or locked account from a wrong password, without a reset.
Recent sign-ins with application, result code and source, which is the evidence for an account compromise.
Cached Kerberos tickets with start and expiry times; a ticket issued before a group change carries the old group list.

pitfalls: Resetting the password for a 403. The sign-in already succeeded, so the reset proves nothing and the user has to change a password for no reason.
Adding a user to a distribution group when the application checks a security group or a role. Mail delivery changes, access does not, and the ticket comes back.
Granting access from a phone call or a chat message to close the ticket quickly. The grant outlives the request, and nobody can show who approved it.
takeaways: A 401 is authentication; a 403 after a successful sign-in is authorization.
Group changes only reach an application when a new token is issued, so sign out and in first.
MFA combines different factor types, and the push prompt is the one that gets approved by mistake.

drill.prompt: On your own machine, run `whoami /groups` and read the SIDs. Find one group that gives you more access than your daily work needs. Write the exact request you would send to the group owner to have it removed, including the end date you would ask for.
checklist: You can point to the group name and its SID in your own `whoami /groups` output.
You named the resource that group actually unlocks, not just its name.
Your request names the group owner and a concrete date.
You can explain why removing it will not break the work you do today.
You did not change any membership yourself to test it.

l4-3.title: Encryption and hashing: what TLS actually proves
l4-3.subtitle: Certificates, handshakes, and the difference between secrecy and integrity.
objectives: Separate encryption, hashing and encoding when a user asks what a value means.
Read a TLS certificate's names, dates and issuer and decide what the warning is about.
State the four things a completed handshake proves and the three it does not.
Verify a file or a certificate with a command whose output you can quote in the ticket.

ticket.subject: Browser says the connection is not private on the reports page
ticket.body: Since Monday everyone on the finance floor gets a full-page warning when they open the reports page in the browser, but the same page works from home. The desk has been telling people to click Advanced and Proceed. One user has already done it twice and entered their password the second time.
ticket.impact: Twelve finance users blocked or clicking through a warning since Monday 08:00; one password entered on the page after a warning.

sections.h: The certificate warning the whole floor learned to click through
sections.body:
An internal app starts showing "Your connection is not private" on Monday morning. Someone on the floor says to click Advanced, then Proceed. By Wednesday the instruction has reached two other departments, and on Friday a user follows it on a look-alike site that asks for a password. Nothing about the browser changed. What changed is that the organization taught its users that a transport warning is noise.

The evidence takes one command, from any machine that can reach the app:

```console
$ openssl s_client -connect app01.corp.example:443 -servername app01.corp.example </dev/null
CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=0 CN = app01.corp.example
verify error:num=10:certificate has expired
verify return:1
---
Certificate chain
 0 s:CN = app01.corp.example
   i:C = US, O = Corp Internal, CN = Corp Issuing CA 01
---
Verify return code: 10 (certificate has expired)
```

The name is right, the issuer is the organization's own CA, and the certificate expired. That is a renewal ticket with a known owner. It is also, until it is fixed, a training exercise in ignoring warnings, and the bill for that lands on the next real phishing page.

**Decision rule:** a browser warning is never closed with "click through". If the name matches, the dates are valid and the chain is trusted, the user should not see a warning at all, and something is intercepting the connection.

sections.h: Encryption, hashing and encoding are three different tools
sections.body:
**Encryption** scrambles data so that only a holder of the key can read it, and it is reversible by design. Symmetric encryption uses one key for both directions, and AES-256-GCM is the common choice for data at rest. Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: a public key anyone may have, and a private key only the owner holds. Asymmetric operations are slow, so they establish a symmetric session key rather than carry the bulk data.

**Hashing** takes any input and produces a fixed-length value, with no key and no reverse. The same input always gives the same hash, and a one-character change gives a completely different one. That makes hashes useful for integrity and for password storage, where the system keeps the hash and compares hashes.

**Encoding** changes the representation and hides nothing. Base64 turns bytes into text so they survive a mail system or a JSON field. It has no key, and anyone can decode it.

| Tool | Reversible | Proves | Example you will meet |
|---|---|---|---|
| Symmetric encryption | with the key | only key holders can read | AES-256-GCM on a disk |
| Asymmetric encryption | with the private key | who holds the private key | TLS key exchange, signatures |
| Hash | no | the data did not change | SHA-256 on a download |
| Encoding | trivially | nothing about safety | Base64 in a URL |

The common L1 error is promising a user that a hash can be "decrypted" to recover an old password. It cannot; the only path is a reset.

sections.h: What the handshake actually proves
sections.body:
The TLS handshake settles four things before any application data moves:

1. The server holds the private key that matches the certificate it presented.
2. The certificate chains to a root the client already trusts.
3. The name the client asked for appears in the certificate's subject alternative names.
4. Both sides derived the same session keys, so everything after this point is encrypted and integrity-checked.

Read it again for what is missing. It does not prove the server is patched, that the business behind it is honest, or that the person typing is who they say. A phishing site with a valid certificate from a free CA passes all four checks, because a certificate is a statement about a name and a key, not a character reference.

That is why "it has a padlock" is not an answer to "is this site safe". The padlock says the traffic is encrypted and the name in the certificate is the name you requested. Whether you typed the right name is the security decision.

sections.h: Reading a certificate in sixty seconds
sections.body:
Three fields answer almost every certificate ticket: the names, the dates, and the issuer.

```console
$ openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName -in web01.crt
subject=CN = web01.corp.example
issuer=C = US, O = Corp Internal, CN = Corp Issuing CA 01
notBefore=Nov 12 00:00:00 2025 GMT
notAfter=Feb 10 00:00:00 2026 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:web01.corp.example, DNS:web01
```

- **Names.** The browser compares the name in the address bar against the subject alternative names. The CN alone is not enough in current browsers.
- **Dates.** Inside the validity window or not.
- **Issuer.** The organization's internal CA for internal apps, a public CA for public sites.

If the name matches and the dates are valid but the browser still warns, the chain is untrusted or something is re-signing the connection. Inside the corporate network a proxy that re-signs traffic is normal, and its CA is pushed to machines by policy. On a home or hotel network the same warning means someone else holds the connection. Stop, do not enter credentials, and escalate with the issuer name.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
```text
app01.corp.example:443 presents CN=app01.corp.example, SAN matches,
issuer Corp Issuing CA 01, expired 11/18/2025 00:00 GMT.
openssl verify code 10 (certificate has expired). Chain otherwise
trusted. All browsers on the finance subnet affected, 12 users.
Action: renewal with the internal PKI team. No workaround issued;
users told not to click through the warning.
```

- Close when a renewed certificate is presented, the verify code is 0, and one user has loaded the page with no warning.
- **Escalate to the security team when** the issuer is not one the organization uses, when the expiry date changes between two checks on the same host, or when a user has already entered credentials after clicking through a warning.

An expired certificate is an availability problem with a boring fix. A certificate nobody in the organization issued is an interception problem, and the only correct answer on the call is to disconnect and report it.

diagram.title: The handshake, and where the proof lives
diagram.caption: Steps 2 to 4 are the proof: the name, the dates, and a chain the browser already trusts. From step 5 the channel is encrypted, and in TLS 1.3 the certificate itself travels inside it.

video.title: TLS Handshake Explained - Computerphile
video.why: Draws the certificate and key-exchange steps by hand, which makes the difference between proving a name and proving a channel concrete.

commands.what: Runs the handshake and prints the verification result, including the exact error number.
The three fields that decide most certificate tickets, without the rest of the output.
Shows the verify result and the expiry date as seen by a client that does not use the browser's trust store.
The Windows way to compare a downloaded file against the vendor's published hash.
The same comparison on Linux, and the value you paste into the ticket as evidence.

pitfalls: Telling a user to click through the warning to clear the call. That teaches the habit, and the habit is what a look-alike site needs.
Calling a Base64 string encrypted. Anyone can decode it, and treating it as a secret is how credentials end up in tickets and logs.
Promising that a password hash can be reversed to recover the old password. A hash is one-way; only a reset restores access.
takeaways: Encryption is reversible with a key, hashing is not reversible, and encoding protects nothing.
A completed handshake proves the key, the chain, the name and the session keys, and nothing about the business.
A warning with valid dates and a trusted issuer means interception, and the call stops there.

drill.prompt: Pick a public site you use and one internal host you are allowed to query. For each, run `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host` and record the verify code, the issuer and the expiry date. Then hash one downloaded file with `Get-FileHash` or `sha256sum` and compare it to the vendor's published value.
checklist: You have two verify codes, and you can say what each one means.
You can name the issuer for both hosts and say whether your machine trusts it by policy.
You recorded both expiry dates and the number of days left on each.
The file hash matches the vendor's published value, or you recorded the mismatch exactly.
You did not click through any warning to complete the exercise.

l4-4.title: Network and endpoint protection: segmentation, EDR and patching
l4-4.subtitle: Why a flat network turns one laptop into an incident.
objectives: Trace which VLANs and server ports a compromised workstation can actually reach, using switch and firewall output
Read an EDR detection for parent process, command line and repeat timing, and decide whether to isolate the host
Prove effective patch state, including pending reboot, on Windows and Linux before calling a host patched
Hand over a containment note that names the segment boundary, the ports found open, and who approved isolation

ticket.from: Service Desk / NOC — endpoint alert queue
ticket.subject: Antivirus alert on ws-0412 and the finance share is full of locked files
ticket.body: At 08:55 the endpoint console raised a detection on ws-0412 for a process writing to many files on a mapped drive. The user on that desk says the finance share on fs01 now shows locked files and nothing opens. The user rebooted the machine once and the alert fired again at 09:04. No change request is open for that host.
ticket.impact: The 12-desk accounts payable team cannot open anything on the finance share since 08:55.

sections.h: One laptop, one flat VLAN, and 200 hosts in the blast radius
sections.body:
The 08:55 alert names one desk. The scope decision is not about that desk. `ws-0412` sits in VLAN 120 with 200 other workstations, two file servers and the print server, and the only thing between them is a switch that forwards whatever it is asked to forward. Ransomware needs no vulnerability for that trip: it opens SMB to TCP 445 on a share the logged-in user can already write to, and encrypts everything the account can reach.

That is the cost of a flat segment. One click becomes twelve desks and a file server before lunch, and recovery becomes a reimage weekend instead of a shift. Nothing you do at the endpoint stops that once the session is authenticated.

Three controls decide how far it spreads, in order of effect: the boundary a host cannot cross, the sensor that notices the write pattern and can cut the host off, and the patch level that closes the ways in. Each has a check you can run and put in the ticket.

sections.h: Segmentation you can prove with a show command
sections.body:
A **VLAN** is a switch-level broadcast domain, and it is not a security boundary on its own. The moment a router or firewall routes between VLANs, every VLAN can reach every other one unless a policy says otherwise. The boundary is the policy between the segments, and the switch tells you where the hosts actually are.

```
sw-core-1# show vlan brief | include 120|130|140
120  AP-Finance-WS   active    Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4, Gi1/0/12
130  SRV-File        active    Gi1/0/21
140  SRV-Print       active    Gi1/0/22
sw-core-1# show ip interface vlan 120 | include Internet
  Internet address is 10.20.120.1/24
```

The segments exist, so the design intent is there. What matters is what the policy between them permits, and the test runs from the workstation:

```
PS C:\> Test-NetConnection 10.20.130.10 -Port 445 | Select-Object -ExpandProperty TcpTestSucceeded
True
PS C:\> Test-NetConnection 10.20.130.11 -Port 445 | Select-Object -ExpandProperty TcpTestSucceeded
True
PS C:\> Test-NetConnection 10.20.130.5 -Port 3389 | Select-Object -ExpandProperty TcpTestSucceeded
True
```

The file server answer is correct, because that is the share the team uses. The backup server on 445 is not: no workflow writes to it from a desk, and it is the target that turns an encryption event into a failed restore. RDP to the domain controller is worse. Both belong in the ticket, with the ports and addresses listed.

Decision rule: if a workstation reaches a port on a server that no documented application needs, that is the finding. Fix the policy before you spend another minute on the endpoint.

sections.h: EDR is a sensor with a remote control, not a wall
sections.body:
**EDR** — endpoint detection and response — records what a process does: its parent, its command line, the files it writes and the addresses it connects to. Antivirus matches known signatures and blocks them. EDR keeps the behavior record, which is why it can show a chain that no signature ever matched.

The console action worth knowing is **isolate**. It cuts the host off the network while keeping the management channel open, so the agent keeps reporting and you can still pull the process tree. Isolating a file server stops the business. Isolating a workstation that is encrypting a mapped drive stops the spread.

On a Windows host with the built-in agent, two commands answer the first questions:

```
PS C:\> Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object RealTimeProtectionEnabled,AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated

RealTimeProtectionEnabled AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated
------------------------- -----------------------------
                     True 11/23/2026 3:14:07 AM

PS C:\> Get-MpThreatDetection | Sort-Object InitialDetectionTime -Descending |
>> Select-Object -First 2 InitialDetectionTime,ThreatID

InitialDetectionTime  ThreatID
--------------------  --------
11/24/2026 9:04:38 AM   2147722
11/24/2026 8:55:12 AM   2147722
```

Two detections nine minutes apart mean the process returned after the first block, so the parent is still running somewhere on that host. That single fact belongs in the ticket. A record that says the machine was cleaned once is not a containment state.

sections.h: Installed is not the same as effective
sections.body:
When someone says a host is patched, three facts are being claimed: the update is installed, the running service uses the new binary, and the host has restarted since the kernel or core library changed. Only the first is easy to check.

On Windows, `Get-HotFix` lists installed updates, and a pending reboot hides the half-applied state underneath it:

```
PS C:\> Get-HotFix -Id KB5040434 | Select-Object HotFixID,InstalledOn

HotFixID   InstalledOn
--------   -----------
KB5040434  11/20/2026 12:00:00 AM

PS C:\> Test-Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Component Based Servicing\RebootPending'
True
```

The update is installed and the reboot never happened, so the old library is still mapped into the running process.

On Linux the same split shows between `updateinfo` and `needs-restarting`:

```
$ sudo dnf updateinfo list --security
CVE-2026-3888 Important/Sec. openssl-libs-1:3.0.7-28.el9_4.x86_64
CVE-2026-3120 Moderate/Sec.  kernel-5.14.0-427.42.1.el9_4.x86_64
$ sudo needs-restarting -r; echo "exit=$?"
Core libraries or services have been updated since boot-up:
  * kernel
  * openssl-libs
Reboot is required to fully utilize these updates.
exit=1
```

`needs-restarting -r` exits 1 when a restart is required, which makes it usable in a script that closes the loop after a patch window. A host that reports zero findings but has not rebooted comes back in next week's scan with the same CVEs.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note has seven lines: hostname and desk, the VLAN the host sits in, the EDR detection time and threat ID, the containment action and the minute you took it, the server ports the host could reach that it should not, patch state including any pending reboot, and the name of the person who approved isolation.

Closing note: do not reimage before the disk or an image of it is preserved for L2. A reimaged host closes the alert and destroys the only record of how the encryption started.

Escalation criterion: if the host reached a server it should not have reached, or a share already shows encrypted files, escalate to L2 incident response immediately and keep the host isolated. Do not clean it and hand it back.

diagram.title: VLAN 120 to the server tier, as routed today
diagram.caption: Workstations reach fs01 on 445 by design. The dashed path to bk01 is the same port on a server no desk workflow needs, and it is what turns one infected laptop into a failed restore.

video.title: What is Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)?
video.why: Shows the detection-to-response path inside an endpoint console, which the text can only describe as a list of record types.

commands.what: which access ports sit in each segment on the switch
whether a workstation can reach SMB on a server it does not use
detection times on the host, to see whether the process returned
exits 1 when updates are installed but the host has not restarted

pitfalls: Treating VLAN separation as a security boundary: once a router routes between the segments, hosts reach each other unless an ACL or zone policy blocks the port, and the flat-network incident repeats.
Reimaging before imaging the disk: the alert closes and L2 loses the process tree, the scheduled task and the initial payload, so the entry path is never found.
Calling a host patched because the update appears in Get-HotFix: without the pending-reboot check the old binary is still serving requests, and the same CVE returns in the next scan.
takeaways: A VLAN is a broadcast domain; the ACL or firewall zone between segments is the boundary.
EDR records behavior and can isolate a host while keeping the management channel open; it is not a signature wall.
Installed, loaded, and rebooted are three different facts, and only the third makes a kernel or library patch effective.

drill.prompt: On your own machine, list the outbound ports that are open from your host to your local network and record which ones you cannot explain. Use `netstat -ano` on Windows or `ss -tunp` on Linux, then map each remote port to a process. Write down three ports you expected and two you did not, and note what each would let an attacker reach if this host were compromised.
checklist: A list of established connections with the remote address and port for each
The process name and PID behind every listening port you can see
At least two connections you cannot justify from a service you knowingly run
One sentence naming the segment boundary that would have blocked the worst of them

l4-5.title: Web security: injection, XSS and misconfiguration
l4-5.subtitle: The three findings behind most application tickets, and their fixes.
objectives: Reproduce a suspected injection with a harmless character and capture the response code, error line and timestamp
Tell an encoding defect from an injection defect by watching what the page does with the text you typed
Read response headers for the three misconfigurations that leak the most: version banners, missing cookie flags, and a missing CSP
Hand over a one-page reproduction the developer can act on without guessing

ticket.subject: Order search returns an error page when a customer name has an apostrophe
ticket.body: The order-desk lead reports that searching for a name with an apostrophe, such as O'Brien, returns a page headed You have an error in your SQL syntax with a file path underneath. Clearing the browser cache was tried, and it happens in Chrome, Edge and Firefox. The same search worked last week and nothing was deployed since.
ticket.impact: About 30 order-desk staff cannot look up roughly one name in twenty since 08:20.

sections.h: The apostrophe that broke the order search
sections.body:
The order desk types `O'Brien` into a search box and gets back a page headed `You have an error in your SQL syntax`, with a file path underneath it. That page is doing three jobs badly at once: it proves the input reached the database without being treated as data, it tells the reader which database engine and which directory the code runs from, and it shows that the application prints its own errors to anonymous users.

Reproduce it with a harmless character before you open any browser console. The status code and the response time separate a rejected query from a dead worker:

```
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" "https://portal.example.com/orders?q=O%27Brien"
500 0.412s
```

A 500 in under half a second is the database parser rejecting malformed SQL, not a timeout or a crash. Three families of defect produce this class of ticket: injection, cross-site scripting and misconfiguration. They are separate fixes, usually separate owners, and one page can carry all three.

sections.h: Injection: when the input becomes code
XSS: the application trusting its own database
sections.body:
**Cross-site scripting** happens when the application puts stored text back into a page as HTML instead of as text. A comment, a ticket title, or a saved search name containing `<script>` runs in every browser that loads that page, carrying that user's session cookie with it. The database is not the problem; the render step is.

The fix is output encoding at render time, not input filtering on the way in. Encode on output (`htmlspecialchars` in PHP, or a template engine that escapes by default), and set the cookie flags so a stolen cookie buys nothing:

```
$ curl -sI https://portal.example.com/account
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx/1.24.0
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.2.14
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=8f2c1d7a; path=/
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
```

`Set-Cookie` has no `HttpOnly` and no `Secure`, and there is no `Content-Security-Policy` header anywhere in the response. `HttpOnly` stops JavaScript from reading the session cookie, `Secure` keeps it off plain HTTP, and a CSP limits which scripts may run at all. Any one of those missing is a finding you can show in a single line of output, with no payload involved.

Decision rule: if the text you typed comes back inside the HTML source and displays as visible characters, that is an encoding problem. If it executes, that is XSS. The fix in both cases sits in one template, not in the database.

sections.h: Misconfiguration: the defaults that ship open
sections.body:
Most application findings are not clever. Directory listing left enabled, a sample application still installed under `/examples`, `X-Powered-By` announcing the exact framework patch level, database admin consoles reachable from the user VLAN, verbose errors in production. None of these needs an exploit; each needs a browser or a scanner.

The header check above is your fastest read. `Server: nginx/1.24.0` and `X-Powered-By: PHP/8.2.14` hand over the exact version, which turns find a bug into find the bug for 8.2.14. Suppressing the version banner and the stack trace is a configuration change with no application logic in it, so it is the cheapest item on the list and usually the slowest to get scheduled.

Decision rule: if an unauthenticated request returns a stack trace, a SQL error, or a framework version, write it up as a finding. The application still working is not a counterargument. The message is the disclosure, and it is the strongest evidence you can attach because it needs no exploitation to prove.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note carries the URL with its parameter, the exact input, the timestamp in UTC, the status code, the first error line or the missing header, the browser and account used, and whether the page showed data belonging to another user. Name the class in the subject line: injection, XSS, or misconfiguration. A developer fixes from a one-page reproduction far faster than from a screenshot of a browser.

Closing note: state what you did not do. A line that says the failure was reproduced with the customer's own input and no payloads were sent protects the customer, the application owner and you.

Escalation criterion: escalate to the application team in the same shift if the page returns another user's records, if an error exposes credentials or internal paths beyond the message text, or if no owner is recorded for the change. Everything else waits for the normal change window.

diagram.title: How one input string becomes a finding
diagram.caption: Steps 2 through 4 are three separate defects: concatenation, error reporting, and logging. A fix at any single step changes the evidence but not the class.

data.footer: The rendered error at step 4 is the evidence you attach and also the disclosure the customer must fix.

video.title: Cross-Site Scripting: A 25-Year Threat That Is Still Going Strong
video.why: Covers the XSS category end to end, including why the browser executes stored text, which this lesson has room to state but not to demonstrate.

commands.what: reproduces the failure and separates a parse error from a timeout
shows version banners, cookie flags and missing security headers
captures the first error line for the ticket
checks whether the server still accepts a deprecated TLS version

pitfalls: Sending a working payload to prove injection on production: a successful UNION or OR 1=1 returns real customer rows, which turns a support ticket into a reportable breach.
Fixing injection by blocking quote characters in the form: the query is still concatenated, and any other metacharacter or an encoded quote walks straight past the filter.
Reading only the page body and never the headers: missing HttpOnly, Secure and CSP do not break the application, so they never appear in a functional test and survive for years.
takeaways: Injection is a concatenation defect; parameterized queries fix it at the only layer that can.
XSS is an output encoding defect, and HttpOnly plus a CSP limits what a successful one can steal.
A stack trace shown to an anonymous user is both the proof of the bug and a finding on its own.

drill.prompt: In your own lab, stand up any intentionally vulnerable web application image locally (DVWA or OWASP Juice Shop in Docker), and on that lab instance only, type a single quote into a search field and capture the response. Then add `HttpOnly` to the lab session cookie and re-read the response headers. Do not run anything against a site you do not own.
checklist: The lab response showing an error or an escaped quote, saved with the URL and timestamp
The response headers before and after the cookie change, side by side
A one-line verdict naming the class: injection, XSS, or misconfiguration
A note of which test you deliberately did not run, and why

l4-6.title: Risk, vulnerability management and the policy you are enforcing
l4-6.subtitle: Severity, likelihood, exceptions and the document nobody reads.
objectives: Separate a scanner's severity score from the risk of a specific host in a specific zone
Sort a scan export by score and port to find the three findings worth a decision
Read an exception register for the three fields that make a deferral valid
Hand over a risk note that forces a recorded decision instead of another email thread

ticket.subject: Scanner says 47 critical on app01 and the owner wants to wait until January
ticket.body: The weekly scan finished at 02:00 and reports 47 critical findings on app01, including a 9.8 in the bundled web framework. The application owner replies that the next maintenance window is in January and the application is internal only. The same export shows the host answering on 8443 from the VPN address pool. The year-end change freeze starts Monday.
ticket.impact: One application server holds 47 critical findings with no signed exception on file since the 02:00 scan.

sections.h: Forty-seven critical findings and an owner who says January
sections.body:
The export lands at 02:00 with 47 critical findings on a single application server, and by 09:00 the owner has replied that the next maintenance window is in January. Both statements are true and neither one is a decision. Forty-seven is a count of findings, not a measure of risk, and January is a date, not a control.

What the desk can settle is narrower and more useful: which findings are reachable, from where, what the host holds, and whether the deferral exists on paper. That is enough to write a note that either closes the queue item or forces a decision from someone accountable for it.

The vocabulary matters here because it is where the conversation goes wrong. A scanner finding is a fact about a host. A vulnerability is a weakness. A threat is someone willing to use it. **Risk** is what you get when all three line up against something the business needs.

sections.h: Severity is the bug. Risk is this host.
sections.body:
**CVSS** — the Common Vulnerability Scoring System — scores the vulnerability largely on its own terms. A 9.8 says the flaw is remotely reachable with no privileges and high impact if reached. It says nothing about whether anyone can reach the component, whether it is enabled, or what data sits behind it.

The environmental factors move the ranking more than the base score does. Is the port exposed to the VPN pool or only to the backup subnet. Is the vulnerable library actually loaded by the running application. Is there a WAF rule or a host firewall in front of it. What does the data classification say about the records on that host. A 9.8 behind a jump server that only two administrators use is a different decision from a 9.8 on a login page.

Decision rule: if CVSS is 9.0 or higher, a working exploit is public, and the host is reachable from a lower-trust zone, treat it as P1 today. The change freeze governs changes, not incidents.

sections.h: Sort the list before you argue about it
sections.body:
The export is a CSV with the columns `host,cve,severity,cvss3_base,port,protocol`. Sort it by score and read the top four. The argument about 47 findings becomes an argument about three, and the port column tells you which of those three needs a maintenance window at all.

```
$ awk -F, 'NR>1 && $4+0>=9.0 {print $2","$1","$4","$5}' scan-app01.csv | sort -t, -k3,3 -nr | head -4
CVE-2026-21445,app01,9.8,443
CVE-2026-31102,app01,9.8,8443
CVE-2025-48871,app01,9.1,443
CVE-2025-36744,app01,9.1,22
```

Port 443 is the service the business uses, so a fix needs a window and a rollback plan. Port 8443 on an application server with no documented admin interface is a service nobody should be able to call, and closing it is a firewall rule that does not need a maintenance window at all. Port 22 answering beyond the jump host is an exposure finding, not a patch finding, and it can be fixed this afternoon.

Attach the counts as well, because the owner will ask for them: `awk -F, 'NR>1 {c[$3]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' scan-app01.csv`. A list without counts invites a debate about the list.

sections.h: The exception is a document with an expiry date
sections.body:
A deferral that exists only in email is not an exception, it is a hope with a timestamp. An **exception** records the asset, the finding, the reason for the delay, the compensating control, the owner, the approver and an expiry date. The expiry is the field people skip and the one that makes the register work: on that date the decision is made again or the finding returns to the queue on its own.

Your job is to read the register, not to grant the deferral. Search by host and by CVE, then check three fields. Is it signed by someone with authority over that asset class. Does the compensating control exist as something you can verify. Is the expiry still in the future. A control written as monitoring in place is not verifiable. A control written as host firewall permits 443 only from 10.20.50.0/24 is, and you can test it in one command.

Decision rule: no signed exception, no deferral. If the owner pushes back, send the scan output and the request to the security manager. Accepting risk is a decision for someone accountable for it, and the desk is not that person.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note carries the asset, the finding count by severity, the top three by CVSS with port and exposure, whether each one is reachable from a lower-trust zone, the exception status and expiry, the owner's requested window, and the freeze dates currently in force.

Closing note: quote the evidence, not the adjective. A line reading CVE-2026-31102, CVSS 9.8, port 8443 reachable from 10.20.0.0/16 ends a meeting that a line reading the server is at risk starts.

Escalation criterion: escalate to the security manager the same day if a critical finding is being deferred with no signed exception, or if the host is reachable from a zone its documentation does not allow. Do not scan production or run exploit checks to prove the point; scanning is intrusive, any such test needs written authorization, and it belongs in the lab.

diagram.title: This week's queue, placed by likelihood and impact
diagram.caption: The top right is what pages you at 02:00. The bottom left is real and is not this week's ticket: the register records it and the next review picks it up.

video.title: CertMike Explains CVSS
video.why: Walks the CVSS metric groups in under five minutes, which makes the gap between a base score and a host-specific risk judgment concrete.

commands.what: the findings that actually need a decision this week

commands.cmd: awk -F, 'NR>1 {c[$3]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' scan-app01.csv
commands.what: findings per severity band, for the note and the pushback
whether the admin port is reachable from your segment or only from the jump host
whether a signed, unexpired exception exists for that host

pitfalls: Reporting the raw critical count as the risk: 47 findings on a host that nobody outside one subnet can reach reads the same as 47 on an internet-facing server, so the number stops meaning anything and gets ignored.
Treating an email approval as an exception: with no expiry and no named approver, the deferral never returns to the queue and the finding is still open two years later.
Running an exploit check to settle the argument: scanning and exploit validation against production without written authorization is an unapproved test against a customer system.
takeaways: CVSS scores the bug; risk depends on exposure, data and controls on that host.
Ports and exposure reorder a scan export faster than the severity column does.
An exception without an approver and an expiry is not a decision, it is a delay.

drill.prompt: Take any published CVE that affected a product you use, read its CVSS vector string, and write two paragraphs: one describing the bug with no reference to your environment, and one describing the risk if it were on a host you administer. Then place three findings from your own lab on a likelihood-versus-impact grid and label each with the control that would move it.
checklist: The CVSS vector string decoded into its four base metrics in plain words
Two separate paragraphs: the vulnerability alone, then the risk on a named host
Three plotted items with a one-line justification for each position
One named compensating control that would move an item down the grid

l5-1.title: Recon and footprinting: what is already public about a company
l5-1.subtitle: Map the exposed surface before you touch a single port.
objectives: List the public sources that describe an estate, and say what each one reveals
Run whois, dig and a certificate-transparency query, and read the fields that change the report
Classify every question as passive or active, and hold the active ones until scope is signed
Produce a one-page asset table where every row carries its source and date

ticket.subject: Client SOC saw scanning from our office IP before the contract was signed
ticket.body: The client's security team says it saw port scans against their web range at 09:40, coming from an address in our office. The engagement letter is still with their legal team. The analyst who ran the scan says they were only checking what was already exposed. The client wants to know what was sent and whether anything was touched.
ticket.impact: Engagement start date is on hold until the client security team gets a written answer; two consultants are idle this week.

sections.h: The scan hit a /24 before the scope letter was signed
sections.body:
The intake call happened on a Friday. The scope letter was signed on Monday. On Wednesday an analyst ran a discovery scan across the range the client had mentioned on the phone, because the range was obvious. The client's SOC opened an incident at 09:40, and the engagement started with an apology instead of a kickoff.

That is the failure this lesson exists to prevent. **Footprinting** means collecting information about a target from sources that already publish it: DNS, certificate logs, company filings, search indexes. **Reconnaissance** is the whole opening phase, and it splits on one question: does a packet reach an address the client owns? Passive work sends none, so it can be done before the contract, from a desk, at any hour. Active work sends packets at their estate, so it needs signed authorization that names the ranges, the dates, and a contact who answers at 22:00.

Two rules hold for the rest of this module. Written authorization is required before any active step, and every active exercise stays in the lab range. Everything in this lesson is passive, and passive answers more than most people expect.

sections.h: The zone answers four questions before you email anyone
sections.body:
DNS is the client's own index of what it publishes, and it is readable without touching them. Four queries cover most of what a first report needs.

```console
$ dig +short example.com NS
ns1.hosting.example.
ns2.hosting.example.

$ dig +short example.com MX
10 mail1.mailprovider.example.
20 mail2.mailprovider.example.

$ dig +short example.com TXT
"v=spf1 include:_spf.mailprovider.example -all"

$ dig +short www.example.com
example.com.
```

The NS records name the DNS provider, which is usually the hosting provider and a hint at where the site actually lives. The MX records name the mail provider, and with it the mail filtering vendor. The TXT record is an SPF policy, and the `include:` entries list every third party allowed to send mail as this domain, which is a list of SaaS platforms somebody bought without telling you. A `CNAME` on `www` that points at a registrar host means the site is hosted, not owned in that rack.

Then try the zone transfer and record the refusal. `dig axfr example.com @ns1.hosting.example.` returning `; Transfer failed.` is the correct, normal answer, and it belongs in the report as a line of evidence, not as a finding.

sections.h: Certificates publish hostnames nobody meant to publish
sections.body:
A public certificate authority must publish every certificate it issues to a Certificate Transparency log. Those logs are searchable, and they keep hostnames that DNS stopped pointing at years ago. That is how you find the staging host and the build server nobody meant to publish.

```console
$ curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" \
    | jq -r '.[].name_value' | tr ',' '\n' | sort -u
*.example.com
jenkins.example.com
staging.example.com
vpn.example.com
```

`%25` is a URL-encoded percent sign, which crt.sh reads as the wildcard, so the query asks for every name under `example.com`. One JSON entry can carry several names in `name_value`, which is why the output is split and sorted. crt.sh is a free service under load: run one query, then wait.

Every name becomes an asset line with its source attached. `jenkins.example.com` came from a certificate issued in March 2024, and if it resolves from the public internet, that is the first paragraph of your report. A build server exposed to the internet is a worse finding than anything you will scan for later.

sections.h: A job post named the firewall version, a search index named the folder
sections.body:
Search indexes hold what the client published and forgot. Two queries do most of the work: `site:example.com filetype:pdf` finds documents, and `site:example.com -inurl:www` finds pages outside the main site. Change the file type to `xlsx` and you find the price list.

Job posts are the quietest source. A vacancy asking for FortiOS 7.0 and Cisco ASA 9.16 on the edge tells you the platform and the generation. A post mentioning Jenkins on 10.20.x tells you the internal addressing scheme. Treat both as claims, not facts: a recruiter wrote them, not the network team.

Shodan indexes what is exposed on the public internet. A query such as `org:"Example Corp"` matches the IP registration name rather than DNS, so it surfaces hosts no name points at. Record the timestamp, because the index changes hourly.

**Decision rule:** if the question can be answered from a cache, a log, a filing or a search index, it is passive and it goes in the report today. If the answer needs a packet to an address the client owns, it is active, it waits for signed scope, and L1 does not start it.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The deliverable is one table, on one page, with no scan output attached.

| Asset | Source | First seen | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vpn.example.com` | crt.sh, cert dated 2024-03 | 24 Nov | remote access, likely SSO in front |
| `jenkins.example.com` | crt.sh, cert dated 2023-11 | 24 Nov | build server, public address, not in scope |
| `mail1.mailprovider.example` | `dig MX` | 24 Nov | mail hosted by a third party |

Then the closing note, which is what the engagement lead forwards:

> Passive footprint of example.com, collected 24 Nov 10:00 to 11:20. Sources: public DNS, crt.sh, one search index. No packets were sent to client addresses. Four subdomains found; jenkins.example.com resolves to a public address and is not covered by the scope letter.

Escalate to the engagement lead, before anyone scans, when a discovered name resolves to a public address outside the documented scope, when a public repository appears to hold a live credential, or when an administrative login is reachable from the internet. None of those are tested from L1. They are dated, quoted with their source, and handed up.

diagram.title: Passive footprint, in order
diagram.caption: Each step feeds the next: DNS names the hosts, certificates reveal the ones DNS hides, and the search step fills in people and versions. No packet leaves your network.

data.footer: All five steps are passive: nothing is sent to a client address.

video.title: Passive Reconnaissance - Whois Lookup Tutorial
video.why: Shows a real whois response field by field, so you can see which lines are worth copying into a report and which are registrar noise.

commands.what: Registrar, creation date and name servers; the creation date tells you how old the estate is
Names the DNS and hosting provider, which points at where the site runs
Names the mail provider and, with it, the mail filtering vendor
The SPF record lists every third party allowed to send mail for the domain
Tests for an open zone transfer; "Transfer failed." is the normal, correct answer
Pulls every hostname ever published in a public certificate for that domain

pitfalls: Running a discovery scan "to check the range" before scope is signed. That is an active step against someone else's estate, it is logged by their SOC, and it can end the engagement.
Reporting a hostname from a certificate log as a live host without resolving it. The log keeps names for years after DNS stopped answering; mark unverified rows as unverified.
Trimming the source column to save space. An asset with no source and no date cannot be defended when the client asks how you found it.
takeaways: Passive means no packet reaches the client; passive work needs no scope letter, active work does.
DNS, certificates, search indexes and job posts each answer a different question about the same estate.
An asset list without a source per row is an opinion, not a footprint.

drill.prompt: Pick a domain you own or a public documentation domain such as example.com. Run the NS, MX and TXT queries, then the crt.sh query, and build a four-column table for every name you find. Do not scan, resolve-and-probe, or send any packet at the addresses.
checklist: The table has the columns asset, source, first seen, why it matters
Every row names the exact command or URL that produced it
At least one row came from the certificate log and not from DNS
You wrote one sentence saying what you deliberately did not test, and why

l5-2.title: Nmap: scanning with a question, not a habit
l5-2.subtitle: Hosts, ports, service versions, and reading the output honestly.
objectives: Choose the scan flag from the question asked, not from memory
Separate open, closed, filtered and unfiltered, and say what each one proves
Run a version probe with a rate limit that will not alarm a SOC
Write a scan handover that quotes the command, the file and the reason column

ticket.subject: Our scan says 443 is filtered but the app team says the site is open
ticket.body: The monthly internal scan reports 443/tcp filtered on app01 at 10.20.30.15, while the application team says the site loads from the office. The previous analyst reran the scan, got filtered again, and closed the ticket as "port blocked". There is no firewall change request for this host this quarter and the app team says nothing was changed.
ticket.impact: The scan report cannot be signed off and the change board wants an answer before Thursday.

sections.h: The scan said filtered and the ticket said the server was down
sections.body:
The monthly scan flagged 443/tcp on app01 as `filtered`. The analyst reran it, got the same word, wrote "port blocked by firewall" and closed the ticket. The application team reopened it that afternoon: the site works from the office, from home, and from a phone on mobile data. Two days went into an argument about a word nobody looked up.

Nmap reports a port state, and that state is evidence about the path, not about the service. **open** means a SYN came back with SYN/ACK. **closed** means a SYN came back with RST, so the host is alive and nothing is listening. **filtered** means no reply came back at all, so a device in the path dropped it, and the only thing proved is that your probe did not arrive. **unfiltered** means the port is reachable but Nmap could not decide whether anything listens.

The skill is not memorizing flags. It is choosing the question first, then the flag that answers it, and writing down what the answer does and does not prove.

sections.h: Four questions, four flags, no guessing
sections.body:
Four questions cover almost every scan an L1 analyst is asked to run, and each has one flag that answers it.

*Which hosts are alive?* `nmap -sn 10.20.30.0/24` sends discovery probes and prints addresses that answer. It is not a port scan.

*Which ports?* `-p` takes a list, a range or a name: `-p 22,80,443`, `-p 1-1024`, `-p-` for all 65535. Without `-p`, Nmap scans its default top-1000 list, which is why "not open" sometimes means "not looked at".

*How?* `-sS` sends a SYN and never completes the handshake, which needs root or sudo on Linux and Administrator on Windows. `-sT` uses a full TCP connect, works without privilege, and is louder in the target's logs. `-sU` is UDP, which is slow and mostly unanswered.

*What is listening?* `-sV` reads banners and probes services for a version. It takes time per port and it is the only way to turn a port number into a service name you can act on.

Then `-oA scan-app01` writes three files at once: normal, XML and grepable. Every scan you may quote later gets that flag.

sections.h: One command, one question, four states to read
sections.body:
Four ports, one command, and output you can read line by line:

```console
$ sudo nmap -sS -p 22,80,443,8080 --reason 10.20.30.15
Starting Nmap 7.94 ( https://nmap.org ) at 2025-11-24 09:14 IST
Nmap scan report for app01.lab.example (10.20.30.15)
Host is up (0.0011s latency).

PORT     STATE    SERVICE    REASON
22/tcp   open     ssh        syn-ack ttl 64
80/tcp   closed   http       reset ttl 64
443/tcp  open     https      syn-ack ttl 64
8080/tcp filtered http-proxy no-response

Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 2.11 seconds
```

Read the REASON column before the STATE column. `syn-ack` means the service answered. `reset` means the host answered and refused, which is a working host with no listener. `no-response` means silence, and silence is a statement about a firewall, a security group, or a route, not about the application. The 8080 row has the same shape as the original ticket: `filtered` with `no-response` points at the path between the scanner and app01, so the next step is a firewall rule lookup, not a call to the application team.

**Decision rule:** SYN sent and SYN/ACK back means the service is reachable, so move to `-sV`. SYN sent and RST back means the host is fine and nothing listens, so check the service. SYN sent and nothing back for three tries means a device in the path is dropping it, so the question goes to the firewall or cloud security group owner with the source address, destination address and port.

sections.h: Version detection buys evidence, not a patch level
sections.body:
Version detection is where a scan turns into a finding, and where it turns into a false finding equally fast.

```console
$ sudo nmap -sV --version-light -p 22,443 10.20.30.15
PORT    STATE SERVICE  VERSION
22/tcp  open  ssh      OpenSSH 8.9p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu0.4 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
443/tcp open  ssl/http nginx 1.18.0 (Ubuntu)
```

`--version-light` limits the probe set to the most common ones, so it finishes in seconds instead of minutes. That banner is what the service announces, not proof of what is installed: a load balancer or a container image can return any string. Before you write "outdated OpenSSH" in a report, confirm the package version on the host.

Timing matters more on a client network than on a lab. `-T4` is the usual choice for a scan with a scheduled window. `-T5` will drop packets, trip an IDS, and produce `filtered` results that look like findings but are your own scan outrunning the path. On a production segment, cap the rate instead: `--max-rate 100` keeps the packet rate predictable and the SOC conversation short.

Every scan in this lesson runs against the lab range or a host you own. Written authorization is required for anything else, and it names your source address, or your scan is indistinguishable from someone else's.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The handover is the command, the output file, and one sentence per port that matters.

> Scan of 10.20.30.15 from 10.20.14.87 on 24 Nov 09:14, `sudo nmap -sS -p 22,80,443,8080 --reason -oA scan-app01`. 22 and 443 open (syn-ack), 80 closed (reset), 8080 filtered (no-response, three retries). Version probe: nginx 1.18.0 on 443. Files: scan-app01.nmap, .xml, .gnmap.

Escalate to the firewall or cloud security group owner when a port the application owner confirms as open returns `filtered`, and attach the exact source address, destination address, port and timestamp. Escalate to the platform team when `-sV` shows a version the vendor no longer supports, because that is a patch decision and not a network one. If the scan was never authorized in writing, stop and escalate to the engagement lead before you run it, not after.

diagram.title: From question to evidence
diagram.caption: The scan is chosen after the question, and the output file is written before anyone reads the result. Skipping the first or last step is what makes a scan impossible to defend.

data.footer: Filtered is a statement about the path. Closed is a statement about the host.

video.title: How Nmap really works // And how to catch it // Stealth scan vs TCP scan // Wireshark analysis
video.why: Captures the packets a SYN scan and a connect scan actually send, which is the part of this lesson the text can only describe.

commands.what: Host discovery only; lists addresses that answer, without scanning ports
Half-open scan of four ports with the reason for each state printed
Full connect scan without root; works from a Windows workstation, leaves a log on the target
Turns port numbers into service names and versions, with a short probe set
All 65535 ports at a capped packet rate, written to three output files
Checks one UDP port; silence is the common answer and is not a finding on its own

pitfalls: Reading "filtered" as "service down". Filtered says a device in the path dropped the probe; the service may be running perfectly and the rule may be a temporary block.
Running -T5 on a production segment to save two minutes. It drops packets, produces false "filtered" states, and trips the client SOC, which costs more time than the scan saved.
Quoting a -sV banner as the installed version. Proxies, containers and rewrites change banners, so confirm from the host itself before writing "outdated".
Scanning without -oA. When the change board asks what you ran, a screenshot of a terminal is not reproducible and cannot be attached to the record.
takeaways: open, closed, filtered and unfiltered are four different claims about two different things: the service and the path.
The reason column is the evidence; the state column is the summary.
A scan without -oA and without a written authorization is not a scan you can quote.

drill.prompt: On your own machine, scan only localhost: run nmap -sT -p 1-1024 --reason 127.0.0.1, then the same with -sV on any port that shows open. Do not scan your office network, your ISP range, or any address you do not own.
checklist: You can name every state that appeared in the output and say which column proved it
You have a saved output file from -oA and can open the .nmap file in a text editor
You ran one scan as a normal user and can say why -sS was refused
You wrote one line stating what the scan did not prove

l5-3.title: Wireshark: seeing the conversation instead of guessing
l5-3.subtitle: Capture, filter, follow a stream, and prove where it stopped.
objectives: Choose the capture point from the question, and name what a capture taken there cannot prove
Write a BPF capture filter that keeps the file small and complete for the case
Apply display filters that each answer one question about a connection
Use Follow TCP Stream and the SYN retry pattern to prove whether the path or the application failed

ticket.subject: Invoice upload fails after 90 seconds, only from the Pune office
ticket.body: Users in the Pune office say the invoice upload sits at "processing" and then fails after about 90 seconds. Users in the London office upload the same file without a problem. The application team says nothing changed on the server and says the network is the problem. Ping and traceroute to app01 from the Pune office look normal.
ticket.impact: Twelve finance users in one office cannot upload invoices since Monday; month-end close is on Friday.

sections.h: The capture was correct and it still named the wrong team
sections.body:
Two engineers captured traffic for a slow upload. One captured on the laptop and found retransmissions, and wrote "packet loss on the WAN". The other captured on the server and found the request arriving 400 ms after the click, then 90 seconds of nothing while the application wrote its temp file. Both were correct; the first produced the wrong ticket.

A capture is only evidence of what crossed the point where you took it. **Wireshark** reads capture files; on a server you usually produce them with `tcpdump` or `dumpcap` and open them later, because both tools write the same format. Decide which side of the problem the capture sits on, take it there, keep it small, and read the conversation instead of the packet count.

Every capture in this module is taken on a host you own or in the lab. A mirror port or SPAN session on someone else's network needs written authorization first.

sections.h: Filter at capture time, decide at display time
sections.body:
The most common failure is not the analysis, it is the capture: no filter, a full disk, and the event you needed overwritten by a Windows update that started at 09:39.

Decide the filter before you start. A **capture filter** is BPF, applied by the kernel, so packets that do not match are never written. A **display filter** is applied by Wireshark to what you already have and can be changed all day. That order is the difference between a 40 MB file you can read and a 4 GB file you cannot.

```console
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -s 0 -w /tmp/app01-0941.pcap \
    'host 10.20.14.87 and tcp port 443' -c 500
tcpdump: listening on eth0, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), snapshot length 262144 bytes
500 packets captured
500 packets received by filter
0 packets dropped by kernel
```

`-i` names the interface, `-nn` stops DNS and port-name lookups, `-s 0` keeps the full packet, and `-c` stops at a number you chose. The summary lines are evidence: "0 packets dropped by kernel" means the file is complete for that filter. On a busy interface the drop count is never zero, so rotate with `dumpcap -b filesize:102400 -b files:20` instead of filling the disk.

sections.h: One display filter per question, or you are reading noise
sections.body:
Wireshark's filter bar takes display filters, and each of these answers exactly one question.

| Filter | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| `ip.addr == 10.20.30.15 && tcp.port == 443` | one client and one service |
| `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0` | connection attempts, complete or not |
| `tcp.analysis.flags` | retransmissions, duplicate ACKs, zero window |
| `tcp.stream eq 3` | one conversation |
| `tls.handshake.extensions_server_name` | the hostname the client asked for |

Start with the address pair and count connections, then switch to bare SYNs and compare attempts against completed handshakes. A client that retries five times in 90 seconds is telling you where the wait went.

**Decision rule:** if the SYN leaves the client and no SYN/ACK comes back, the loss is in the path, and no application log will show it, so check the firewall, NAT and route first. If the handshake completes and the server resets 90 seconds later, the path did its job and the finding belongs to the application team.

sections.h: Follow the stream and make the server confess
sections.body:
Once the right conversation is on screen, right-click a packet and choose Follow, then TCP Stream. Wireshark reassembles the stream: what each side sent, in order, client in one color and server in the other. That view is where "processing failed" becomes a status line or a TLS alert.

TLS stops you at the payload. For HTTPS you see the handshake in clear, including the server name and the certificate, then encrypted application data. Do not install a private key on a user's browser to get around that. What the handshake proves is already useful: whether the certificate was accepted, which hostname the client asked for, and whether the connection ended in an alert.

`tshark` runs the same display filters on a saved file without the GUI:

```console
$ tshark -r /tmp/app01-0941.pcap -Y "tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0" \
    -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e tcp.dstport | head -5
Nov 24, 2025 09:41:02.118402 IST	10.20.14.87	443
Nov 24, 2025 09:41:04.219771 IST	10.20.14.87	443
Nov 24, 2025 09:41:08.221004 IST	10.20.14.87	443
Nov 24, 2025 09:41:16.226118 IST	10.20.14.87	443
```

Those four SYN lines, 2, 4 and 8 seconds apart, are the client's retry backoff. That pattern with no SYN/ACK in between is a path problem, and it is the most useful thing a capture hands you.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note has four parts: where the capture was taken, the exact filter, the one conversation that matters, and what it proves.

> Capture on app01 eth0, 24 Nov 09:41, `tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -s 0 -w /tmp/app01-0941.pcap 'host 10.20.14.87 and tcp port 443' -c 500`, 0 packets dropped. Client 10.20.14.87 sent SYN at 09:41:02 and retried at +2s, +4s and +8s. No SYN/ACK in the file. The handshake never completed, so the request never reached the application.

Attach the pcap file, not a screenshot, and name the stream index if you used Follow TCP Stream. Say which side of the path the capture sits on, because a capture taken on the client cannot prove the server did not answer.

Escalate to the network team when the handshake never completes from a client that otherwise works, with the timestamps and source address. Escalate to the application team when the handshake completes and the server resets or returns 5xx, with the Follow TCP Stream text. If the capture would need a mirror port on a network you do not own, stop: written authorization is required, and the request goes to the engagement lead.

diagram.title: Where a 90-second upload stops
diagram.caption: The handshake completes and the request is sent, then the server resets after 90 seconds. That sequence puts the failure above the transport layer, which is the opposite of what the first capture suggested.

video.title: How TCP Works - The Handshake
video.why: Shows the handshake and its flags in a live capture, so the SYN, SYN/ACK and RST rows you filter for here look familiar before your first real incident.

commands.cmd: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -s 0 -w /tmp/cap.pcap 'host 10.20.30.15 and tcp port 443' -c 500
commands.what: Captures full packets for one host and port only, and stops at 500
Rotating capture on a busy interface so the disk cannot fill
Lists bare SYNs, which shows every connection attempt and its retry spacing
Narrows a large file to one client-service pair before you open the GUI
Surfaces retransmissions, duplicate ACKs and zero-window events in one view
Shows the hostname the client asked for during the TLS handshake

pitfalls: Capturing with no filter on a busy interface. The file fills the disk, capture stops, and the packets you needed are the ones that were never written.
Treating retransmissions as proof of packet loss on the network. A retransmission shows a segment was not acknowledged, which also happens when the receiving application stops reading.
Reading a capture taken on the client as proof about the server. It proves what left and what came back at that point, and nothing beyond it.
Using a display filter and assuming the file is small. Display filters hide packets; they do not stop them being captured and they do not reduce disk use.
takeaways: The capture point is a decision: a file can only prove what crossed that point.
A BPF capture filter protects the disk; a display filter protects your attention.
SYN retries with no SYN/ACK are a path problem; a completed handshake followed by a reset is an application problem.

drill.prompt: Capture your own traffic while a single web page loads: sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -s 0 -w /tmp/mine.pcap -c 200 "tcp port 443", then open the file in Wireshark. Filter to bare SYNs, then to one conversation, and follow the TCP stream. Capture only on your own machine and only your own session.
checklist: The file opens in Wireshark and the summary counts match what tcpdump printed
You can show one completed handshake and the three packets that make it
You applied tcp.analysis.flags and can explain one row it returned
You have the Follow TCP Stream text for one connection, and can say what stays encrypted

l5-4.title: Burp Suite: testing a web app the authorised way
l5-4.subtitle: Proxy, intercept, replay, and keep a record of every request.
objectives: State what written authorization must name before a proxy points at a host
Capture a request in Burp Proxy and replay it in Repeater against an in-scope target
Tell a server-side check from a client-side one by changing one value at a time
Hand over a test record an application owner can reproduce without you

ticket.subject: Confirm the portal login cannot be bypassed before Friday
ticket.body: The application team asked the desk to confirm that the portal login cannot be bypassed before Friday's release. The request has no host list, no test window and no test account, and the person who raised it is on leave. A previous engineer opened the production login page once, said it looked normal, and closed the ticket.
ticket.impact: One release is waiting on the answer since Monday; the app team has no date.

sections.h: The ticket says "check the login page" and stops there
sections.body:
Monday, 09:20. The application team wants to know whether the portal login can be bypassed before Friday's release. The ticket says "check the login page" and names no host, no window and no test account.

That sentence is not written authorization. A proxy pointed at the customer's production portal without a written scope is an unapproved test against a live system, and the authenticated requests in your history carry session tokens that belong to real people. The proxy history becomes the incident.

The quieter failure: a verbal yes, a test against staging, nothing found, and a report that says "no issue". Staging has no WAF, a different build and a seeded database, so the result describes staging.

Before a request leaves your machine you need two things in writing: the scope (hosts, test window, excluded paths such as payment pages, the stop condition, who to call when something breaks) and a test account you are allowed to use. Burp makes the requests easy to read. It does not make them permitted.

sections.h: Scope first, then a listener you can trust
sections.body:
Burp Suite runs a local proxy. The default listener is `127.0.0.1:8080`, so only your machine can use it. For web work, use Burp's own Chromium from `Proxy` > `Intercept` > `Open browser`; it already trusts Burp's CA certificate, so HTTPS pages load without warnings. If you use your own browser, set its HTTP and HTTPS proxy to `127.0.0.1:8080` and install the CA from `http://burp`, or every HTTPS page throws a certificate error and you debug your own setup.

Then set scope. In `Target` > `Scope`, tick `Use advanced scope control` and add one entry per authorized host. In `Proxy` > `HTTP history`, turn on `Show only in-scope items`. Scope in Burp is a filter, not an access control. It hides what you should not see and does nothing to stop the browser requesting it. The real control is the tab you have open.

A first capture with `curl` gives the same request in a form you can paste into a ticket:

```bash
$ curl -sS -i -X POST http://10.20.30.15/login \
    --data-urlencode 'email=helpdesk@lab.local' --data-urlencode 'password=Passw0rd123'
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Date: Mon, 24 Nov 2025 09:41:07 GMT
Server: nginx/1.24.0
Location: /dashboard
Set-Cookie: SESSIONID=8f21c0d4e7aa9b31; Path=/; HttpOnly
Content-Length: 0
```
