Two facts are already there. The redirect on a correct login says the session is checked on the server. The `Set-Cookie` line has `HttpOnly` but no `Secure` and no `SameSite`, so that cookie travels over plain HTTP if anything ever serves this host on port 80. That is a finding you can write up without attacking anything.

sections.h: Intercept is a pause button, and it is still on
sections.body:
`Intercept is on` holds every request until you forward it. Leave it on and walk away, and the browser spins, the user sees a hung page, and a second incident gets raised against the application while you are the cause. Intercept one request, read the method, path, headers and body, then switch it off and work from `HTTP history`, which is a complete record and does not break the page.

Replay is where testing happens. Right-click a request, choose `Send to Repeater` (or `Ctrl+R`). Change one thing, send, read the response, keep the tab. One thing is the rule: if you edit the cookie and the price in one send, the response cannot tell you which change mattered, and the record is useless to the next reader.

**Decision rule:** if the page loads with the proxy off and hangs with intercept on, the fault is your proxy, not the app. Turn intercept off before you write a word about the application.

sections.h: Change a value you should not control
sections.body:
The cheapest test in Repeater needs no payload. Take a request that works, then change one value the application should be checking itself.

Remove the `SESSIONID` cookie and resend `/dashboard`. A `302` to `/login` means the check runs on the server. A `200` with account data means the page served it with no session at all, which is broken access control, the first entry on the OWASP Top 10.

Change a hidden field, `role=user` to `role=admin`, or the `price=249.00` in a checkout post. If the admin menu renders, or the total changes to your number, the server accepted a value it should have looked up. If it returns `403` or recalculates the total, the check is in the right place and this attempt is a dead end.

A difference that appears only in the browser, with identical HTML from the server, is client-side behavior. Read the JavaScript before writing it up: hiding a button is not access control if the endpoint still checks the role.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
```text
TEST RECORD — portal login, ref APP-4471
Scope: portal.lab.local (10.20.30.15), 24 Nov 09:00-12:00, payment pages excluded
Account: qa.tester@lab.local, test account issued by the app team
Request: POST /login  email=helpdesk@lab.local  password=Passw0rd123
Response: 302 /dashboard, Set-Cookie SESSIONID (HttpOnly; no Secure, no SameSite)
Second request: GET /dashboard with SESSIONID removed -> 302 /login
Result: session checked server-side; cookie flags are the finding
Not tested: admin area, payment pages (out of scope)
```

- Close when the record names the host in scope, the account used, the exact request, the response, and what you did not test.
- **Escalate to the application security team when** a replay returns another user's data, changes a stored value, or reaches an admin function from a low-privilege account. Escalate the same minute if the `Host` in Repeater is not on the written scope list: that request was out of scope, and the customer must hear it from you, not from their logs.

Burp Suite Community Edition has no scanner and throttles Intruder, so do not promise a full automated test with the free edition. A careful manual pass with a saved request record closes more tickets than a scan button.

diagram.title: Burp loop: scope, capture, replay, record
diagram.caption: Steps 2 to 4 repeat for every question you ask the app. Step 1 is checked before the first request and again before the last.

steps.label: Intercept once
steps.detail: read the raw request, then off

data.footer: Step 1 cannot be fixed later. Every other step can be repeated.

video.title: How to intercept HTTP requests and responses using Burp Suite
video.why: Shows the real Proxy UI, the intercept toggle and the request and response panes, which the text can only describe.

commands.what: Shows whether the proxy listener is up and bound to loopback only.
The same request Burp captures, with headers intact, ready to paste into a ticket.
Proves a browser or script is actually sending its traffic through the proxy.
Returns 200 when the Burp CA is trusted, or error 60 when it is not installed.

pitfalls: Leaving intercept on and walking away. The page hangs, the app team raises a second incident, and the cause is the person testing.
Replaying with a real user's session cookie copied from a support ticket. The test now touches that person's data, and a valid token sits in a proxy history on your laptop.
Reporting "no vulnerability found" after an unauthenticated look at three pages. Burp Community has no scanner, and a pass over the login page says nothing about the admin area.
takeaways: Written authorization names hosts, window, excluded paths and a stop condition. A chat message is not authorization.
Burp's scope list filters what you see; it does not stop a browser from requesting anything.
One changed value per replay, with the request and the response kept together.

drill.prompt: Install Burp Suite Community Edition. Start `python3 -m http.server 8000` in an empty folder and set the target scope to `http://localhost:8000` only. Load the page in Burp's browser, send the request to Repeater, and resend it once with the User-Agent header changed.
checklist: Your scope list holds exactly one entry, `http://localhost:8000`.
HTTP history shows the request with its method and status code.
Repeater holds two sends of the same request, differing only in one header.
You can name what changed in the response, or say that nothing did.
No request went to a host you do not own.

l5-5.title: OWASP Top 10 in practice: break SQLi and XSS, then fix them
l5-5.subtitle: Exploit in the lab, read the code, write the fix.
objectives: Place a scanner finding in the right OWASP Top 10 category
Reproduce SQL injection and reflected XSS in a lab with one request each
Name the code change that fixes each: a bound query, encoded output
Decide when a candidate finding escalates the same day

ticket.subject: External scan says our item page is open to SQL injection
ticket.body: The quarterly external scan lists `https://portal.example/item?id=1` as SQL injection, high severity. The application team says the page has been live for four years, and a developer opened it in a browser, typed a quote into the id parameter, and got a normal error page. The report carries no request, no parameter and no evidence, and the scan ran from outside without credentials.
ticket.impact: The customer signs off the quarterly scan on Friday; this finding is blocking it.

sections.h: The scan says SQL injection and the app team says the page is fine
sections.body:
A quarterly external scan comes back with `SQL injection` against `https://portal.example/item?id=1`. The application team replies that the page has run for four years and "nobody can inject anything". Both statements are opinions and the ticket sits for a week.

Proving it on the customer's production page is the wrong move. A working injection test against live data is an unapproved attack, and the first thing it does is read rows you are not allowed to read. The right move is a lab copy of the same build, where a request that breaks the page costs nothing.

What settles a ticket like this is a request and a response you can show. These are the two findings that produce most injection tickets, how to reproduce each in a lab, and the code change that closes it.

Every payload below belongs in a lab or inside an authorized engagement. Written authorization names the host, the window and the accounts, and it exists before any request leaves your machine.

sections.h: The list, and the two entries that arrive as tickets
sections.body:
The OWASP Top 10 is a list of categories, not a checklist of vulnerabilities. The 2021 edition is the current published one, and it moved two things that matter on this desk: broken access control to first place, and cross-site scripting into injection, as one of its forms.

| Category | Where you meet it |
| --- | --- |
| A01 Broken access control | data appears after you change the id in the URL |
| A03 Injection | a quote or a tag changes what the page returns |
| A05 Security misconfiguration | directory listing, default page, verbose error |
| A06 Vulnerable components | an old library version named in a scan |

Categories are a vocabulary for the report. The evidence is always a request.

sections.h: SQLi: one quote changes the query
sections.body:
A login form that pastes strings into SQL is the classic case:

```php
$sql = "SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '" . $_POST['email'] . "' AND pw = '" . $_POST['pw'] . "'";
```

The database receives one string and cannot tell the developer's quote from the user's. In the lab, submit `' OR '1'='1' -- ` in the email field: the condition becomes true for every row, and everything after `--` is a comment, so the password is never checked.

```bash
$ curl -sS -i http://lab.local/login.php \
    --data-urlencode "email=' OR '1'='1' -- " --data-urlencode "pw=wrong"
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Date: Mon, 24 Nov 2025 10:02:18 GMT
Location: /dashboard.php
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=6c1f0a9d42e7; path=/
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
```

A `302` to the dashboard with a wrong password is the proof. No rows were dumped, nothing was changed, and the ticket now has a request anyone can replay.

The fix is a query shape, not a filter. Bind the values so the driver sends the statement and the data on separate paths:

```php
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT id, pw_hash FROM users WHERE email = ?');
$stmt->execute([$_POST['email']]);
$row = $stmt->fetch();
if ($row && password_verify($_POST['pw'], $row['pw_hash'])) { /* ... */ }
```

`mysqli_real_escape_string` and hand-written blocklists still appear in old codebases, but they depend on every call site remembering, and they fail when the character set changes. Prepared statements do not depend on memory. The pattern to grep for on a call is a query string built with `.` or `+` that contains `$_GET` or `$_POST`.

sections.h: XSS: the tag that runs in someone else's browser
sections.body:
Cross-site scripting is the same mistake aimed at a different interpreter. The server takes a search term and writes it into the HTML unencoded, so the browser reads the user's `

``` The tag came back exactly as sent, which is the evidence. In a browser, it executes. Reflected XSS needs a victim to open a crafted link. Stored XSS sits in a comment or a profile field and is served to every visitor, which is the version that becomes an incident. The fix is output encoding at the point of rendering: `htmlspecialchars($q, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` in PHP, auto-escaping in a modern template engine, `textContent` instead of `innerHTML` in JavaScript. A Content-Security-Policy is a second layer that limits what an injected script can reach. It does not repair the missing encoding. `HttpOnly` on the session cookie limits cookie theft and does not stop the script from acting as the logged-in user. **Decision rule:** if the payload comes back unchanged in the response body, the page reflects input without encoding, and that is reflected XSS until you see the encoding applied. If the same value is stored and shown to another account, it is stored XSS, and every visitor is exposed.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
```text
FINDING — SQL injection in login (reproduced in lab)
Asset: portal build 4.2.1, lab host lab.local (10.20.30.40), work order WO-2211
Parameter: email, POST /login.php
Request: email=' OR '1'='1' --   pw=wrong
Response: 302 /dashboard.php with a session cookie
Impact: authentication bypass for any account, no credentials needed
Fix: prepared statement in includes/auth.php; query is concatenated today
Line: includes/auth.php:38
```

- Close a candidate finding when the record shows the request, the response and the line that builds the sink.
- **Escalate to the application owner the same day when** the parameter is reachable without login, or when the same input is stored and shown to other accounts. Both mean anyone can trigger it, not only a tester with a proxy.

The exploit is a quote. The fix is a query shape and one encoding call. A report that names the file and the line gets fixed faster than one that repeats the scanner's paragraph.

diagram.title: Two interpreters, two fixes
diagram.caption: Both columns start with the same user-controlled string. The second interpreter decides the fix, and neither fix is an input blocklist.

data.verdict: Same input, different interpreter. Fix the sink, not the payload.

video.title: 2021 OWASP Top Ten Overview
video.why: Introduces the 2021 list and why the categories were reordered, which is the context the table here compresses into four rows.

commands.what: The replay that proves authentication bypass without reading anyone's data.
Counts how many times the payload came back unencoded in the response body.
Lab-only confirmation of the database banner; never run outside the written scope.
Lists concatenated query call sites for the code review that follows a confirmed injection.

pitfalls: Confirming the finding on the customer's live page. Reading one row of real data turns a scan ticket into a reportable incident the authorization did not cover.
Treating HTTPS as a fix. Injection happens inside the encrypted request, and TLS changes nothing about how the database reads the string.
Rating stored XSS as low because "the user has to click". A stored payload fires for every visitor of the page, including the admin who reviews comments.
takeaways: SQL injection changes the query; XSS changes the page. The interpreter tells you the fix.
Prepared statements and output encoding are the fixes; escaping every call by hand and blocklists are habits that fail.
A scanner finding is a hypothesis until a request and a response reproduce it in scope.

drill.prompt: Write a four-line page in any language on your laptop that echoes a query parameter with no encoding, serve it on `localhost:8000`, and send it the XSS payload from this lesson. Add output encoding, send it again, and keep both responses side by side.
checklist: The first response contains `<script>alert(1)</script>` exactly as sent.
The second response contains `<script>` and no executable tag.
A browser loads the second version as text, not as script.
You can name the line you changed and the function that encoded it.
Nothing was sent to a host you do not own.

l5-6.title: Vulnerability scanning, Metasploit and the report that follows
l5-6.subtitle: Validate findings, rate them honestly, and write for the client.
objectives: Tell a credentialed scan result from an unauthenticated guess
Validate a scanner finding with an auxiliary module without exploiting it
Rate a finding against exposure and business context, not color alone
Write a finding an engineer can fix and a manager can fund

ticket.subject: 412 findings from last night's scan and the customer wants a fix date
ticket.body: The authenticated scan of 10.20.30.0/24 finished at 02:10 and the portal lists 70 critical findings. The account manager forwarded the PDF to the customer before anyone validated it. The customer's IT lead replied that three of the named hosts were decommissioned in August and wants them removed. An analyst has started deleting those rows by hand. No finding has been reproduced.
ticket.impact: The weekly security call is tomorrow at 10:00 and the report cannot be defended as written.

sections.h: The scan finishes at 02:00 and the report is 412 findings
sections.body:
The authenticated scan of a customer's /24 finished at 02:10. The portal shows 412 findings, 70 of them critical. The account manager forwarded the PDF at 08:00. By 10:00 the customer's IT lead has replied that three named hosts were decommissioned in August and that one "critical" is a printer which only accepts jobs from two addresses.

Nobody reproduced anything. The list is technically a scan result and practically unusable, and the cost is paid on the next call, when a real finding is read as another false alarm.

The work between the scan and the report is the job: triage what the scanner produced, validate what survives, rate it against this customer's exposure, and write it so a manager and an engineer can both act on it. Everything below belongs to a lab or to an engagement with written authorization naming the range, the window and the accounts.

sections.h: Credentials decide how much of the list is real
sections.body:
An unauthenticated scan sees what a stranger sees: open ports, banners, TLS settings, sometimes a version string. A credentialed scan logs in with a read-only scanning account and reads the actual patch level from the registry or the package database. On the same host the second one reports the real build, so backported patches that fixed a CVE without changing the version string stop appearing as findings. Most false positives in a fresh report disappear with credentials, not with a better scanner.

The scan does not decide whether it is safe to run. A full port scan with default settings across a /24 can saturate a WAN link or stop an old device. Scan inside the window written in the authorization, exclude the hosts the customer listed as fragile, and use the safe-checks option where the product has one. If a scan causes an outage, the outage is yours.

sections.h: Validate: the scanner says likely, not proven
sections.body:
An auxiliary module proves reachability, not exploitation. Start by asking which modules can answer the question at all:

```text
msf6 > search ms17_010
Matching Modules
================
   #  Name                                     Disclosure Date  Rank    Check  Description
   -  ----                                     ---------------  ----    -----  -----------
   0  exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue  2017-03-14      average Yes    MS17-010 EternalBlue SMB Remote Windows Kernel Pool Corruption
   1  exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec       2017-03-14      normal  Yes    MS17-010 EternalRomance/EternalSynergy SMB Remote Windows Code Execution
   2  auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010                         normal  No     MS17-010 SMB RCE Detection
   3  auxiliary/admin/smb/ms17_010_command      2017-03-14      normal  No     MS17-010 EternalRomance/EternalSynergy SMB Remote Command Execution
```

The `Check` column is the answer to whether `check` works in that module, and many modules say `No`. The auxiliary scanner prints one line per host that answered as likely vulnerable. `likely` is the honest word: the scanner saw the SMB dialect, not a shell.

Confirmation means running the matching exploit module until a session opens, and that is a different authorization from scanning because it changes state on the host. When the scope covers scanning only, the finding stays "likely vulnerable" and the report says exactly that.

sections.h: Rate with the customer in the room
sections.body:
CVSS v3.1 gives a base score from 0 to 10 and a vector string that explains it. The bands most reports use: 9.0-10.0 critical, 7.0-8.9 high, 4.0-6.9 medium, 0.1-3.9 low. The base score assumes a generic worst case, and the vector `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N` — network reachable, no privileges, no user action — is what makes one 9.8 worse than another.

Two findings can share a score and not share a risk. A 9.8 on a test host with no route from the office and no data is a maintenance item. A 7.5 on the VPN gateway, with a public exploit and no compensating control, is this week's problem. Exposure, data sensitivity, existing controls and whether an exploit is already in use decide the order. `searchsploit` answers the last question for a known CVE in seconds.

**Decision rule:** internet-facing, public exploit, no compensating control, it leaves the desk the same hour. Internal, needs credentials, already covered by another control, it goes in the report with that context written next to the score.

sections.h: The report has two readers
sections.body:
The executive summary is for the person who signs the invoice: what was tested, when, the two or three things that matter, and the business consequence in plain words. No CVE numbers in that paragraph.

Each finding is for the engineer who has to fix it: title, severity and vector, affected asset, evidence, reproduction steps, business impact, the specific remediation (the patch, the setting, the code change), references, and retest status. Evidence means the request and response, the command and its output, or a screenshot with the hostname visible. A finding without a reproduction step is a rumor; put it in the appendix or leave it out.

The scope section protects both sides. It lists hosts, accounts, tools, dates and what was not tested, so a later "you missed the database" has an answer.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
```text
SCAN SUMMARY — 10.20.30.0/24, authenticated, 24 Nov 02:10
Raw: 412 findings / 70 critical
After triage: 96 findings / 9 critical (duplicates, dead hosts, false positives)
Validated: 7 reproduced with evidence, 2 marked likely-only (scan scope, no exploit)
Top: MS17-010 on 10.20.30.21, Windows Server 2008 R2, no owner recorded
Report: v0.9 to the app owner 25 Nov, retest window 8 Dec
```

- Close when every finding in the report has an asset, an evidence line, a severity with a reason, and an owner.
- **Escalate to the engagement lead when** a validated finding is internet-facing with a public exploit, when a host answers that is not on the authorized list, or when someone asks you to test something the authorization does not cover.

A scan is a measurement. The report is the argument about what the measurement means, and the argument is the part the customer pays for.

diagram.title: One engagement day, from scope to draft
diagram.caption: The scan is one hour of the day. Triage, validation and rating take the rest, and the report is written from what survived them.

video.title: Launch a Credentialed Scan with Nessus Professional
video.why: Shows where the scanning account is attached in the scan policy, the step that removes most false positives in a fresh report.

commands.cmd: msfconsole -q -x 'use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010; set RHOSTS 10.20.30.0/24; set THREADS 4; run; exit'
commands.what: Runs the check across the range and prints one line per host that answered as likely vulnerable.
Confirms one host's SMB version and the script verdict, which becomes the evidence line in the report.
Shows whether the module supports check and which references to cite.
Shows whether a public exploit exists, which moves the rating more than the base score does.

pitfalls: Scanning the whole /24 with default settings at 10:00. A full scan can saturate a WAN link or reset an old device, and that outage is yours, not a finding.
Copying the scanner's severity into the customer report. A 9.8 on a dead host and a 9.8 on the VPN gateway read the same, so the customer stops reading the list.
Firing the exploit module because the scope allowed scanning. Exploitation changes state and needs its own authorization, and "likely vulnerable" is a complete finding without it.
takeaways: Credentials remove more false positives than any scanner setting.
An auxiliary check says likely; only a reproduction in scope says confirmed.
Severity is a starting point. Exposure, data and controls decide the order.

drill.prompt: Scan only your own machine: `nmap -sV 127.0.0.1`, then look up one open service with `searchsploit`. Write the finding in report form, with title, severity and vector, evidence, impact, remediation and retest, in under 150 words.
checklist: The scan target is 127.0.0.1 and nothing else.
The finding names one service, its port and its version.
Severity has a vector string next to it, not a color alone.
Remediation names a version, a setting or a patch, not "update".
The whole finding fits in 150 words.

l6-1.title: Logs to SIEM: how raw events become one queue
l6-1.subtitle: Sources, normalisation, indexing, and why the timestamp is the argument.
objectives: Trace one event from the source device to the alert queue and name the stage where it can be lost.
Prove whether an alert time and a device log time describe the same instant, using the offset and not the clock face.
Explain what normalization buys a correlation search, and why a missing field produces a partial count instead of an error.
Write a data-fault handover note that names the owner instead of re-opening the same alert.

ticket.subject: Your brute force alert fired at 09:40, but the DC log says 04:10
ticket.body: The queue raised a high-severity alert against dc01 for 412 failed logons by svc-backup at 09:40. The AD admin opened the security log on dc01 and found the failures at 04:10, before the office opened, and says the alert is wrong. The alert is still open, the on-call analyst wants to close it as a false positive, and nobody has checked whether a logon succeeded after the failures.
ticket.impact: One high-severity credential alert open for three hours; the controller log rolls over in two days and is the only copy of the evidence.

sections.h: The alert that was five and a half hours out
sections.body:
The SOC queue raised a high-severity alert against `dc01` at 09:40: 412 failed logons for `svc-backup`. The AD admin pulled the security log on the domain controller, found the same 412 failures at 04:10, before the office opened, and told the SOC the alert was wrong. Nobody had asked the only question that mattered: did any logon succeed after the failures?

Both were telling the truth. The controller wrote its own local time and no offset. The pipeline that parsed the event applied a zone the device never sent, so one instant became another instant.

You can see the missing offset in the raw event, before any search runs:

```text
11/18/2025 04:10:02 AM
LogName=Security
EventCode=4625
ComputerName=dc01.example.net
Keywords=Audit Failure
Message=An account failed to log on.
    Account Name:  svc-backup
    Source Network Address:  203.0.113.44
```

No time zone appears anywhere in that block. Whether this event lands at 04:10 or 09:40 is decided by a zone nobody wrote down, and the parser guessed one.

sections.h: Six stages, and the four that fail without making a sound
sections.body:
The queue only shows the end of the pipeline. Everything before it can fail without producing an error anywhere.

The most common silent failure is a source that never emits. Event ID 4625 exists only if failure auditing is enabled for logon events on that host. A server left on default audit policy produces nothing, and the queue reads that silence as a quiet week. Check the policy before you trust the absence of alerts:

```powershell
PS C:\> auditpol /get /category:"Logon/Logoff"

Subcategory   GUID                                    Inclusion Setting
Logon         {0CCE9215-69AE-11D9-BED3-505054503030}  Success and Failure
Logoff        {0CCE9216-69AE-11D9-BED3-505054503030}  Success
```

Next is the shipper. An agent installed but not connected to an indexer, or a syslog receiver on the wrong port, leaves a gap with a start time and no end.

Then the parser, which decides where one event stops and the next begins. A Java stack trace split into forty one-line events is a parser problem, not a log problem, and it buries the timestamp of all forty.

Last is retention. Hot buckets roll to warm, warm to frozen, and frozen is deleted. A thirty-one-day-old alert cannot be investigated if the index keeps thirty days.

sections.h: The timestamp is the argument you can settle
sections.body:
`_time` is stored as an epoch number, one instant in UTC. Every date on a screen is that number rendered in some zone, so there are two separate questions: what instant did this happen, and what does my screen say.

The instant is set once, at parse time, by `TIME_FORMAT`, `MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD` and `TZ` for that sourcetype. When `TZ` is not set, the parser falls back to the search head's own zone for timestamps that carry no offset. On a datacenter host that zone is usually UTC while your profile renders in local time, which is how a device clock in one zone becomes a stored time in another. The repair is one setting on the parsing tier plus a re-index of the window. It is not a change to the alert, and L1 cannot make it from the queue.

Compare the two clocks before you compare the attack:

```splunk
index=wineventlog host=dc01 EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h
| stats count min(_time) AS first max(_time) AS last BY user
| eval first=strftime(first,"%H:%M:%S %Z"), last=strftime(last,"%H:%M:%S %Z")

user         count  first          last
svc-backup     412  09:40:02 IST   09:42:47 IST
j.okafor         3  09:41:11 IST   09:41:19 IST
```

Two facts in that output decide the ticket. If the clocks are seconds apart, the drift is NTP's problem and the alert is safe to analyze. If every row sits exactly five and a half hours from the console clock, the source is mis-parsed, and nothing in that index lines up with a source that was parsed correctly.

**Decision rule:** when the alert clock and the device clock differ by a whole or half-hour offset, stop analyzing the alert and fix the parse. Seconds mean drift. Hours mean zone.

sections.h: Normalization: why one search hits three firewalls
sections.body:
Vendors do not agree on field names. A firewall calls the source address `srcip`, a proxy calls it `client_ip`, an identity provider calls it `IpAddress`. **Normalization** maps those onto one set — `src`, `dest`, `user`, `action` — so one question can be asked of any product. In Splunk that set is the Common Information Model; in Elastic the same idea is the Common Schema.

Normalization makes a rule portable, and it makes a broken rule silent. A correlation search written against `src` returns rows for the firewalls whose add-on maps the field and nothing for the one whose add-on was never installed, or whose sourcetype changed after an upgrade. The rule keeps running, keeps returning a number, and the number is a partial count nobody questions because it is not zero.

The fast path is `| tstats` against an accelerated data model: it reads normalized fields instead of raw events, and with a bad mapping it returns zero rows and no error, the same trap wearing a performance badge.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note on this ticket has five lines and no theory:

- Source, sourcetype and host: `WinEventLog:Security` on `dc01`.
- Both clocks, with values: 04:10 on the controller against 09:40 in the queue.
- Audit policy on the host: failure auditing on or off.
- The pairing result: how many 4624 events followed the 4625 burst, from which source.
- What you did not check, in plain words.

That note closes as a data fault with a named owner, or it escalates with the evidence attached. It must never say "timestamps look weird" — an offset is a measurement, so measure it.

**Escalation criterion:** hand off to the logging platform team, not the SOC, when one sourcetype shows an exact zone-sized offset or a flat zero across more than one host. Every alert built on that data is wrong and no analyst can repair it from the queue.

diagram.title: One event, six chances to be lost
diagram.caption: The queue shows the last step. Every step before it can drop the event or change its meaning without raising an error anywhere.

data.footer: A security alert is usually a data fault wearing a security label.

video.title: What is Microsoft Azure Sentinel? Cloud-native SIEM.
video.why: Shows connectors, analytics rules and incidents inside one product interface, so the six-step flow in the plate has a working example instead of only labels.

commands.what: Shows whether 4625 and 4624 can exist at all on that host, before you read an empty search as a quiet week.

commands.cmd: index=wineventlog host=dc01 EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h | stats count min(_time) AS first max(_time) AS last BY user
commands.what: Puts the first and last failure on one line, which is what you compare against the console clock.

commands.cmd: | metadata type=sourcetypes index=* | eval age=now()-recentTime | where age > 3600
commands.what: Lists sourcetypes that stopped arriving more than an hour ago, which is how a dead shipper shows up as a number.

commands.cmd: | tstats count FROM datamodel=Authentication WHERE Authentication.action=failure BY Authentication.src
commands.what: Reads the normalized field instead of the raw event, so a zero here points at field mapping, not at attacker behavior.
Confirms the agent thinks it is connected to an indexer, and names the target it believes it is sending to.

pitfalls: Closing the alert because the device log disagrees with the alert time. The disagreement is a parse fault, and the attack may be real in either timeline.
Reading zero events as zero activity. With logon failure auditing off, 4625 never exists and the queue shows silence, not safety.
Using a field name from a dashboard without checking the add-on that produced it. When the mapping is missing, the correlation search counts a subset and reports it as the total.
takeaways: Six stages sit between the device and the queue; the queue only shows the last one.
An exact zone-sized gap between two clocks is a parsing fault, not an attack finding, and it breaks cross-source correlation.
Normalization is what lets one search span three vendors, and a missing mapping returns a partial count rather than an error.

drill.prompt: On your own Windows machine, open Event Viewer, pick one Security event, and note the time it shows. Then run `Get-Date -Format o` and `Get-TimeZone`. Write the three values down, work out what UTC instant the event really is, and state what a SIEM in a different zone would display for the same event.
checklist: You wrote the event time, the current UTC time and the zone name on one line.
You converted the event time to a UTC instant by hand and showed the arithmetic.
You stated what a viewer in another zone would see, and why that is not a different event.
You can say from memory which two props.conf settings decide that conversion.
No real hostname, user name or address from a customer environment appears in your notes.

l6-2.title: Splunk, Sentinel and Elastic: same job, different syntax
l6-2.subtitle: Pick the query that answers the question, not the one you memorised.
objectives: Write the same counting question in Splunk SPL, Sentinel KQL and Elasticsearch, without copying field names between them.
Name the table or index and the time field for a platform before adding any filter.
Read a zero-row result as a data-source, time-window or field fault, in that order, and prove which one it is.
Hand a ported rule over with counts that a detection engineer can act on.

ticket.subject: The Sentinel copy of our Splunk brute force search returns nothing
ticket.body: The failed-logon search was ported from Splunk to Microsoft Sentinel for the new cloud estate. The KQL runs without an error but returns no rows for the last 24 hours, while the Splunk original shows 412 failures for dc01 in the same window. The SecurityEvent table exists in the workspace, and the analyst has been asked to sign the ported rule off today.
ticket.impact: One scheduled detection rule cannot be enabled, so the cloud estate has no brute-force coverage until the port is signed off.

sections.h: The ported query that returned an empty grid
sections.body:
Detection engineering ported the failed-logon search to Microsoft Sentinel for the new cloud estate. The KQL runs without an error and returns no rows for the last 24 hours. The Splunk original returns 412 failures for `dc01` in the same window. The analyst is asked to sign the ported rule off before the end of the shift.

An empty result is hard to argue with: nothing fails and nothing explains itself. Three faults produce it: the query points at a table where those hosts never write, the time filter names a column that is not the table's time column, or the filter compares a field to a value that never appears. The first one costs ten seconds to rule out:

```kusto
SecurityEvent
| take 10
```

Ten rows with none from `dc01` means the table is fine and that host's connection is not: check the data collection rule first. An empty grid means you are in the wrong workspace.

sections.h: Every query is the same four moves
sections.body:
Restrict by time and value, count, group, then order and cut. Every platform here does those four things, and the clause order is the same: filter before you aggregate, or the engine aggregates everything and throws most of it away.

| Move | Splunk SPL | Sentinel KQL | Elastic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Restrict | `earliest=-24h` plus a term | `where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)` | a `range` on `@timestamp` |
| Count | `stats count` | `summarize count()` | a `terms` aggregation |
| Group | `BY src` | `by IpAddress` | `"field": "source.ip"` |
| Cut | `sort` then `head` | `top 5 by` | `"size": 5` |

Two habits survive every port: filter on time first, and count before you list. A list of forty thousand rows is not evidence; a count grouped by source address is.

```splunk
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h
| stats count AS failures BY src
| sort -failures
| head 5

src            failures
10.20.14.31         412
10.20.14.90          23
10.20.14.77           6
```

The Sentinel version differs in two places: the table name and the field that holds the address.

```kusto
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize failures = count() by IpAddress
| top 5 by failures desc
```

sections.h: Name the index, the table and the time column first
sections.body:
In Splunk, `index=` and `sourcetype=` open the search and are also the largest performance control you have. Leave the index out and the search head looks at everything you are allowed to see, which is how a five-second question becomes a fifteen-minute one that may still hit a job limit.

In Sentinel, the table name opens the query: `SecurityEvent` for Windows security events, `SigninLogs` for Entra ID sign-ins, `DeviceProcessEvents` for Defender for Endpoint process telemetry. The time column is not universal. Log Analytics tables carry `TimeGenerated`; the Defender XDR hunting tables carry `Timestamp`. Filter on the wrong one and the query returns nothing, or searches all retained history.

In Elastic, `FROM logs-windows.security-*` opens the query and `@timestamp` is the field everything else is measured against.

The Sentinel portal also doubles the time filter. The Logs blade has its own picker above the query, so a `where` clause asking for 24 hours inside a picker set to one hour returns an hour of data and looks like a rule that stopped matching.

**Decision rule:** say out loud which field carries time in the platform you are in, and what the picker above the query is set to, before you add a single filter. If you cannot name the time field, the query is not ready to write.

sections.h: Field names are where a port actually costs you
sections.body:
The same source address is `src` in Splunk's Windows add-on, `IpAddress` in the `SecurityEvent` table, and `source.ip` in Elastic's Common Schema. Those are three fixed namespaces, and only one of them is yours to choose.

The platforms also fail differently, and the failure type is a diagnostic. Kusto stops at compile time on a column that does not exist, so a green KQL query with zero rows is never a field-name fault: it is data, time, or a value that matched nothing. Elasticsearch does not stop. A term query against an unmapped field returns zero hits with a 200 response, which reads exactly like "no failures today". Splunk sits in the middle: an unknown field in a `where` clause often evaluates to null and drops the row.

That difference is why one mistake produces three different tickets.

**Decision rule:** when a ported query returns zero rows, run `Table | take 10` (KQL) or `index=... | head 10` (SPL) with no filters before you touch the logic. Empty means the data source; rows mean the time window or the field.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
A port handover is one note with the question in English at the top, and none of the syntax above it:

- The question: how many failed logons per source in the last 24 hours, per host.
- Where the data lives: workspace, table or index, and the time field that was used.
- What each step returned: the bare table count, the count after the time filter, the count after the value filter.
- The two counts side by side, Splunk against Sentinel, for the same window and the same host.
- What you did not verify: agent health on the source host, and whether throttling would suppress a second alert.

That note lets the detection engineer fix a rule instead of re-running an investigation you already did.

**Escalation criterion:** escalate to the detection engineering owner when both platforms return the same counts for the same window and the rule still produces nothing, which points at rule scope or throttling rather than at the query.

diagram.title: Same question, two dialects
diagram.caption: Both columns answer "how many failed logons per source". What changes is what you name first, and where the time filter lives.

data.verdict: Same four moves; the platform decides whether you name an index or a table first.

video.title: Basic Searching in Splunk Enterprise
video.why: Shows a base search being narrowed one pipe at a time in the real search bar, which makes the filter-before-aggregate order visible instead of abstract.

commands.cmd: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h | stats count AS failures BY src | sort -failures | head 5
commands.what: The reference answer for the port: a count per source address, cut to the top five.

commands.cmd: SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | where EventID == 4625 | summarize failures=count() by IpAddress | top 5 by failures desc
commands.what: The same question in KQL, where the table name replaces the index and the schema replaces the add-on.
Proves the table has rows in this workspace at all, which separates a data fault from a query fault.

commands.cmd: Heartbeat | summarize LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer | where LastSeen < ago(1h)
commands.what: Lists agents that stopped reporting, so you know a quiet table is not a quiet estate.
The Elasticsearch equivalent: index pattern, @timestamp range, and a terms aggregation on the schema field.

pitfalls: Copying src into a KQL query and then rewriting the logic when it returns nothing. Kusto rejects an unknown column at compile time, so zero rows was never a field-name problem.
Comparing counts taken over different windows: earliest=-24h runs on the search head clock, ago(24h) runs on the query service clock, and the portal time picker then cuts the result a third time.
Porting stats count BY src as summarize count() by IpAddress without checking that every event carries that column. A local logon has no source address, so the empty value becomes the largest group.
takeaways: Every platform does the same four moves: restrict, count, group, cut.
You must be able to name the time field and the visible time picker before you write a filter.
Zero rows is a data answer until proven otherwise; each platform fails differently on a bad name, and that difference is the diagnostic.

drill.prompt: Open the lab SIEM without changing the time range. Run the loosest query it allows (`index=wineventlog | head 5` or `SecurityEvent | take 5`) and list which hosts answered. Then write the failed-logon count for one host in that platform's own syntax, and compare your number with the count on the host itself.
checklist: You wrote down the table or index, the time field, and the picker setting before running anything.
The loose query returned rows, and you can name three hosts that appear in it.
Your count query uses the platform's own aggregation rather than a list of raw rows.
Your number and the host-side count agree, or you can state which filter caused the difference.
You used lab data only, with no customer hostnames or addresses in your notes.

l6-3.title: Alert triage: true positive, false positive, and severity
l6-3.subtitle: Decide in three minutes whether to escalate, close or investigate.
objectives: Sort an alert into true positive, benign true positive or false positive, and quote the evidence for the verdict.
Run the identity, asset and timing checks in that order and stop as soon as one of them settles the ticket.
Set priority from the rule severity and the asset urgency instead of from the caller or the clock.
Write a closure note that another analyst can audit and a detection engineer can tune from.

ticket.subject: Night shift closed our 4625 burst on dc01 as false positive
ticket.body: A 4625 burst against dc01 was closed at 05:50 with the note "user locked out, AD reset the password". At 07:10 the identity team reported the same service account authenticating from a VPN pool address outside the office ranges, and the account is in Backup Operators. The closed alert is the only record of the earlier failures.
ticket.impact: A privileged service account may be compromised; the triage decision was made before anyone paired the failures with a successful logon.

sections.h: The alert that was closed at 05:50
sections.body:
The night shift closed a 400-failure logon alert on `dc01` with one line: "user locked out, AD reset the password." At 07:10 the identity team called. The same service account had authenticated from an address outside the office ranges at 04:12, two minutes after the last failure. The closed alert was the only record of the burst, and the closure note had overwritten the one detail that mattered.

The missing check takes one search: pair the failures with the successes in the same window, from the same source.

```splunk
index=wineventlog host=dc01 (EventCode=4625 OR EventCode=4624) earliest=-6h
| stats count BY EventCode, src, user
| sort -count

EventCode  src            user         count
4625       203.0.113.44   svc-backup     412
4624       203.0.113.44   svc-backup       1
4625       10.20.6.15     j.okafor         3
```

412 failures and one success from one address inside one hour is a compromise. A lockout is failures with no success behind them. That single row was available before the shift ended, and the address here is from the documentation range, not a real one.

The lesson is not that the night analyst was careless. It is that the queue hands you a category with the alert, and that category is often wrong.

sections.h: Three checks, and the order is part of the method
sections.body:
Identity first. Does this account normally do this, from here, at this hour? Service accounts have the most rigid patterns of anything on the network: no interactive logon, no VPN address, no browsing. A human account with a new laptop is ordinary; a service account sourcing from a residential range is not, whatever the password state says.

Asset second. The same alert on a developer laptop and on a domain controller are different tickets. Blast radius decides urgency, and urgency decides whether you escalate now or finish the shift first.

Timing third. Check the change calendar, the backup window, the patch schedule and the authorized test scope. The point is not to find an excuse: "the AD team was working on it" is a claim, while a change record with a window and an owner is evidence, and only one belongs in a closure note.

The order matters because each check can end the triage early. Identity settles most alerts in under a minute and needs no tooling. Asset decides who is woken up. Timing saves you from escalating a scanner, and only after you know it is a scanner.

sections.h: The category nobody writes down: benign true positive
sections.body:
The queue offers two words, and there are three answers.

A **true positive** is a rule that fired correctly on activity you do not want. A **false positive** is a rule that fired because the logic matched something it was never meant to catch. In between sits the **benign true positive**: the rule worked, the activity happened, and the activity is allowed. A vulnerability scanner inside its authorized window is the standard example.

The distinction is not pedantry. Closing a scanner hit as a false positive tells the detection engineer the rule is broken, and the usual response is to weaken it. The rule that was correctly catching credentialed scanning is now the rule that misses a real one. Every closure note is a tuning input whether you meant it that way or not.

There is a fourth category that never appears in your queue: the false negative, activity nobody wrote a rule for.

**Decision rule:** if you can name the authorized activity, the window and the owner, close it as a benign true positive with those three facts. If you cannot name all three, you do not have an explanation yet.

sections.h: Severity belongs to the rule, urgency belongs to the asset
sections.body:
**Severity** comes from the rule author and describes the damage if the alert is true: credential access on a domain controller is high, a blocked outbound connection from a lab machine is low. You do not get to lower it because the user was polite or because the shift is ending.

**Urgency** comes from the environment: is the account privileged, is the asset production, is the activity still happening, and is it spreading. A medium-severity alert on a backup server with a privileged service account can outrank a high-severity alert on an isolated test host.

Set priority from both, and write both down: they are what the next shift cannot reconstruct from the alert title.

Two failure modes cost L1 engineers their credibility. Escalating everything at high teaches the SOC to ignore the queue. The other is quieter: downgrading at handover so the queue looks clean, which hands the next shift an alert with your note and none of your context.

**Decision rule:** if the activity is still running, escalate on the facts you have without waiting to finish the investigation. A stopped attack can wait for a complete note; a running one cannot.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The note is the ticket. It carries four lines and a verdict:

- The category, in the right word: true positive, benign true positive, or false positive.
- The evidence that decided it, quoted: the source address, the event IDs, the one success after 412 failures.
- Severity from the rule, urgency from the asset, and the priority you set from both.
- What the next analyst should check first, in one sentence.

If the account was privileged and the source external, the closing line is not a closure but a request for the incident process.

**Escalation criterion:** escalate the moment a burst of failures is followed by a success from the same source, or when the source is external and the account holds privileged group membership. Both are true positives on evidence, and neither needs a second opinion before you pick up the phone.

diagram.title: Three minutes, five questions
diagram.caption: The top branch is the one the night shift skipped. One successful logon from the failing source settles the ticket before the other questions are asked.

video.title: Same Alert. Real Attack or False Positive? (How SOC Analysts Decide)
video.why: Works one alert through the real-or-benign decision out loud, which shows the reasoning order that the tree can only draw.

commands.cmd: index=wineventlog host=dc01 (EventCode=4625 OR EventCode=4624) earliest=-6h | stats count BY EventCode, src, user
commands.what: Puts failures and successes side by side per source, which is the evidence that separates a lockout from a compromise.
Reads the newest failures straight from the controller, including the sub status that tells a wrong password from an unknown account.

commands.cmd: SigninLogs | where UserPrincipalName == "svc-backup@example.com" | project TimeGenerated, IPAddress, Location, ResultType
commands.what: Checks whether the same account also signed in to the cloud identity provider, which the on-premises log cannot show.
Shows group membership and password age, which is what turns a medium alert into an urgent one.

commands.cmd: index=wineventlog EventCode=4672 earliest=-6h | stats count BY user, host
commands.what: Lists special-privilege logons, so you can see whether the suspicious account was handed administrative rights when it authenticated.

pitfalls: Accepting "the password was reset" as the explanation. A reset ends the lockout, not the attempts, and it says nothing about the success that followed them.
Closing a scanner hit as a false positive. It is a benign true positive, and that label asks the detection engineer to weaken a rule that was working.
Downgrading severity at handover so the queue looks clean. The next shift inherits the alert with your note and none of the context that produced it.
takeaways: Pair failures with successes before you categorize anything; one success changes the ticket.
Benign true positive is a real category, and the words you close with become tuning instructions.
Severity is fixed by the rule, urgency moves with the asset, and priority needs both.

drill.prompt: Take three closed alerts from the lab queue, including one closed as false positive. Re-triage each with the tree, and write one evidence line per alert: the category, the artifact that proves it, and the priority you would set. Use lab data only, and redact any address that is not from a documentation range.
checklist: Each alert has one category from the three, not a hedge.
Each evidence line quotes a concrete value: an event ID, a source address, a timestamp or a group name.
At least one alert changed category from what the original note said.
Each priority line states severity and urgency separately before combining them.
You can say which of the three you would have escalated on the first call, and why.

l6-4.title: Correlation and detection engineering: writing a use case
l6-4.subtitle: Turn one alert into a rule that finds the behaviour, not the symptom.
objectives: Split an alert into the behavior it names and the data that can prove it
Write a correlation search that joins two event types on one key inside a time window
Set a threshold from a week of real events instead of from a guess
Hand a rule to another analyst with an owner, a test event and a version

ticket.subject: Same account, 30 failed logons, and nobody saw the two that worked
ticket.body: The overnight queue took 41 Windows logon alerts from dc01, dc02 and fs01. Each one was a single bad-password event, triaged alone and closed. The 07:00 review found the same service account had 30 failures across both domain controllers and then two successful logons from a workstation. No rule in the console groups those records, so nobody received one alert that said so.
ticket.impact: A possible credential compromise sat closed in the queue for nine hours.

sections.h: Forty-one alerts, and the one that mattered was split into four
sections.body:
The queue handed over at 07:00 held 41 Windows logon alerts. Each alert was one event: a 4625 bad-password record on dc01, dc02 or fs01. Each was triaged on its own, judged not worth escalation, and closed. The queue was empty by 07:10, which looked like a quiet night.

The pattern was never on the screen. One service account, `svc_backup`, failed 30 times across the two domain controllers between 03:04 and 03:26, then authenticated successfully to fs01 at 03:27 from 10.20.14.87 — a user workstation, not a backup server. The successful logon arrived as a separate alert. It was closed too, because a success is not a failure.

That is what per-event alerting costs: the signal exists, spread over records nobody joins. **Correlation** is the join. **Detection engineering** is deciding what to join, on which field, over how long, and writing it down so the next analyst gets one alert instead of forty.

sections.h: An alert is a sentence, and a detection is a test of that sentence
sections.body:
Write the behavior as a sentence before you touch the query language: `One account fails authentication on more than one server and then succeeds within ten minutes.` That sentence has a subject (the account), a condition (failures on more than one host), a second condition (a success) and a window. Every clause maps to a field you either have or do not have.

If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to write a rule. A query you copied from someone else is not a detection until you can say what it would look like when it is wrong.

A use case has six parts: the sentence, the data sources that can witness it, the join key, the threshold, the time window, and an owner who answers when it fires.

Decision rule for a call: if the alert describes one event but the behavior needs two, you are looking at a symptom. Go to the raw search before you decide anything.

sections.h: The join key is where most rules fail quietly
sections.body:
Correlation joins records on a shared field inside a bounded window. That shared field is the **join key**: the account, the host, the source address. If the key is spelled differently in two indexes — `user`, `Account`, `TargetUserName` — the join returns nothing, and nothing reads to a tired analyst as "no activity".

SPL does this with `stats` grouped by the key. Grouping is cheaper than `join` and has no subsearch row limit:

```console
index=win sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4624 OR EventCode=4625)
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count(eval(EventCode=4625)) AS fails,
        count(eval(EventCode=4624)) AS oks,
        values(ComputerName) AS targets
        BY _time, user
| where fails >= 10 AND oks > 0
| table _time, user, fails, oks, targets

_time                 user          fails  oks  targets
2025-11-24 03:10:00   svc_backup       14    0   dc01, dc02
2025-11-24 03:20:00   svc_backup       16    2   fs01
```

Two rows, one bucket apart: failures on both domain controllers, then two successes on a file server. The alert that should have reached the queue is one line, and it names the account, the hosts and the count.

Sentinel does the same join with `summarize ... by`: `SecurityEvent | where EventID in (4624, 4625) | summarize fails=countif(EventID==4625), oks=countif(EventID==4624), hosts=make_set(Computer) by Account, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m) | where fails >= 10 and oks > 0`. Same key, same window, different words.

sections.h: Tune on a week of real events, not on a guess
sections.body:
Run the rule backwards before you enable it: add `earliest=-7d latest=now` and count the rows. If it returns 900, the threshold is wrong, the field is wrong, or the data is wrong, and you have to find out which before it becomes 900 alerts. Read twenty of the hits in full. They split into two groups.

The first group is real but expected: `svc_backup` fails every night at 03:10 because the job starts before DNS is up. That needs a threshold or a scoped exclusion with an expiry date, not a permanent silence. The second group is artifacts: `user` is empty because that forwarder does not send it. That needs a field fix, and an exclusion would hide the next real event.

Ship the rule the way you ship code: in version control, with the sentence in the description, the search or analytics rule itself, a sample event you can replay, and a changelog line. Detection-as-code is not a product you buy. A folder of YAML in git is enough.

Decision rule: a rule that fires more than 20 times a day with no confirmed true positive in a week is queue filler. Raise the threshold, add a scoped exclusion, or delete it, and write down which one you chose.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Your note has seven lines: rule name, the sentence, the data sources, the join key, the threshold and window, the seven-day hit count split into true and false positives, and the owner. Add the saved-search name or the file path in git. Another analyst should be able to re-run the rule from that note without asking you a question.

Closing note for the overnight ticket: "svc_backup had 30 failed logons on dc01 and dc02 between 03:04 and 03:26, then two successful logons to fs01 from 10.20.14.87 at 03:27. Source is a user workstation and the account is a backup service account. Correlation search corr-logon-fail-then-success enabled; historical baseline 3 hits per week, 1 confirmed true positive."

Escalation criterion: escalate to L2 the moment the correlated result shows a successful logon for a service account or a domain admin after failures from a host that should never run that account. Password typos do not succeed on a file server at 03:27.

diagram.title: From one alert to a rule with an owner
diagram.caption: Six steps. The fourth is the one people skip: a rule is not shipped until it has been run backwards over a week of real events and someone has read the hits.

data.footer: A rule with no owner is muted in week one and never returns.

video.title: SIEM Correlation Rules for Beginners
video.why: Walks correlation rules from the rule logic to the events they group, which is the step this text can only describe in prose.

commands.cmd: splunk search 'index=win EventCode=4625 | stats count AS fails BY user' -auth admin:changeme
commands.what: run the detection from the CLI before you save it as a search

commands.cmd: curl -k -u admin:changeme https://splunk01:8089/services/saved/searches -d name=corr-logon-fail-then-success --data-urlencode 'search=index=win (EventCode=4624 OR EventCode=4625) | bin _time span=10m | stats count(eval(EventCode=4625)) AS fails BY _time, user'
commands.what: create the scheduled correlation search from a script so every site gets the same object

commands.cmd: az monitor log-analytics query -w 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 --analytics-query 'SecurityEvent | where EventID in (4624,4625) | summarize count() by Account, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)'
commands.what: run the same join in Sentinel without opening the portal

commands.cmd: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Group-Object {$_.Properties[5].Value} | Sort-Object Count -Descending
commands.what: which account is failing on this host, asked of the host itself

pitfalls: Joining on a field name that exists in only one index: `user` is populated in the Windows log and empty in the VPN log, so the join returns nothing and the ticket is closed as "no matching activity".
Trying to correlate inside one alert: the rule sees a single event, so 30 failures and a success can never appear in the same record, and no threshold will ever fix that.
Shipping with no baseline: the rule fires 600 times on day one, someone adds a blanket exclusion for `svc_*`, and the rule is blind to the next compromise of exactly that account.
takeaways: A detection is a sentence plus a data source plus a threshold plus an owner; the query is the easy part.
`stats ... BY` is the correlation: one key, one window, then filter on the counts.
Run the rule backwards over a week before you enable it, and put that hit count in your note.

drill.prompt: In your training Splunk instance, take the sentence "one account fails on more than one host and then succeeds within ten minutes" and build the correlation search for it. Run it with `earliest=-7d`, count the hits, open the top three, and write the sentence, the join key, the threshold and the hit count into a four-line note.
checklist: A written sentence with a subject, a count and a window
The search returns a table with one row per account and time bucket
A seven-day hit count, with at least three hits read in full
One line naming the field you had to fix or the threshold you had to raise

l6-5.title: MITRE ATT&CK and threat intelligence: mapping what you see
l6-5.subtitle: Where IOCs fit, where they fail, and how to use ATT&CK for coverage.
objectives: Separate an indicator of compromise from the behavior that produced it
Name the technique and sub-technique behind an alert, with the ATT&CK ID
Judge an indicator by its shelf life before you block anything with it
Turn a technique list into a coverage check with a rule or a documented gap against each

ticket.subject: VirusTotal says 3 of 70 and the application team says the file is theirs
ticket.body: A user reported an attachment that would not open. The analyst submitted its SHA256 to VirusTotal, saw 3 of 70 engines flag it, and escalated the ticket as malware. The application team says the file is their own installer, signed last week. The user has been off the network since the escalation and cannot work.
ticket.impact: One user offline since 11:20, with the SOC and the application team disagreeing about the same file.

sections.h: Three of seventy is a question, not a verdict
sections.body:
The ticket said malware because a file scanner showed 3 of 70. That number has no denominator of trust. The engines are not independent, a week-old installer built in-house trips heuristic engines that have never seen it, and a file that was never submitted shows 0 of 70 for a different reason: nothing has looked at it yet.

Two hours went into an argument about a verdict. Nobody opened the endpoint log to see whether the document ran, what it spawned, or where the host connected. An **indicator of compromise (IOC)** — a hash, an address, a domain — is a fact about a file or a host. It is not a fact about intent.

The work on the call is to walk from the indicator to the behavior: what executed, under whose account, with which parent process, and what touched the network. ATT&CK gives you the vocabulary for that sentence.

sections.h: A tactic is why, a technique is how, a sub-technique is the log line
sections.body:
**MITRE ATT&CK** is a public knowledge base of adversary behavior, built from observed incidents and maintained by MITRE. Three levels matter at L1.

A **tactic** is the goal: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Credential Access, Exfiltration. Enterprise ATT&CK has 14 of them.

A **technique** is how the goal is reached, and it has an ID: T1566 Phishing, T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter, T1547 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution.

A **sub-technique** is the level that matches a log field: T1059.001 PowerShell, T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder, T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment.

That last level is the useful one. "Execution" does not tell you which field to alert on. "T1059.001, `powershell.exe` whose parent is `WINWORD.EXE`" does. When you write a ticket, name the sub-technique and the field that showed it, and the L2 analyst can check your work in one search.

sections.h: An indicator is only as good as its shelf life
sections.body:
The useful question about any indicator is how long it stays true. David Bianco's pyramid of pain ranks them by how much it costs an adversary to change them.

| Indicator | Stays true for | What it proves |
| SHA256 of a file | until the file is rebuilt | that exact file |
| IP address | days to weeks | a host that was reachable |
| Domain name | weeks | a name someone resolved |
| Technique | years | behavior, after a rebuild |

Read it as a shelf life. A hash match answers a question about one file. It does not clear the host, because the loader that dropped the file can be recompiled in a minute. An address match can be worse than useless: CDN ranges, cloud egress ranges and shared hosting are used by thousands of unrelated customers, and blocking one takes a business service down with it.

Decision rule: if the only thing tying an alert to an adversary is a hash or an address, treat it as enrichment and keep the ticket open on behavior. If you can name the technique and show it in your own logs, you have a detection.

sections.h: Map the activity, then look for the gap
sections.body:
Take one phish and walk it. The attachment is opened: T1566.001. The document spawns a shell: T1204.002 User Execution, then T1059.001. A Run key is written: T1547.001. The host talks to 203.0.113.66 on 443: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol.

Now the part that earns its keep: for each of those four IDs, ask whether a rule exists that would have fired. Each answer is either a detection or a documented gap, and the four lines together are a coverage review. That is why ATT&CK is used for defense. It is not a way to name an attacker.

The knowledge base is a downloadable bundle, so you can check an ID on a machine with no internet access:

```console
$ curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mitre-attack/attack-stix-data/master/enterprise-attack/enterprise-attack.json \
    | jq -r '.objects[] | select(.type=="attack-pattern" and .revoked==false)
             | [.external_references[0].external_id, .name] | @tsv' \
    | grep '^T1059' | sort
T1059	Command and Scripting Interpreter
T1059.001	PowerShell
T1059.002	AppleScript
T1059.003	Windows Command Shell
T1059.004	Unix Shell
```

Mapping is not emulation. Running Atomic Red Team, Caldera or any technique against a host is an offensive act. It requires written authorization that names the hosts, the window and the person accountable, and in this course it stays inside the lab range.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Six things go in the note: the hash with its size and signer, the scanner ratio plus the first and last submission dates, whether the file executed (parent, child, account), the technique IDs you can show in the logs, the rule that did or did not fire, and the gap that leaves behind.

Closing note: "SHA256 of installer.docm, 3/70 on VirusTotal, first submitted 2025-11-20, signed by the app team build certificate. Endpoint log shows WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe -enc on ws-0412 at 09:13; no rule exists for T1059.001. Releasing the file is not the same as clearing the host."

Escalation criterion: escalate to L2 when you can name a sub-technique and show the log line that proves it. Do not escalate on a scanner ratio alone. That is the ticket that burned two hours and took a user offline for an installer.

diagram.title: One attachment, four technique IDs
diagram.caption: Read the times as evidence order rather than as a story: the Run key at 09:18 is what makes the earlier PowerShell persistent, and 09:22 is the first moment data may have left.

video.title: MITRE ATT&CK® Framework
video.why: The maintainer of ATT&CK shows the tactic column and the technique entry side by side, which fixes the shape of the matrix faster than a written description.

commands.what: look up a technique ID and its name without internet access to the ATT&CK site
the detection ratio, and how old the first submission is
what your own intelligence platform already knows about the address
the hash of the file that is actually on the endpoint, not the one in the email

pitfalls: Blocking a shared address because it appeared in an alert: CDN and cloud egress ranges serve unrelated customers, so the block takes a business service down and the real traffic keeps flowing elsewhere.
Calling a 0/70 ratio clean: a private build has never been submitted, so the scanner has nothing to compare and returns zero for lack of evidence.
Mapping an incident to a tactic only, such as "Execution": without a sub-technique you cannot check whether a rule exists, so the gap you found stays open.
takeaways: A tactic is why, a technique is how, and a sub-technique is the level that matches a field in your logs.
An IOC has a shelf life measured in days; a technique stays true after the file is rebuilt.
Coverage is a list of technique IDs, each with a rule or a documented gap against it.

drill.prompt: Take the four IDs from the diagram and, for each one, search your lab SIEM for the field that would prove it. Write one line per ID in the form "T-ID, field, rule name or GAP". Then look up T1059.001 in the downloaded bundle and confirm the name matches what you wrote.
checklist: Four lines, each with a technique ID and a named field
At least two lines that say GAP and name the data source that is missing
The jq lookup returns T1059.001 with its official name
One sentence on why an indicator alone would not have changed any of the four answers

l6-6.title: A SOC shift: five alerts, one incident
l6-6.subtitle: Walk a shift: triage, correlate, escalate, hand over.
objectives: Triage five related alerts as one timeline instead of five tickets
Pivot on the host and the account across SIEM, EDR and firewall data
Choose containment you can reverse, and record it with a time and a console
Write a handover that an L2 analyst can act on without calling you

ticket.from: Service Desk — SOC queue, 06:00 to 14:00 shift
ticket.subject: Five alerts on one laptop between 09:12 and 09:40, all closed separately
ticket.body: The shift took five alerts on ws-0412 within half an hour: a macro-enabled document, an encoded PowerShell command, a registry Run key, an outbound connection to 203.0.113.66 and failed logons on fs01 from the same host. Two were closed as benign and three went to two different L2 queues as separate tickets. The user called at 10:05 to say the laptop was slow.
ticket.impact: One host, three tickets and two queues, with no single timeline since 09:12.

sections.h: Five alerts, one host, and no timeline anywhere
sections.body:
Between 09:12 and 09:40 the queue took five alerts on ws-0412. A macro-enabled document opened. An encoded PowerShell command ran. A registry Run key was written. The firewall logged 41 MB outbound to 203.0.113.66:443. And fs01 recorded six failed logons from 10.20.120.42, which is ws-0412.

Two of the five were closed as benign. Three went to two different L2 queues as separate tickets. The user called at 10:05 because the laptop was slow. Nobody had put the five records in one place, so nobody could see that the same host had executed a payload, made it persistent, and then tried a file server.

A shift is not a list of alerts. It is one timeline per entity, and the entity is usually a host or an account. The ticket number is the one thing that will not help you.

sections.h: Read the event, not the rule name
sections.body:
Rule names carry verdicts written weeks ago by someone who is not on your call: "Suspicious PowerShell", "Malware Detected". The verdict is a summary. The event is the evidence.

Open the raw event and answer four questions: which account, which parent process, which command line, and when this rule last fired for this host. A rule that has fired 40 times for ws-0412 in a month is either badly tuned or watching something normal. Either way, its name tells you nothing about this event.

Two minutes on the raw event saves the twenty you would spend arguing about a rule name that never mentioned the parent process.

Decision rule: when the alert name contains a verdict, ignore the verdict and read the command line. `powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA...` under `WINWORD.EXE` is not the same event as `powershell.exe -File \\fs01\share\login.ps1` under `explorer.exe`, and only the command line separates them.

sections.h: Correlate across the queue, not inside the alert
sections.body:
Pivot on the entity, not the alert ID. Pull every index that mentions the host or its address for the hour, and sort by time:

```console
index=edr OR index=proxy OR index=win (host=ws-0412 OR src=10.20.120.42) earliest=09:00 latest=10:00
| eval t=strftime(_time,"%H:%M:%S")
| table t, index, sourcetype, EventCode, Image, dest, url
| sort t

t         index  sourcetype    event
09:12:04  win    Security      4624 logon ws-0412\a.sharma
09:12:51  edr    Security      WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe
09:13:02  edr    Security      -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA...
09:18:37  win    Security      Run key HKCU\Software\...\Run\OneDriveSync
09:22:10  fw     pan:traffic   203.0.113.66:443 out, 41 MB
09:31:48  win    Security      4625 x6 on fs01 from 10.20.120.42
```

One line changes the incident, and it is not the PowerShell alert. The 41 MB went out on 443 with no proxy record at all, so either the host bypassed the proxy or it had a direct egress path. That is a finding about your network, not about the user, and it goes in the ticket.

The six 4625 records on fs01 matter for the same reason. They are the only evidence that the host had credentials and was reaching for more, and they are the point where an incident stays contained instead of becoming a file server problem.

sections.h: Contain only what you can undo
sections.body:
At L1 you may isolate and you may disable. You may not reimage, and you should not shut the machine down. A powered-off host loses its memory and its open channels, and L2 loses the process tree that proves what ran.

Isolation from the EDR console keeps the management channel open, so collection continues and the user sees a message explaining why the network is gone. Disabling the switch port is the fallback when the agent is not responding. It also kills remote collection, and on most sites it needs the network team to approve it.

Record the action with a time and a console. "Isolated ws-0412 at 09:52 from the EDR console, agent still checking in, user notified by phone" is a containment record. "Contained" is a word.

You are not solving the incident on this call. You are stopping the spread and keeping the evidence, in that order, and anything that serves neither is L2 work.

Decision rule: if the host is encrypting files or pushing data out, isolate first and investigate second. If it is a macro document that never spawned a shell, collect the evidence and leave the machine running for L2.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
One timeline, one host, five alerts, and the evidence paths. State what changed and what did not: isolated at 09:52, account a.sharma still enabled, fs01 logons failed so no session was established, no data confirmed leaving.

Closing note: "5 alerts 09:12 to 09:40 on ws-0412 (10.20.120.42). WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe -enc at 09:13, Run key written 09:18, 41 MB to 203.0.113.66:443 at 09:22, six 4625 on fs01 at 09:31. Host isolated 09:52, EDR agent live. a.sharma password reset pending. Proxy has no record of the 41 MB."

Escalation criterion: raise it to P1 immediately, without waiting for shift end, if the account that succeeded holds write access to a file server or if traffic to 203.0.113.66 is still rising. Otherwise it stays P2 with the timeline attached.

diagram.title: From first alert to isolation
diagram.caption: The analyst asks the SIEM about the entity, not the ticket. The two answers that changed the severity came from the EDR console and the firewall, both outside the alert that started the work.

video.title: A Day in the Life of a SOC Analyst: Coffee, Alerts, Repeat
video.why: A former analyst describes what a critical alert does to the rest of a shift, which shows the queue pressure this lesson can only state as a timeline.

commands.cmd: index=edr OR index=proxy OR index=win (host=ws-0412 OR src=10.20.120.42) earliest=09:00 latest=10:00 | eval t=strftime(_time,"%H:%M:%S") | table t, index, sourcetype, EventCode, Image, dest, url | sort t
commands.what: one timeline for the entity across every index in the hour
whether the endpoint agent was actually protecting the host when the payload ran
the logon records behind the alert, including the ones no rule saw
