whether the access port is up before you ask the network team to shut it

pitfalls: Keeping five tickets open on one host: the L2 analyst who receives the third one has no idea the other two exist, and rebuilds the timeline from scratch.
Shutting the laptop down to stop the malware: memory and the process tree go with it, and the parent process can no longer be proved.
Writing "isolated" without a time or a console: nobody can tell whether containment happened before or after the 41 MB left.
takeaways: The unit of work is the entity, host or account, not the alert.
Isolation is reversible and keeps the agent channel; a port shutdown is not, so it needs approval.
A handover is a timeline with times, not a summary paragraph.

drill.prompt: Build the timeline by hand. Take the five alerts from the diagram and put them in one table with three columns: time, system, evidence. Then write the two-sentence handover you would send to L2, including one thing you did not do and why.
checklist: Five rows ordered by time, each with the system it came from
One row that only appears because two sources were joined
A containment action written with a time and a console name
One line stating the escalation criterion you applied

l7-1.title: Identification and classification: is this an incident?
l7-1.subtitle: Separate a nuisance from a breach, and set severity without drama.
objectives: Decide whether an alert is an event or an incident, and name the fact that settled it
Read failed and successful logon events and tell a stale credential from a working guess
Assign a severity from functional impact, information impact, and recovery effort
Write an identification note that lets L2 reconstruct your reasoning without calling you

ticket.subject: User says her mailbox was hacked, please advise urgent
ticket.body: The user called at 08:05 saying a colleague received mail from her account at 23:40 that she did not write, and that Outlook asked her to sign in again this morning. She changed her password from her phone before calling. Her manager wants to know whether the account should be disabled and whether anyone else is affected. Nobody has opened the sign-in logs yet, and the ticket is already flagged urgent because the manager said the word breach.
ticket.impact: One mailbox is in question, an invoice run that uses that address is paused, and two other users on the same floor are asking whether they were hit.

sections.h: The 03:10 page was a stale password, and it cost three engineers an hour
sections.body:
The alert fired at 03:10: 41 failed logons for `svc-backup` from 10.30.4.88 in four minutes. The on-call analyst paged the security lead, who woke the backup engineer, and by 04:20 three people had proved that a scheduled task still held the password rotated at 22:00.

The same queue held a ticket from 08:05: a user reporting that a colleague got mail from her account at 23:40 that she did not write. It was picked up at 11:30, because the night shift spent the morning on the backup account.

Only one of those was an incident, and the queue sorted them backwards. **Identification** is the work of deciding which one you are holding. **Classification** is the answer to how bad it is, who has to know, and how fast. Both come before containment, because containment costs money and destroys data you will want later.

sections.h: An event is something that happened; an incident is something that is harming you
sections.body:
An **event** is an observable occurrence: a logon, a blocked connection, a scheduled task that ran. An **incident** is an event, or a group of them, that actually or imminently harms confidentiality, integrity, or availability. NIST SP 800-61 draws that line. The 2025 revision reorganized the lifecycle around the CSF 2.0 functions and did not move the line.

Three tests turn it into something you can run at 03:10.

1. **Is there an action, or only a name?** A rule titled `Possible Cobalt Strike` that fired on a blocked outbound connection is a signature match. A process on a host that made that connection is an action.
2. **Does it touch something that holds value?** A shared `billing@` mailbox or a domain controller is not a test VM that has been powered off since March.
3. **Is it still happening?** An attempt that ended is evidence. An attempt in progress is an incident with a clock on it.

Two yes answers means incident. Three no answers means event: record it, close it, keep the row so the pattern is visible next month. "Not an incident" never means "no work" — the user still gets an answer.

sections.h: The logon log answers test one in one command
sections.body:
Windows Security event 4625 is a failed logon and 4624 is a successful one. The fields that matter are the target account, the source address, and on the success side the logon type.

```console
PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625} -MaxEvents 4 |
>>   Select-Object TimeCreated,
>>     @{n='Account';e={$_.Properties[5].Value}},
>>     @{n='Source';e={$_.Properties[19].Value}} | Format-Table

TimeCreated            Account        Source
-----------            -------        ------
11/18/2026 2:41:07 AM  svc-backup     10.30.4.88
11/18/2026 2:41:09 AM  svc-backup     10.30.4.88
11/18/2026 2:41:12 AM  svc-backup     10.30.4.88
11/18/2026 2:41:14 AM  administrator  10.30.4.88
```

The account column is `TargetUserName` and the source column is `IpAddress`. The property order for 4625 is fixed, so the indexes work. Read the last line first: a service account failing from its own subnet and then switching to `administrator` is a script working through a list, not a user with a stale password.

**Decision rule:** if no success follows those failures from that source within the hour, classify it as an event and fix the credential. If a success follows, stop reading logs and open an incident — that account is compromised until someone proves otherwise.

sections.h: Severity is three facts, not the volume of the caller
sections.body:
NIST SP 800-61 builds severity from functional impact (what stopped working), information impact (what was or may have been read, changed, or taken), and recoverability (how much work restores service). Score all three, then pick a number.

| Sev | Test | Who is called |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Privileged account confirmed compromised, data confirmed leaving, or a production service down | Security lead and duty manager now, by phone |
| 2 | Two or more hosts or accounts, or one host showing lateral movement | L2 IR within 15 minutes, security lead informed |
| 3 | One host or one account, contained, no spread | L1 owns it, IR ticket, L2 review next business day |
| 4 | Attempt blocked, nothing touched | Document and close |

Severity is provisional: you will move tickets between rows as facts arrive. Containment is not provisional: disabling an account or isolating a host stops work and starts a restore clock. Take the cheapest reversible step first — a password reset and a session revoke — and leave disabling to the incident owner.

**Decision rule:** a Sev 1 or Sev 2 is decided by a fact, never by a request. "The manager wants this treated as critical" is not a fact. "The account is in Domain Admins and signed in from 10.30.4.88" is.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Write the identification note in the ticket, not in chat. Five lines:

```text
What:     4 x 4625 for svc-backup, then a 4624 success from 10.30.4.88 at 03:14
Scope:    one service account, no other account seen from that address
Evidence: exported to \\fs01\ir\INC0048211\logons.evtx
Sev:      2 - backup account brute-forced, no data confirmed taken
Next:     password reset 03:31, sessions revoked, L2 IR paged 03:34
```

Write timestamps in UTC and say which clock produced them. If you cannot answer what you saw, where it is stored, and who knows, you are not ready to hand over.

Do not open the mailbox, the share, or the host to "take a quick look" unless the incident owner gives you written authorization naming what you may access. It also protects you in a later review.

**Closing note:** the ticket closes when the note names the evidence, the severity, and the next owner. It does not close when the user stops calling.

**Escalate to Sev 2 and page L2 IR** the moment the same indicator appears on a second host or account, or when the account holds privileged rights. Below that line, L1 can close it.

diagram.title: From queue item to severity
diagram.caption: Three questions, asked in order. The first branch that answers yes sets the floor for severity; the last one sets the ceiling.

video.title: Incident Triage: Severity vs Priority, Timeline & Escalation (Hands-On Lab) | CySA+ CS0-004
video.why: Runs a real alert export through a triage decision, which is the same scoring you do on paper, and shows why severity and priority are separate fields.

commands.what: Failed logons with the target account and source address
Successful logons; the logon type tells remote from local
Entra ID sign-ins with IP, app, and MFA result, when the account is cloud-joined
Which address is connected to Remote Desktop on this host right now
Whether the account you are holding the ticket for is privileged
Mailbox rules created recently, the usual trace of a business email compromise

pitfalls: Treating the rule name as the finding. A rule called "Possible Cobalt Strike" fires on a blocked connection, and escalating it without checking the host spends someone else's night.
Disabling the account first because it feels decisive. It locks the user out of the recovery path and destroys the sessions you needed to inspect; reset the password and revoke sessions instead.
Marking a ticket Sev 4 to clear the queue. The classification is the only record that the attempt happened, and a later review will ask who saw it and what they did.
takeaways: An incident is an event that harms confidentiality, integrity, or availability; a signature match is an event until a host proves otherwise.
Failed logons followed by a success from the same address are a compromise, not a password problem.
Severity comes from impact and recoverability, and L1 can move it as facts arrive.

drill.prompt: On your own Windows machine, check whether the account you use every day is privileged, and list every process listening on a port. Then write the five-line identification note for a made-up ticket in which that account failed 30 logons from 10.30.4.88 and succeeded once.
checklist: whoami /groups output is pasted, and you state in one sentence whether the account is local admin
You can name at least one listening port and the process that owns it
The note states a severity and points at one fact, not at how the manager sounded
The note names where the evidence would be stored and says UTC

l7-2.title: Investigation and evidence: chain of custody for people who are not examiners
l7-2.subtitle: What to capture, what to stop touching, and how to record it.
objectives: Preserve a live system in volatility order without destroying what you came to capture
Image a disk through a write blocker and prove the copy matches the source
Record each handoff so the exhibit survives a question six months later
Recognize the point where the case leaves L1 and goes to an examiner

ticket.subject: Finance wants to know why an invoice payment went to a new account
ticket.body: A payment of 41,000 went to an account that was not the supplier's usual one, after an email thread that looked normal. The user says her laptop was "fixed" three weeks ago because Word was slow, and the desk reimaged it. Finance needs to know whether her mailbox was accessed and when the bank details were changed. The laptop is back in service and has been used every day since.
ticket.impact: The payment may be lost, the client is asking for a timeline this week, and the only host that could explain the change has been in daily use for three weeks.

sections.h: The laptop was wiped before anyone took a copy
sections.body:
The user reported an invoice attachment that asked her to enable a macro. The desk remoted in, found Word slow, and reimaged the machine that afternoon. That is the standard fix.

Three weeks later a payment left for an account nobody recognized, and the only machine that could have shown how the mailbox rule was created had been wiped and returned to stock.

Nobody broke a rule. The desk did what it does every day. The failure was that nobody treated the laptop as evidence before treating it as a broken workstation. **Evidence collection** is capturing the state of a system before you change it. **Chain of custody** is the record that proves the copy you hold is the copy you took, and who held it in between.

Your job on the first call is to preserve and to record. The examiner's job starts when you hand over.

sections.h: Touching the machine changes it, so decide before you click
sections.body:
Every action on a live system writes to it. Logging in creates a profile and a logon record, mounts the user's drive, starts scheduled tasks, and may sync OneDrive. Opening Event Viewer writes to the log you are reading, and even a clean shutdown updates timestamps and clears memory.

Pick the least destructive action that answers the question, then write down what you did and when. The sequence is fixed:

- **Get written authorization.** The incident owner, HR, or the client names the host, the scope, and who may access it. Without that in writing, document and escalate. You do not image a colleague's laptop on a hunch, and any practice run happens on a lab machine you own.
- **Record the scene.** Time in UTC, hostname, serial number, and who is in the room.
- **Isolate the network.** Pull the cable or disable the switch port. Keep the power on: memory holds the running process, the open connections, and often the key material.
- **Capture volatile state, then disk.** If the machine is already off, leave it off. Booting it changes hundreds of files before you have looked at one.

**Decision rule:** if the host is on and connected, pull the cable, not the cord. If it is off, do not press the button to see whether it still works.

sections.h: Hash before you move, and hash again after
sections.body:
An image is evidence only if someone can show it matches the original. Hash the source, hash the copy, compare. On Linux, with the disk attached read-only through a write blocker:

```console
$ sudo dd if=/dev/sda of=/mnt/evidence/ws-0142-sda.img bs=4M conv=noerror,sync status=progress
12582912000 bytes (13 GB, 12 GiB) copied, 204 s, 61.7 MB/s
3143+0 records in
3143+0 records out
13182779392 bytes (13 GB, 12 GiB) copied, 214.402 s, 61.5 MB/s

$ sha256sum /dev/sda /mnt/evidence/ws-0142-sda.img
3f8a1c0d94b2e7f6a5c1d0e8b7a2946c5d3e1f0a9b8c7d6e5f4a3b2c1d0e9f8a  /dev/sda
3f8a1c0d94b2e7f6a5c1d0e8b7a2946c5d3e1f0a9b8c7d6e5f4a3b2c1d0e9f8a  /mnt/evidence/ws-0142-sda.img
```

`conv=noerror,sync` keeps `dd` going past a bad sector and pads the output so every offset still lines up with the original. Without it, one bad block shifts every byte after it. A write blocker stops the operating system from writing to the source while you read it. If the disk is failing, stop: that imaging job belongs to the examiner.

The same check on Windows, which also runs on a memory capture:

```console
PS C:\evidence> Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 .\ws-0142-memory.raw | Format-List

Algorithm : SHA256
Hash      : 4d2b7e19c8f3a6051b9e4d7c2a8f6b3e0d9c5a1f7e2b8d4c6a0f3e9b1d7c5a28
Path      : C:\evidence\ws-0142-memory.raw
```

Memory is captured with a tool built for it, such as WinPmem or Magnet RAM Capture, run from removable media and written to external storage. Record the tool name and version.

sections.h: The form is the evidence; the file is only a file
sections.body:
A hash proves the bytes did not change. It does not prove who held them. The chain-of-custody form does, with one line per transfer:

| Field | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Exhibit | INC0048211-E01 |
| Description | SATA SSD, serial S4EVNX0R512309, from ws-0142 |
| Collected by, at | R. Menon, 2026-11-18 09:12 UTC |
| Hash at collection | 3f8a1c0d...9f8a, SHA-256 |
| Stored at | Evidence locker B, shelf 3, sealed bag 118 |
| Transferred to, at | K. Alvarez (L2 IR), 2026-11-18 14:40 UTC |

Write in the ticket system, never leave an unsealed exhibit unattended, and never make a second copy without logging it. A copy that exists off the record is worse than no copy: the first question in any review is why it exists.

**Decision rule:** if you cannot say who held the item between 09:12 and 14:40, the item is not evidence. Say so in the note and let the examiner decide, rather than filling the gap from memory.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Take the user's statement before you touch the machine: what they clicked, when, and what they saw. Their memory is the most volatile evidence in the building, and it disappears the moment they start worrying about blame.

```text
Host:     ws-0142, Dell Latitude, serial 7H2K3L4, user a.okafor
Arrival:  powered on, VLAN 30, Word and Outlook open, no external media
Action:   switch port Gi1/0/14 disabled 09:05 UTC; memory captured 09:12
          (WinPmem, version recorded on E01 form); disk removed 09:40
Disk:     write-blocked, imaged by L2 at 14:40, hash verified against source
Chain:    INC0048211-E01, sealed bag 118, locker B shelf 3
Open:     inbox rule forwarding to an external address, created 11/17 21:48 UTC
```

**Closing note:** an L1 handover is complete when the exhibit is sealed, hashed, logged, and named in one place, and the user's statement is attached. A photograph of the screen is not a capture, and a file on your desktop is not an exhibit.

**Escalate to L2 IR or the examiner** as soon as the case may reach HR, a client contract, or law enforcement, or when the disk holds data you are not authorized to read. A second unrecorded copy can void the first.

diagram.title: First responder sequence
diagram.caption: Each step is recorded before the next one starts. The only step you can skip is none of them, and the only one that destroys evidence is a reboot.

data.footer: Power off between step 2 and step 3 and steps 3 and 4 become impossible.

video.title: Evidence Acquisition
video.why: Walks the first ten minutes of a live acquisition in order, including isolating without powering down and verifying the copy with a hash, which the text can only list.

commands.what: Serial and model for the exhibit description, before the disk leaves the host

commands.cmd: sudo dd if=/dev/sda of=/mnt/evidence/ws-0142-sda.img bs=4M conv=noerror,sync status=progress
commands.what: Byte-for-byte image that survives bad sectors without shifting offsets
Proves the copy matches the source; the two lines must be identical
Hash of a memory capture, for the exhibit form
Open connections and owning processes, captured before the cable comes out
ISO 8601 timestamp with the UTC offset, for the chain-of-custody line

pitfalls: Reimaging the machine to "clean it up" before capture. It is the fastest way to destroy the only record of how the intruder got in, and it cannot be undone.
Powering off to preserve the disk. A powered-off host loses memory, and memory is where the running process and the session keys were.
Copying the image to a desktop and emailing it to L2. The exhibit now exists in three places with no hash on two of them, and the chain is broken.
takeaways: Preserve first, examine later: the cheapest action that answers the question is the one to take.
Pull the cable, keep the power, and never reboot a host you have been asked to preserve.
A hash proves the bytes; the form proves the people. A case needs both.

drill.prompt: Create a small file on your own machine, hash it with Get-FileHash, copy it to another folder or a USB stick, and hash the copy. Then write the four-line chain-of-custody entry for the transfer, including a UTC time.
checklist: Both hashes are pasted and identical
The entry names the file, the serial of the media if you used one, and the UTC time
You wrote one sentence on what you would have had to do differently if the file were a live disk
No real customer or colleague data appears in the file you hashed

l7-3.title: Digital forensics: disk, memory and log artefacts
l7-3.subtitle: Order of volatility, and the three artefacts that answer most questions.
objectives: Order capture by volatility and say what a power-off costs at each layer
Read logon events by type and tell a console logon from RDP from a service start
Resolve a process to its parent and explain what that proves
Build a UTC timeline from three artifacts and mark which source supports each line

ticket.subject: Client wants the exact time of the intrusion and our three systems disagree
ticket.body: The client's security team has the EDR console, our firewall logs, and a file listing from the host, and none of them agree on when the attacker started. EDR shows a PowerShell process at 02:02. The file listing shows the script written at 21:02 the previous evening. The firewall shows the outbound connection at 02:04. The client is asking which one is right and wants a timeline to the minute.
ticket.impact: The client's report is due tomorrow, and the account team cannot answer whether the intrusion happened before or after the patching window.

sections.h: Three systems, one question, three different answers
sections.body:
The EDR console showed `powershell.exe` starting at 02:02 on ws-0142. The file listing showed the script written at 21:02 the previous evening. The firewall showed the outbound connection at 02:04. One story, three clocks, and a client asking when the attacker got in.

The gap was the time zone: the EDR console shows UTC, the file listing showed local time at UTC+5:30, and the firewall logged UTC. Nobody lied and nobody converted anything.

**Digital forensics** is the work of answering what happened on a system from the traces it left behind. The first requirement is not a tool. Every timestamp carries its source and its zone, and every line says which artifact supports it. This lesson covers the three artifacts that answer most questions on this floor, and the order in which to take them.

sections.h: Volatility sets the order; importance does not
sections.body:
RFC 3227 sorts evidence by how long it survives: registers and cache, memory, network and kernel state, disk, remote logs, backups. The stack in the diagram is that list, most fragile at the top, and it is a capture order rather than a ranking of importance.

Memory is the layer people skip, and it answers what logs cannot: which process opened the connection, what its command line was, what was decrypted in that session, and often the key material itself. Power the host down and that row is gone, along with the process tree you could have read with one command.

Disk survives a reboot. It does not remember what was running, so it cannot tell you whether a file was opened by a user or by a script with the user's token.

Remote logs sit near the bottom of the list and are the fastest to collect, because you never touch the host: pull the firewall, the domain controller, and the EDR records from your desk first. If the host is wiped, those copies still describe the same minutes.

**Decision rule:** if the host is running and you cannot capture memory, do not reboot it to clear the problem. Ask for the capture first, and write down why if you are refused.

sections.h: The logon record names the account, the type, and the address
sections.body:
Event 4624 is a successful logon, and the `LogonType` field is what makes it readable. Type 2 is someone at the console, 3 is a network logon such as a share or a remote service, 5 is a service starting under its own account, 10 is Remote Desktop, and 11 is a cached credential on a domain-joined laptop that cannot see a domain controller.

```console
PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4624;
>>   StartTime='2026-11-18 01:45'; EndTime='2026-11-18 02:20'} |
>>   Select-Object TimeCreated,
>>     @{n='User';e={$_.Properties[5].Value}},
>>     @{n='Type';e={$_.Properties[8].Value}},
>>     @{n='From';e={$_.Properties[18].Value}} | Format-Table -AutoSize

TimeCreated             User        Type From
-----------             ----        ---- ----
11/18/2026 2:02:11 AM   a.okafor      10 10.30.7.21
11/18/2026 2:02:44 AM   a.okafor       3 10.30.7.21
11/18/2026 2:03:09 AM   svc-backup     5 -
```

A type 10 followed by a type 3 from the same address is somebody on Remote Desktop who then reached a share. At 02:02 that pattern is the finding. The type 5 line is a service starting, and it is only noise when the service name matches the account.

Read 4625 and 4624 as a pair, and quote timestamps as logged rather than as your console redraws them.

sections.h: The process tree and file times answer what the logon cannot
sections.body:
4624 says who got in. It does not say what ran. Event 4688 gives process creation and the parent process ID, but only when `Audit Process Creation` is enabled under Advanced Audit Policy, Detailed Tracking, and command line capture is turned on under Administrative Templates, System, Audit Process Creation. On a default build 4688 may be missing entirely. That is a fact for the report, not a dead end.

```console
PS C:\> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='powershell.exe'" |
>>   Select-Object ProcessId, ParentProcessId, CreationDate, CommandLine | Format-List

ProcessId       : 6120
ParentProcessId : 4488
CreationDate    : 11/18/2026 02:02:07
CommandLine     : powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoA
```

`ParentProcessId` 4488 resolves to `winword.exe`. A word processor that started PowerShell with an encoded command is the intrusion in one line. Record the encoded string and hand it to L2.

File times supply the when. NTFS keeps four timestamps on each file, and a second set in the file name entry, so an MFT parser can show a change that a file listing hides. On Linux, `stat` prints the three times with nanoseconds, and access time may not update at all unless the mount options say so.

**Decision rule:** when memory and disk disagree, memory tells you what ran and disk tells you what persisted. Report both, and name which source you trust for which claim.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
The deliverable is one table in UTC with a source column, not a paragraph of narrative:

```text
15:32 UTC   script written to C:\Users\a.okafor\AppData\Roaming\...  (disk, local 21:02 UTC+5:30)
02:02:07    powershell -enc started by winword.exe, PID 6120          (memory)
02:02:11    RDP logon a.okafor from 10.30.7.21, type 10                (Security 4624)
02:04:02    outbound TCP 443 to 203.0.113.44                          (firewall, UTC)
```

The 21:02 that started this ticket is the same event as 15:32 UTC. Saying so, once, ends the argument about which system is wrong.

**Closing note:** a timeline line is only worth writing when it names the artifact, the time in UTC, and what the artifact proves. Lines with no source are how a report gets pulled apart in a client meeting.

**Escalate to L2 IR or a forensic examiner** when the answer needs a disk image, when the host holds other users' data, or when the case may go to law enforcement. L1 reads logs and builds a timeline; L1 does not acquire evidence from a disk it has no written authorization to read.

diagram.title: Order of volatility, top to bottom
diagram.caption: The top rows vanish first and are the least likely to be captured. The bottom rows survive longest and take the longest to retrieve, which is why remote logs are pulled from a desk while memory is still available.

layers.name: Registers and cache
layers.fn: gone in seconds; almost never captured

data.footer: Capture downward. The rows you skip are the rows you cannot get back.

video.title: Episode 6: Order of Volatility
video.channel: SANS Digital Forensics and Incident Response
video.why: A SANS instructor walks the volatility order in under four minutes, which fixes the sequence in your head before you are standing at a powered-on host.

commands.what: Successful logons; Properties[8] is the logon type
Recent process creation with parent, when audit policy records it
Live process tree, if you get to the host before it is powered off
Linux access, modify, and change times with nanosecond precision
Logon and reboot history with full timestamps, on a Linux host
Whether the host clock was synchronized, which decides whether its timestamps can be trusted

pitfalls: Rebooting to "get a clean look". Memory is gone, the process tree is gone, and the disk now shows a shutdown event that will be read as the start of your investigation.
Mixing local and UTC times in one timeline. The first line the client checks will be the one where the two clocks disagree by five and a half hours.
Reading 4688 as proof of what ran on a host where process auditing was never enabled. An empty result means the policy was off, not that nothing happened.
takeaways: Volatility is the capture order, and memory is the layer that answers what was running.
Logon type 10 followed by type 3 from one address is remote access that reached a share.
A timeline line needs a UTC time, an artifact, and the claim that artifact supports.

drill.prompt: On your own machine, capture a five-line timeline: current UTC time, your time zone offset, the start time of your two oldest running processes, the last boot time, and one entry from the System event log. Convert everything to UTC and mark the source of each line.
checklist: Every line carries a source and a UTC time
The time zone offset is stated, and you can say whether the host clock is synchronized
At least one line came from an event log rather than from a command that reads live state
You can name one artifact you did not capture, and why

l7-4.title: Malware analysis without becoming the next victim
l7-4.subtitle: Safe handling, hashes, sandboxes and what a report must contain.
objectives: Preserve a suspicious file and produce its SHA256 with two tools that agree
Get a detection verdict from a hash lookup without uploading the client's file
Decide when a sample must not be run, and name the authorization a run would need
Write a six-field sample note that the malware desk can act on without asking you questions

ticket.subject: Opened the invoice attachment, now Excel opens a blank page
ticket.body: A finance user opened Remittance_8841.zip from an external sender at 09:14 and says a blank Excel window appeared for a second, then closed. The mail gateway now blocks the same attachment for the rest of the team, but the file is still on the user's desktop and a copy sits in quarantine. The laptop is on the office VLAN with a mapped drive to the finance share. Month-end processing starts at 14:00.
ticket.impact: One user offline since 09:20; the finance share is reachable from that laptop and month-end closes today.

diagram.title: From a suspicious file to a sample note
diagram.caption: Steps one to three never execute the file. Step four does, and only inside an authorized lab. Most L1 samples stop at step three.

data.footer: Detonation and upload are the steps that leave your control. Both need written approval.

video.title: Cybersecurity Tool for Beginner Security Analysts - VirusTotal
video.why: Walks the search-by-hash workflow on the VirusTotal site, so the panes you quote in a sample note are ones you have already seen on screen.

commands.what: The sample's identity for the ticket, the report and every later lookup
Same hash from a second tool; a mismatch means the copy changed
Publisher and signature status; NotSigned on an invoice is a finding
Detection stats for a hash without sending the file anywhere
Enables Windows Sandbox for an isolated run, admin rights required
URLs, registry paths and mutex names readable without executing anything

pitfalls: Double-clicking the sample on your own laptop to see what it does. Your session carries SSO tokens and mapped drives, so the second infection has more reach than the first.
Uploading the client's file to a public multi-scanner. Those services share submissions with the vendors behind their engines, which is a disclosure and needs written approval first.
Calling a sample clean because a sandbox showed nothing. Many families check for virtual hardware or sleep past the run window, so absence of behavior is not absence of capability.
takeaways: A hash is the sample's identity; get it from two tools before you write anything down.
A hash lookup gives a verdict without moving the file, and uploading it is a disclosure decision, not a technical one.
Detonation happens in a named lab under written authorization; outside that, "not detonated" is a complete answer.

drill.prompt: Pick any installer already in your Downloads folder. Hash it with Get-FileHash and certutil and confirm the two strings match, check Get-AuthenticodeSignature, look the SHA256 up on VirusTotal, then write the six-field sample note for it. Do not download a real sample and do not run the installer.
checklist: Both tools return the same SHA256 and you can say why a mismatch would matter
Signature status and publisher are recorded, or NotSigned is recorded as the finding
The lookup result includes the detection ratio and the first submission date
The note has all six fields and ends with what you did not do

sections.h: The user opened it once; do not open it twice
sections.body:
The ticket says the user opened an invoice attachment and a blank Excel window appeared. The file is still on the desktop, the laptop is on the office VLAN, and the obvious next step, double-clicking it to see what happens, is the mistake that turns one infected machine into two.

Your laptop is not a clean room. It holds a browser session with SSO tokens for the ticketing system, mapped drives to the file server, a VPN profile, and cached credentials for other systems. Malware that runs there inherits all of it. **Malware analysis at L1** is three actions in order: preserve the sample, identify it from data that does not execute, and leave the running of it to a lab.

Written authorization for that lab names the environment, the sample hash, the owner and the time window. Outside that boundary the answer in your note is "not detonated", and that is a complete answer.

sections.h: Hash the copy before you look at anything else
sections.body:
Take the sample out of circulation without destroying it. If the mail gateway quarantined the attachment, export it from the console, not from the user's desktop. If the desktop copy is the only one, put it on a labeled USB stick, record who copied it and when, and do not rename, open or edit it.

Then hash it. The SHA256 becomes the sample's identity for the rest of the incident: it goes in the ticket, in the report, and into every search you run.

```console
PS C:\Samples> Get-FileHash .\invoice_8841.zip -Algorithm SHA256

Algorithm  Hash                                                             Path
---------  ----                                                             ----
SHA256     9f2c41b7d0e8a36c5f19be72d4a8c0e3f61d5b28ca97f04e1d3b6a8c2f5e9071 C:\Samples\invoice_8841.zip

PS C:\Samples> Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\setup.exe

SignerCertificate Status     StatusMessage
----------------- ------     -------------
                  NotSigned  The file C:\Samples\setup.exe is not digitally signed.
```

`certutil -hashfile invoice_8841.zip SHA256` must return the same string. If it does not, the copy changed and the hash you are about to report is wrong. `NotSigned` on a document that claims to be an invoice is a finding by itself.

sections.h: The hash answers the first question without an upload
sections.body:
One request to a multi-scanner returns a detection ratio, a first-seen date and the names other engines use for the sample. VirusTotal indexes files by SHA256, so nothing leaves your network.

```console
$ curl -s -H "x-apikey: $VT_API_KEY" \
    "https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/files/9f2c41b7d0e8a36c5f19be72d4a8c0e3f61d5b28ca97f04e1d3b6a8c2f5e9071" \
  | jq '.data.attributes.last_analysis_stats'

{
  "harmless": 58,
  "type-unsupported": 4,
  "suspicious": 0,
  "confirmed-timeout": 0,
  "timeout": 0,
  "failure": 0,
  "malicious": 12,
  "undetected": 8
}
```

Twelve detections across 82 engines is enough to isolate the host and escalate. Zero detections proves nothing: fresh samples and targeted ones are often unknown, so read `first_submission_date` as well as the ratio.

Do not upload the file to get this answer. A public multi-scanner shares submissions with the security vendors that run its engines, so a client contract or an internal build leaves the estate the moment you click upload. Uploading needs written approval; a hash lookup does not.

**Decision rule:** an unknown hash on a file that arrived by mail means isolate the host and hand it up. Do not detonate it to learn more.

sections.h: It only runs in a lab, under a named authorization
sections.body:
Sometimes the question is behavioral: what does it do after it starts. That question belongs in a lab, and the lab is never a production machine.

An isolated environment has no shared folders, no clipboard, no mapped drives and no route to production. Windows Sandbox is the lightest option on a Windows 11 Pro or Enterprise workstation: enable it, then start a session from a `.wsb` file that sets `<Networking>Disable</Networking>` and mounts the sample folder as read-only. A virtual machine with a snapshot is stronger, because you keep the disk and the network capture afterward.

Neither is proof of anything. Many families check for virtual hardware, sleep for ten minutes, or wait for a mouse click. A note that says "no malicious behavior observed" without saying "the sample may detect a sandbox" misleads the next analyst, who will act on it.

**Decision rule:** if you cannot name the isolated environment and the person who authorized the run, you do not run the file.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
One ticket note and one indicator block. No sample attached, no link to a live sample store.

> Sample `invoice_8841.zip`, SHA256 `9f2c41b7...9071`, 41,208 bytes, ZIP containing `setup.exe`. Source: external mail to a finance user, subject "Remittance 8841", delivered 09:14. 12 of 82 engines malicious, first submitted 2025-11-16. Authenticode: NotSigned. Host 10.20.14.62 isolated at 10:05, awaiting the malware desk. Not detonated.

Write the indicators defanged so nobody clicks them inside the document:

```text
sha256  9f2c41b7d0e8a36c5f19be72d4a8c0e3f61d5b28ca97f04e1d3b6a8c2f5e9071
domain  cdn-update[.]example[.]invalid
ip      203.0.113[.]44:8443
```

Escalate to the malware desk when the hash is unknown, when the file is a document that asks for macros or a password, or when the host it ran on had administrative rights over other systems. A known hash, a contained host and a written note close at L1.

l7-5.title: Containment, eradication and recovery
l7-5.subtitle: Isolate the blast radius, remove the root cause, restore with proof.
objectives: Choose a containment action by disruption, and name who must approve it
Isolate a host and disable an account without destroying the evidence on the machine
Enumerate the persistence that survives a file deletion, and decide clean versus rebuild
Close a recovery with proof and a monitoring window instead of an announcement

ticket.subject: Account locks an hour after every password reset
ticket.body: A finance user reports a taskbar window they do not recognize and an account that locks within an hour of each reset. This is the third reset in two days. The same laptop was reimaged two weeks ago for a similar report and that ticket was closed as resolved. The laptop has a mapped drive to the payroll share.
ticket.impact: User blocked since 07:40; the payroll share is reachable from a device that has already been reimaged once for the same symptom.

diagram.title: One incident, from beacon to monitoring window
diagram.caption: Isolation comes 25 minutes after the alert and never powers the host off. The last event opens a monitoring window, so the incident is not closed yet.

video.title: Incident Response - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 4.8
video.why: Walks preparation, isolation and recovery as separate phases, which is the order the floor rushes when a host is still beaconing.

commands.what: Stops new logons; tokens already issued keep working until they expire
Invalidates issued sessions so a stolen cookie stops being useful
Cuts a confirmed command address while the host stays up for analysis
Services whose binaries live outside the system directory, which is where persistence hides
Scheduled tasks created by someone other than the OS or an installer
What Defender caught, when, and which process it was attached to

pitfalls: Reimaging to close the ticket. It removes the evidence of the initial access and the account abuse, and this ticket shows what happens when the cause was never removed.
Shutting the host down to contain it. Memory disappears with the power, and memory holds the running process, the injected code and any credentials still in use.
Disabling the account and stopping there. Existing sessions and refresh tokens stay valid, so the intruder keeps the access without needing the password.
takeaways: Containment is picked by disruption and approved by name; the cheapest action that stops the spread wins.
Eradication means nothing restarts the malware, and a host that held reusable credentials gets rebuilt, not cleaned.
Recovery ends with a monitoring window and a business owner's confirmation, not with a service answering on its port.

drill.prompt: On your own laptop or a lab VM, record a baseline of the three persistence locations: services outside C:\Windows, non-Microsoft scheduled tasks, and the HKCU and HKLM Run keys. Then write the five-row containment record you would fill in for an infected workstation, with the column headings and one example row per action type. Do not disable any account, block any address, or stop any service.
checklist: Baseline captured for all three persistence locations with timestamps
The record has time, action, by and proof columns before any row is filled
Every row names an approver, including the one you would not need approval for
The escalation criterion is written at the bottom, not remembered

sections.h: The laptop was reimaged and the answer left with it
sections.body:
The user reports a taskbar window they do not recognize and an account that locks an hour after every password reset. It is the third reset in two days. Two weeks ago the same laptop was reimaged for a similar report, and that ticket was closed as resolved.

The reimage is the problem. It removed the dropped file and, with it, every process, registry key, logon record and network connection that explained how the file arrived. The user is happy, the laptop is back, and the question the client will ask next week has no answer.

The opposite failure costs more. A host stays online for two days while three people discuss whether it can come off the network, and in those two days the same credentials reach the payroll share.

**Containment** stops the spread and keeps the evidence. **Eradication** removes what restarts the malware. **Recovery** returns the service and proves it is clean. They run in that order, and the clock starts at the first evidence, not at the first approval.

sections.h: Containment is a decision with an owner and a clock
sections.body:
Pick the smallest action that stops the spread, and pick it quickly. From least to most disruptive:

| Action | Stops | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| Block the command address | beaconing from every host | nothing, if the address is confirmed |
| Isolate the host in the EDR console | C2 and lateral movement | user offline, memory intact |
| Disable the account and revoke sessions | reuse of stolen tokens | user cannot work at all |
| Power the host off | everything, including evidence | memory is gone |

Powering off is last, not first. Memory holds the running process, the injected code and any credentials in flight, and none of it survives a shutdown. Isolate at the network layer and leave the machine running.

Isolating a workstation is usually L1 with the on-call engineer's nod. Taking a production server offline or disabling a service account is the client's decision in writing, with a named business owner. Find out who that person is before the incident, because at 02:00 nobody remembers.

**Decision rule:** if the host is still talking to a command address, isolate it now and capture memory after. If it went quiet an hour ago, capture memory first and isolate second.

sections.h: Eradication is about what restarts the malware
sections.body:
Deleting the dropped file removes one artifact. Whatever starts it again is still in place: a Run key, a scheduled task, a service, a startup folder, a browser extension, or an account created for the purpose.

```powershell
PS C:\> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.PathName -notlike 'C:\Windows\*' } |
>>   Select-Object Name, State, StartName, PathName | Format-Table -AutoSize

Name       State   StartName   PathName
----       -----   ---------   --------
WinUpdSvc  Running LocalSystem C:\ProgramData\WinUpd\svc.exe -k netsvc
```

A service whose binary sits in `C:\ProgramData` and runs as `LocalSystem` is persistence, not a Windows component. Cross-check it against `Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.Author -notmatch 'Microsoft' }` and the Run keys under `HKCU` and `HKLM`.

**Decision rule:** if the intruder had administrative rights, or the host held credentials that are valid elsewhere, clean is not enough. Rebuild from a known-good image and rotate every credential the host could touch. A cleaned host that held domain credentials leaves you with a clean machine inside a compromised domain.

sections.h: Recovery is proven, not announced
sections.body:
Recovery ends with evidence, not with an email saying the server is back.

1. Restore from a backup taken before the first evidence timestamp, not before the alert.
2. Change the credentials the host used, and confirm MFA on every account that logged on to it.
3. Scan the restored host with current signatures, and compare restored files against their known-good hashes.
4. Watch the host and its subnet for 48 to 72 hours for the same indicator or the same account activity.
5. Get the business owner to confirm the service does what it is supposed to do. A web server that answers on 443 but returns stale prices is not recovered.

If the same indicator appears inside that window, eradication failed. Do not repeat the same step on the same host. Isolate it again and escalate with the new evidence, because the second clean-and-release cycle is how a small incident becomes a long one.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Isolation needs its own record, separate from the ticket narrative. One row per action, with a time, a name and a proof:

| Time (UTC) | Action | By | Proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10:05 | Host 10.20.14.62 isolated | L1, ticket 4471 | EDR console entry |
| 10:20 | Account disabled, sessions revoked | L1 | `Get-ADUser` output |
| 11:15 | Command address blocked at edge | network on-call | firewall rule ID |

Then the closing note:

> Contained 10:05 UTC. Host network-isolated, not powered off, memory intact for the lab. Account disabled and sessions revoked. Command address blocked at host and edge. Not eradicated: one service and one scheduled task found, sample still under analysis. Business owner approved the isolation at 09:58.

Escalate to the IR lead when the blast radius reaches a domain controller, a hypervisor, a backup server or more than five hosts, and when the same indicator returns after eradication. One workstation with a confirmed indicator is L1 work.

l7-6.title: Root cause, documentation and the report a client reads
l7-6.subtitle: Write the timeline, the cause, the fix and the prevention — plainly.
objectives: Build a UTC timeline where every row names its source
Separate the proximate cause from the control that failed, and fix the control
Draft the six blocks of a client report in plain language with numbers instead of adjectives
Turn every prevention item into an action with an owner, a date and a proof

ticket.subject: Client compliance wants to know what the intruder read
ticket.body: The mailbox compromise from 18 November was closed the same day: password reset, forwarding rule removed, user re-enabled. The client's compliance manager has now asked for a written report covering which messages were exposed and for how long. There is no timeline in the ticket, and the analyst who handled it is on leave. The client wants the report by Friday.
ticket.impact: Client asked Monday; the account manager cannot answer the regulator question and the Friday deadline is two working days away.

diagram.title: From raw logs to a report the client signs off
diagram.caption: The cause is agreed before the prose starts, and nothing is sent before the IR lead has seen the scope statement.

data.footer: A report without a source column is a story. The client's auditor reads the footnotes first.

video.title: What is Root Cause Analysis (RCA)?
video.why: Explains RCA on a whiteboard as a repeatable method for finding a cause you can fix, which is the reasoning the client's follow-up question tests.

commands.what: The host's offset; a timeline built from local times across hosts is wrong by hours
Failed logons in a window, with the account and source address for the timeline
Shows whether the audit log was cleared, and when
Linux service events in ISO timestamps with the offset included
Files changed closest to the incident window, which is where a web shell shows up

pitfalls: Building the timeline in local time. Three hosts in three offsets produce a sequence that never happened and a cause that cannot be defended.
Naming the user as the root cause. It reads as blame, it cannot be fixed, and it hides the missing control the client is paying to close.
Sending the draft straight to the client. Scope statements and redaction are the IR lead's call, and a report released early cannot be recalled.
takeaways: First evidence and first alert are different times, and the exposure window is what the client asks about.
A root cause names a setting, a permission or a missing control, never a person or a job title.
A prevention item with no owner, date and proof is a wish, and the client's auditor treats it as one.

drill.prompt: Take the mailbox case in the ticket and build the report skeleton: six block headings, a timeline table with four rows taken from logs on your own machine (4624, 4625 or 1102), and a three-sentence summary. Do not use any real client data, and do not open anyone else's mailbox.
checklist: Every timeline row carries a UTC time and a named source
The summary is three sentences and contains no tool names
Each prevention item has an owner, a date and a proof column
The unknowns are written down as unknowns, with the log retention limit stated

sections.h: The ticket said resolved and the client asked what was read
sections.body:
Three weeks after a mailbox compromise, the client's compliance manager asks which messages the intruder read and whether anything about their customers was in them. The ticket is closed. The notes say password reset, forwarding rule removed, resolved. There is no timeline, no scope, and no record of the rule that forwarded mail outside the organization. Nobody can answer, so the client answers for us and assumes the worst.

A report is not paperwork that follows the fix. It is the part of the incident the client keeps. The fix disappears when the host is rebuilt; the report goes to auditors, insurers and, sometimes, the client's own customers.

Write it for a reader with one hour, no security background and a decision to make. That reader needs four answers on page one: what happened, when, what was affected, and what has changed.

sections.h: A timeline is a table, and every row has a source
sections.body:
Build the timeline before the prose: the prose is the timeline explained.

```console
PS C:\> Get-TimeZone | Select-Object Id, BaseUtcOffset

Id         BaseUtcOffset
--         -------------
UTC        00:00:00

PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime='2025-11-18T05:00:00'; EndTime='2025-11-18T07:00:00'} |
>>   Select-Object -First 2 TimeCreated, @{n='User';e={$_.Properties[5].Value}}, @{n='IP';e={$_.Properties[19].Value}}

TimeCreated          User        IP
-----------          ----        --
11/18/2025 6:04:11 AM svc-backup 10.20.4.31
11/18/2025 6:07:02 AM svc-backup 10.20.4.31
```

Every row carries a UTC time, what happened, and where the fact came from: an event ID and log, a firewall entry, an EDR alert, a mail header, or a call with the user. A row without a source is a rumor, and the auditor asks for the source on the first one.

Two distinctions change the document. **First evidence** is not **first alarm**: the failed logons started on 12 November, the alert fired on the 18th, and the report states both, because the exposure window is the number the client cares about. Absence is evidence too: "no successful network logon from 203.0.113.0/24 between 12 and 18 November" is a finding, provided you name the log and its retention.

sections.h: Root cause is the control that failed, not the person who clicked
sections.body:
"User opened a phishing email" is where the investigation stops, not where it ends. That user will open mail tomorrow, so the statement cannot be tested or closed.

Work down from the event. The message was delivered because that attachment type was not blocked at the gateway. It ran because macro execution from internet-marked files was allowed. It reached a file server because the account had write access to a share it did not need. Three causes, three fixes, none of them a person.

Call the action closest to the damage the **proximate cause**; it belongs in the timeline. Call the fixable one the **root cause**, and be honest when there are several. A report that names one cause for a four-step intrusion reads as tidy and gets challenged on the first follow-up.

**Decision rule:** if a cause line contains a job title or a person's name, rewrite it until it names a setting, a permission or a missing control.

sections.h: Write the summary for someone who gets one page
sections.body:
Structure beats eloquence. Six blocks in this order: summary, impact, timeline, cause, what we did, what changes. The summary is three sentences on what happened and what it means. Impact states systems, data, account count and duration with units: "one mailbox, 41 days, two external recipients".

Rules that keep it readable:

- Past tense, active voice, numbers not adjectives: "The attacker created three forwarding rules", not "a forwarding rule was observed to have been created".
- No tool names in the summary. `Get-WinEvent` belongs in the appendix; "the security log" belongs in the summary.
- Every finding gets a "so what" line. A mailbox rule matters because it forwarded mail outside the organization, not because rules are interesting.
- State the unknowns: "we cannot confirm whether the attachment was opened on the file server" is stronger than silence.

Redact other tenants: hostnames, address ranges, ticket numbers. Name the shared platform, not the neighbor.

sections.h: Prevention needs an owner, a date, and a test
sections.body:
"Improve monitoring" is not an action. An action has an owner, a date and a proof.

| Action | Owner | Due | Proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| Block external macro attachments | mail team | 2025-12-05 | rule ID and a test send |
| Remove finance group write access to the finance share | AD team | 2025-12-12 | `Get-Acl` before and after |
| Deny egress to 203.0.113.0/24 except via proxy | network | 2025-12-19 | rule ID and a blocked test |

Keep detective and preventive items apart. A new alert detects the next attempt; a removed permission prevents this one. Clients test what they can, which is why every row has a proof column.

Leave out anything the team cannot deliver. A report that commits to a 30-day project nobody has staffed becomes the reason the next report is not believed.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Two artifacts, one email.

The report: a PDF with the six blocks, a timeline table, an appendix of raw log lines, page numbers, and a version and date on page one. Name it `IR-2025-11-18-mailbox-compromise-v1.2.pdf`, not `report-final-final`.

The ticket note, which is what the account manager quotes to the client:

> Report v1.2 attached, 14 pages. Scope: one mailbox, one workstation, 12 to 18 November. Cause: a mailbox without MFA using a reused password, plus an inbox rule forwarding to an external address. Contained 18 November 10:05 UTC. Three preventive actions with owners and dates. Open: whether the file server attachment was opened; logs kept 30 days. Reviewed by the IR lead before release.

Escalate and do not send when the draft raises a possible regulatory notification, when the client's legal team has not seen the scope statement, or when the incident crossed into another client's environment. Reports leave through the IR lead, not the technician's mailbox.

l8-1.title: Python you actually need: values, loops, functions, files
l8-1.subtitle: Enough Python to read a log, count things and write a CSV.
objectives: Read a sixty-line Python script and name what each block does
Parse a real nginx access log into timestamp and status code with one regex
Count events per hour and write the result to a CSV that another team can open
Prove the count is right before you put the number in a ticket

ticket.subject: Need 5xx count per hour for yesterday, app team is blocked
ticket.body: The app team asked for 5xx responses per hour on 23 November so they can point at the window that broke. The log is on web01 at /var/log/nginx/access.log. A colleague ran grep -c for 500, got 1,204, and put it in the ticket. The app team says their dashboard shows 1,880 for the same day and wants to know which number is real. The log rotates at midnight, so part of yesterday is in access.log.1, and nobody on the shift knows how long this should take.
ticket.impact: One app team is holding a fix until it has a trustworthy hourly number; the afternoon shift is doing the count by hand between calls.

sections.h: The hourly count took a shift and still came back wrong
sections.body:
The app team asked for one thing: how many 5xx responses per hour on 23 November. The log is on `web01` at `/var/log/nginx/access.log`. A colleague ran `grep -c '" 500 ' access.log`, got 1,204, put it in the ticket and moved to the next call. Three hours later the app team replied that their dashboard showed 1,880 for the same day, and asked which number was real.

Neither was. `grep -c` counts one code and gives no hour. It reads one file, and nginx rotated at midnight, so most of the day was already in `access.log.1`. And 502, 503 and 504 come from the same failure as 500, so one pattern was never going to answer the question.

Splitting 40,000 lines by hour by hand is four hours of a shift. It cannot be re-run for the previous day, and nobody can check the result. This lesson is the smallest amount of Python that replaces it.

sections.h: Six constructs cover almost every floor script
sections.body:
You need to recognize these, not master the language.

- **Values** are strings (`"500"`), integers (`500`), or `None`. A line read from a file is always a string, so a status code stays text until you call `int()` on it.
- **A list** keeps order: `rows = ["500", "502", "200"]`.
- **A dict** maps a key to a value, which is how you count by hour: `counts["14"] = 486`.
- **A loop** runs the body once per line: `for line in fh:`.
- **A function** is a named block you call twice instead of pasting it twice.
- **`with open(path) as fh:`** closes the file even when the loop raises.

Two standard-library modules do the boring parts. `collections.Counter` is a dict that counts for you, and `csv.writer` handles quoting and commas inside a field. Both ship with Python, so a server with no internet access runs your script unchanged.

One habit matters more than the syntax: open the file with `encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"`. A log with one bad byte otherwise kills the run at line 31,000, and you spend the shift finding out why.

sections.h: Read every rotation, count per hour, write the CSV
sections.body:
The script reads every rotation, pulls the timestamp and status code out of each line with one regular expression, and counts codes per hour.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import csv, glob, re
from collections import Counter

LINE = re.compile(r'\[(?P<ts>[^\]]+)\] "(?P<req>[^"]*)" (?P<code>\d{3})')

counts = {}
for path in sorted(glob.glob("/var/log/nginx/access.log*")):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
        for line in fh:
            m = LINE.search(line)
            if not m:
                continue
            hour = m["ts"].split(":")[1] + ":00"
            counts.setdefault(hour, Counter())[m["code"]] += 1

with open("/tmp/5xx-by-hour.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    w = csv.writer(out)
    w.writerow(["hour", "requests", "errors_5xx"])
    for hour in sorted(counts):
        c = counts[hour]
        err = sum(n for code, n in c.items() if code.startswith("5"))
        w.writerow([hour, sum(c.values()), err])
```

Two lines carry the accuracy. `m["ts"].split(":")[1]` is the hour, because the nginx timestamp is `23/Nov/2025:14:02:11 +0000` and the hour sits between the first and second colon. The code comes from the field after the quoted request, which is where nginx puts it. The rest is counting.

```text
$ python3 count5xx.py
$ head -5 /tmp/5xx-by-hour.csv
hour,requests,errors_5xx
00:00,1841,3
01:00,1702,1
02:00,1655,0
03:00,1608,2
```

Before you send that file anywhere, add up the `requests` column and compare it with `wc -l` over the same two files. If the numbers differ, the regex skipped lines, and the CSV is wrong in a way that still looks tidy.

sections.h: Two runs is the line for writing the script
sections.body:
If the same count is asked for again this week, write the script. If you need one number once, `grep -c` is faster and the number goes straight into the ticket. What the script costs is not the writing; it is proving it is right.

Three checks take two minutes:

1. **Row count.** `wc -l /var/log/nginx/access.log*` against the sum of your totals.
2. **One hour by hand.** Pick 14:00, run `grep -c '23/Nov/2025:14:' /var/log/nginx/access.log`, compare with the CSV row.
3. **Timezone.** nginx writes `+0000`. The app team's dashboard may show local time. State which one your CSV uses.

The decision rule for the call: when the totals disagree, stop recounting and find the lines the parser skipped. `grep -vc '\[[^]]*:[0-9][0-9]:[0-9][0-9]:[0-9][0-9]' access.log` counts lines with no timestamp. On a healthy file that number is zero; anything else is a format you have not handled.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Four lines close this ticket: script path, output path, window with timezone, totals.

> Ran `/home/ops/count5xx.py` on web01 at 16:40 UTC over `access.log` and `access.log.1` for 23 Nov. Output `/tmp/5xx-by-hour.csv`, 24 rows, 41,208 requests, 1,884 5xx. Peak 14:00 with 486 errors, first non-zero row after the 13:40 deploy. Row total matches `wc -l` on both files.

Attach the file instead of pasting 24 rows into the ticket body, because the app team needs to sort it.

Escalate to the app team when the row total still differs from the line count after both files are included, or when the disputed window contains lines the regex cannot parse. Send the script path, both numbers, and three sample lines that did not parse. That is a log format change, and guessing at it is how a second wrong number reaches the customer.

diagram.title: From a repeated question to a checked CSV
diagram.caption: The script is the middle of this, not the whole of it. Step 5 is what turns a number into an answer you can defend.

steps.label: See the question twice
steps.detail: same count asked again this week

steps.label: Write the CSV
steps.detail: header row, one row per hour

data.footer: A count you cannot check is a number, not an answer.

video.title: Python Tutorial: File Objects - Reading and Writing to Files
video.why: Shows a file being iterated line by line, the open modes, and why the with block closes the handle, which the text can only name in one line.

commands.what: which interpreter your script actually runs under; the syntax here needs 3.6 or later
raw line count per file, the total your CSV has to add up to
one code, one file, no hour: the number that started the argument
the run and its first rows, one per hour
lines the regex cannot parse; zero on a healthy file

pitfalls: Counting only access.log and forgetting the rotation. Half the day is in access.log.1, and the missing hours are exactly the ones the app team is asking about.
Matching the code with a loose pattern like ' 5' . It also catches byte counts and URLs, and it inflates the error total in a way nobody notices until the numbers are quoted in a postmortem.
Sending the CSV without a line-count check. A skipped format produces plausible rows and a wrong total, and you will be the person who confirmed it.
takeaways: A line read from a file is a string; convert before you compare or add.
Counter plus csv.writer covers nearly every count-and-report task on the floor.
A number is only finished when it reconciles with an independent count.

drill.prompt: On your own machine, create a fake log of 200 lines in the nginx format with three status codes, then write a ten-line script that prints a count per code and the total, and save the same data as a CSV. Break one line on purpose and confirm your script skips it instead of crashing.
checklist: The script prints one count per code and a total, and the total equals 200 minus the broken line
The broken line is skipped, not silently counted as a 200
The CSV opens in a spreadsheet with two columns and a header row
You can name the line that reads the hour, and say what happens at 00:00

l8-2.title: Python for operations: requests, JSON, APIs and logging
l8-2.subtitle: Pull a ticket list, parse it, and leave a trail when it fails.
objectives: Call a REST endpoint with requests and decide from the status code whether to retry, stop or escalate
Recognize a JSON body that is not the shape your code expects, including an HTML login page
Page through a result set until it is exhausted and report the total
Write a log line for every step so the next person can reconstruct the run

ticket.subject: Morning ticket export is missing the reopened ones
ticket.body: Every morning someone exports open tickets from the service management tool and pastes them into a spreadsheet. Today the export had 96 rows and the queue badge said 137. The tool has an API and the previous L2 left a note with a token and the word page. Nobody knows whether the missing rows are reopened tickets, a pagination problem or a filter. Handover is at 09:00 and the shift lead wants a number that matches the queue before it starts.
ticket.impact: Two analysts are triaging from an incomplete list, and tickets reopened overnight have no owner.

sections.h: The export said 96 and the queue badge said 137
sections.body:
The morning handover starts with a list of open tickets. Someone opens the service management tool, sets the filter to Open, exports CSV and pastes it into a shared spreadsheet. The badge on the queue says 137. The sheet has 96 rows. Overnight reopened tickets are missing from it, and two analysts are already triaging from that sheet.

The tool has an API. The previous L2 left a note with a token and one word, `page`. That word is the ticket: the API returns 100 rows per request and expects a second request for the rest, and the export only ever read page one.

A copied export cannot be checked or repeated. A script can, and its log says what it asked for and what came back.

sections.h: A 200 says the request was understood, not that it worked
sections.body:
`raise_for_status()` turns the status class into a decision you can make on a call:

- **401** means the token is missing, expired or revoked. It will not fix itself.
- **403** means the token is valid but the account lacks the scope for this endpoint or this queue.
- **429** means you asked too often, and the `Retry-After` header says the wait in seconds.
- **5xx** means the server failed. Retry once, then escalate.
- **200** means the request was understood. Nothing more.

Three further checks decide whether a 200 is real data. The `Content-Type` header should be `application/json`; if it says `text/html`, the API sent a login page or a proxy error page, and `r.json()` raises `JSONDecodeError`, which is a `ValueError`. The body shape has to match your code: `{"data": [...]}` is not the same as a bare list, and reaching for a key that is not there returns nothing at all. The count has to agree with the `total` the API reports.

Then pagination. If the response carries a `Link` header with `rel="next"`, there is more data. If it does not, and you asked for 100 rows and received exactly 100, assume there is more data anyway.

sections.h: Fetch, page, and leave a trail when it breaks
sections.body:
The script keeps a session so the token header is set once, loops until a page comes back short, and writes each step to a log file.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, logging, os, time
import requests

logging.basicConfig(filename="/var/log/l1/tickets-pull.log",
                    level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
BASE = "https://sm.example.com/api/v1/tickets"

def fetch(session, params):
    for attempt in (1, 2):
        r = session.get(BASE, params=params, timeout=10)
        if r.status_code == 429 and attempt == 1:
            wait = int(r.headers.get("Retry-After", "30"))
            logging.warning("429, sleeping %ss", wait)
            time.sleep(wait)
            continue
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r
    raise RuntimeError("rate limited twice")

def main():
    s = requests.Session()
    s.headers.update({"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['SM_TOKEN']}",
                      "Accept": "application/json"})
    page, rows = 1, []
    while True:
        batch = fetch(s, {"state": "open", "page": page, "per_page": 100}).json()["data"]
        rows.extend(batch)
        logging.info("page %s: %s rows", page, len(batch))
        if len(batch) < 100:
            break
        page += 1
    logging.info("done, %s rows", len(rows))
    with open("/tmp/open-tickets.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
        json.dump(rows, out, indent=1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

`timeout=10` is not optional. Without it a stalled API holds the shift until TCP gives up, which can take minutes. The token comes from the environment, so a colleague can read the script without being handed a credential. Log the wait, never `s.headers`, because that log file is readable by the whole ops group.

```text
$ SM_TOKEN=$(cat ~/.sm_token) python3 pull_tickets.py
$ tail -4 /var/log/l1/tickets-pull.log
2026-03-11 08:41:02,113 INFO page 1: 100 rows
2026-03-11 08:41:03,240 WARNING 429, sleeping 30s
2026-03-11 08:41:34,905 INFO page 2: 37 rows
2026-03-11 08:41:35,010 INFO done, 137 rows
```

137 is the number on the badge. The 41 missing rows were on page two, and the count line is the only reason you can say so.

sections.h: Retry once, then escalate with the evidence
sections.body:
Decision rules for the call:

- **401 or 403:** stop. Retrying with the same token produces the same answer and can trip an account lockout. The token owner issues a new one, which is a two-minute request, not an investigation.
- **429:** read `Retry-After`, sleep that long, retry once. A second 429 means another job is pulling the same endpoint. Tell your lead, because two scripts competing will keep each other rate-limited all morning.
- **5xx:** retry once after 30 seconds. If it fails again, escalate with the timestamp, the endpoint and the `X-Request-Id` header, which the API team uses to find that request in its own logs.
- **200 with an empty list:** not an outage. Print the parameters you sent. A typo in `state=open`, or a token scoped to another team's queue, returns `[]` with a perfectly happy status code.

The rule that keeps the script honest: it must exit non-zero when it did not get the rows it came for. A script that prints a stack trace and exits 0 is ignored by cron and by the next person.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Hand over the log lines, the row count and the file.

> Pulled open tickets at 08:41 UTC with `/home/ops/pull_tickets.py`. 137 rows to `/tmp/open-tickets.json`, matches the queue badge. One 429 on page 2 with `Retry-After: 30`, retried once, succeeded. Log: `/var/log/l1/tickets-pull.log`.

Escalate to the API owner when the same non-2xx comes back twice, when the `total` the API reports disagrees with the rows you received after the last page, or when a 200 arrives with HTML. Send the endpoint, the query parameters, the status code, the `X-Request-Id` and the log lines. Never send the token, and never paste it into a ticket comment.

diagram.title: One morning pull, including the 429
diagram.caption: The retry is one attempt, not a loop. The log line is written before the retry, so the delay is explained even if the run dies there.

video.title: Master Python Requests In 15 Minutes. Call Any API
video.why: Shows the request and response objects live, including query parameters and reading a JSON body, which is the part the text describes but cannot demonstrate.

commands.what: which library version is installed; the 2.x API used here, no upgrade needed
the status code alone, before you write any Python
response headers: Content-Type, Retry-After, Link for the next page
pretty-print the saved body so the field names are readable
row count in the file you are about to hand over
every step of the last run, with timestamps

pitfalls: Retrying a 401 in a loop. The token is dead, the loop burns the retry budget and can lock the service account, and the fix is a new token from its owner.

Calling r.json() and assuming a dict. An HTML error page raises JSONDecodeError, and a bare list where you expected {"data": []} raises TypeError on the key lookup; both are diagnosed by reading Content-Type first.
Logging the Authorization header or the token in a URL. The log file outlives the incident and is readable by anyone in the ops group.
takeaways: Status class decides the action: 401 stop, 429 wait once, 5xx retry once then escalate, 200 with an empty list means check your parameters.
A 200 with text/html is a login page, not data, and the JSON parser is where you find out.
Pagination is the usual reason an export has fewer rows than the queue badge.

drill.prompt: Against a test API you are allowed to call, pull a list with page size 10 and log each page. Then force a failure by removing the token, and confirm the script stops with a non-zero exit code and one clear log line.
checklist: Two or more pages are logged with a row count each
The final log line states the total, and it equals the sum of the pages
With the token removed the script exits non-zero and logs the 401 once
No credential appears anywhere in the log file

l8-3.title: Bash: turning ten commands into one script
l8-3.subtitle: Arguments, loops, exit codes, and the safety line before rm.
objectives: Write a script with set -euo pipefail and explain what each part stops
Take an argument, refuse bad input with a usage message and exit code 2
Loop over a host list and return a non-zero exit code when any host fails
Add a dry run and a guard against an empty variable before any destructive command

ticket.from: Service Desk - NOC queue, night shift
ticket.subject: Disk check script reported all green and dc02 filled up
ticket.body: The nightly disk check is a script the previous admin wrote. Last night it printed done for all eighteen hosts and exited 0. At 06:00 the backup job failed because dc02 had been at 96 percent on /var since 02:00. The script reads /root/hosts.txt, loops over ssh, sends errors to /dev/null and ends with echo done, so it always looks successful. The night lead wants a failure to be visible and the host list passed as an argument instead of a hardcoded path.
ticket.impact: A datastore filled overnight; the morning backup failed and two VMs on that host are degraded while the storage team clears space.

sections.h: All green at 03:00 while /var was at 96 percent
sections.body:
The nightly script looked at eighteen hosts and reported nothing wrong. At 06:00 the backup failed because `dc02` had been at 96 percent on `/var` since 02:00. The script had checked that host and printed `done`, because of three lines:

```bash
while IFS= read -r host; do
  ssh "$host" 'df -P /var | tail -1' 2>/dev/null || true
done < /root/hosts.txt
echo done
```

`2>/dev/null` threw away the message that said the host was unreachable. `|| true` turned a failed check into a success. `echo done` as the last line made the exit code 0 no matter what happened, and cron has nothing to alert on.

A check that cannot fail is not a check. The fix is not a longer script. It is five lines at the top, a real exit code at the bottom, and a dry run in between.

sections.h: The first four lines decide what the rest may do
sections.body:
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'
```

`-e` stops at the first failing command instead of walking into the next one with broken state. `-u` makes an unset variable an error, which is the cheapest defense against `rm -rf "$DIR"/` with an empty `DIR`. `-o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail when any part fails, not only the last one; without it, `df | awk` hides a broken `df`. `IFS` narrows word splitting to newline and tab, so a path containing a space stays one item.

Then take the input as an argument and refuse to run without it:

```bash
[[ $# -ge 1 ]] || { printf 'usage: %s <hostlist> [--dry-run]\n' "${0##*/}" >&2; exit 2; }
LIST=$1
[[ -r $LIST ]] || { printf 'cannot read %s\n' "$LIST" >&2; exit 2; }
```

Exit code 2 for bad usage is a convention worth keeping, because it separates three outcomes: 0 means the check passed, 1 means the check found a problem, 2 means the script was called wrong. Cron, an alert rule and a person holding the ticket can all tell those apart, and they route to different places.

sections.h: Loop over the hosts and keep each result
sections.body:
The loop reads the file line by line instead of expanding it, so a comment can be skipped and a hostname is never split.

```bash
fail=0
ok=0
while IFS= read -r host; do
  [[ -z $host || $host == \#* ]] && continue
  if [[ ${2:-} == --dry-run ]]; then
    printf 'would check %s\n' "$host"
    continue
  fi
  if ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 "$host" \
       'df -P /var | awk "NR==2 && \$5+0 > 90 {exit 1}"'; then
    printf 'ok   %s\n' "$host"
    ok=$((ok + 1))
  else
    printf 'FAIL %s /var over 90%% or unreachable\n' "$host" >&2
    fail=$((fail + 1))
  fi
done < "$LIST"
printf 'checked %d, failed %d\n' "$((ok + fail))" "$fail" >&2
(( fail == 0 ))
```
