`BatchMode=yes` fails immediately instead of prompting for a password nobody is there to type at 03:00, and `ConnectTimeout=5` keeps one dead host from stalling the run. The `\$5` is escaped because that string is read by a second shell on the remote side; without the backslash the local shell substitutes it.

```text
$ bash -n check-var.sh && echo syntax ok
syntax ok
$ ./check-var.sh hosts.txt --dry-run
would check dc01
would check dc02
checked 0, failed 0
$ ./check-var.sh hosts.txt; echo "exit=$?"
ok   dc01
FAIL dc02 /var over 90% or unreachable
ok   dc03
checked 3, failed 1
exit=1
```

`FAIL` goes to stderr and the exit code is 1, so the person reading the output and the cron job that ran it see the same fact.

sections.h: The line before rm, and the authorization line
sections.body:
These scripts read state. The moment a script changes state, by restarting a service, moving a file or removing a directory, three rules apply.

1. **Refuse an empty target.** `${TARGET:?}` aborts when the variable is unset or empty. A script that runs `rm -rf "$TARGET"/*` with an empty `TARGET` runs `rm -rf /*`, and it does not ask twice.
2. **Default to a dry run.** Print every target and change nothing unless the caller passes `--yes`.
3. **Print what you will touch before you touch it.** Twelve hostnames take four seconds to read and are the only thing that catches a typo in the host file.

Anything that reaches hosts outside your own lab needs written authorization from the system owner, naming the hosts and the time window, before the first run. That is the same boundary as any other security automation: a loop reading `df` on hosts you own is inventory work, and the identical loop pointed at a range nobody signed for is not. Build and test against lab hosts, keep the host list in the repository with the script, and do not run a new script from a shift account without a second pair of eyes.

`shellcheck -S warning check-var.sh` catches most of this class of bug. SC2086 fires on an unquoted variable, SC2181 on checking `$?` instead of testing the command directly. Run it before you ask anyone else to run your script.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Hand over the script, the host list and the last run.

> `check-var.sh` at `/home/ops/bin/`, takes the host list as `$1`, supports `--dry-run`. Last run 03:10 UTC: 18 hosts checked, `dc02` failed at 96 percent on /var, exit 1. Cron: `10 3 * * * /home/ops/bin/check-var.sh /home/ops/hosts.txt >> /var/log/check-var.log 2>&1`.

Escalate to the storage team when the same host fails twice in one night, because that is growth rather than a one-off. Escalate to the platform team when a host reports `FAIL` because `ssh` could not authenticate, since a `BatchMode` failure is a key problem and not a disk problem. Sending those two to the wrong team is how a filled datastore waits another day.

diagram.title: Rebuilding a check so it can fail
diagram.caption: Every step exists because the old script skipped it. Step 6 is the one that made the difference at 03:00.

data.footer: A check that exits 0 cannot fail, so nobody is ever told.

video.title: you need to learn BASH Scripting RIGHT NOW!! // EP 1
video.why: Writes and runs a first script with a variable, a conditional and a positional argument, which is the same shape as the disk check and faster to watch than to type.

commands.what: syntax check with nothing executed, the first thing to run after an edit
static check for unquoted variables (SC2086) and misuse of $? (SC2181)
the single check the loop wraps, and proof that key auth works
capacity of /var as one field, readable by the script
prints the target list without touching a host
the exit code cron and the alert rule will read: 0 pass, 1 failed check, 2 bad usage

pitfalls: Ending the script with echo or an unconditional exit 0. The exit code is the only signal cron has, and this makes every run look successful.
Redirecting ssh errors to /dev/null. A host that is down and a host with a full disk print different messages, and you deleted the one that tells them apart.
Running rm -rf with a variable that may be empty. There is no confirmation prompt and no undo; ${VAR:?} costs nothing and prevents the whole class.
takeaways: set -euo pipefail turns silent failures into stops, and pipefail is the part people forget.
Exit 0 is a claim the check passed; a script that always exits 0 makes no claim at all.
Anything that changes state needs a dry run, a printed target list, and an authorization line if it leaves your lab.

drill.prompt: Write a script that takes a directory as its only argument, counts files larger than 1 MB in it, and exits 1 if there are none. Then add a dry-run flag that lists the matching files without counting, and run shellcheck on the result.
checklist: Running it with no argument prints usage and exits 2
An empty directory gives exit 1, not exit 0
The dry run lists paths and does not print a count
shellcheck reports no warnings, or you can explain the ones left

l8-4.title: PowerShell automation: objects, filters and scheduled checks
l8-4.subtitle: One pipeline that answers 'which services are stopped and should not be'.
objectives: Read a cmdlet result as objects and list its properties with Get-Member before filtering
Filter services by StartMode and State instead of reading a console by eye
Run one check across a server list with Invoke-Command and export a CSV
Register a scheduled task as SYSTEM and prove it ran from LastTaskResult

ticket.subject: Printers down again on the file server, second time this week
ticket.body: Users on the second floor have not been able to print since about 10:00. The spooler service on fs01 was stopped when we looked and someone started it, but this is the second time in four days. The morning service check was logged as clean at 06:40. No change was made to the server that we know of.
ticket.impact: About 60 users on one floor are blocked, and the shift has no way to tell whether another server has the same fault right now.

sections.h: Spooler was down for four hours and the check said clean
sections.body:
Every morning the Windows queue runs the same check on 34 servers: open a remote console, type `Get-Service`, read down the Status column, and write "clean" in the shift log. On 14 November nine minutes of reading produced a clean log. The print spooler on fs01 had stopped at 06:12 and a user started it at 10:05. In between, about 60 people sent print jobs into a queue that did nothing.

The engineer was not careless. The filter was a human eyeball reading 34 console windows, and an eyeball that misses one line is doing what an eyeball does. The same check written as a pipeline does not get tired, and it leaves a file that says what it saw. That is the whole of L1 PowerShell automation: **get objects, filter them, export the result**.

sections.h: Get-Service returns objects, which is why you stop parsing text
Filter on StartMode, because "stopped" alone is noise
sections.body:
A stopped service is normal: dozens are Manual and start when needed. The finding is a service set to start at boot that is not running.

`Get-Service` exposes `StartType` only on Windows Server 2016 and later. `Get-CimInstance Win32_Service` exposes `StartMode` as `Auto`, `Manual` or `Disabled` on every supported version, so use that one:

```console
PS C:\> Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service |
>>   Where-Object { $_.StartMode -eq 'Auto' -and $_.State -eq 'Stopped' } |
>>   Select-Object Name, DisplayName, State, StartMode

Name     DisplayName                            State   StartMode
----     -----------                            -----   ---------
MSDTC    Distributed Transaction Coordinator    Stopped Auto
Spooler  Print Spooler                          Stopped Auto
WinRM    Windows Remote Management (WS-Manag... Stopped Auto
```

`$_` is the current object inside the block, `-eq` compares, and `Where-Object` keeps the objects that pass. Prefer `-eq 'Stopped'` over `-ne 'Running'`, because the second one also catches a service in transition, and a service coming up is not a finding.

Decision rule: Automatic and stopped is a finding, Manual and stopped is not. If the same Automatic service is stopped on several hosts at once, suspect a shared dependency before you restart anything by hand.

sections.h: Run it once across every server with Invoke-Command
sections.body:
`Invoke-Command` runs a block on remote hosts over WinRM (TCP 5985, or 5986 for HTTPS) and returns rows with a `PSComputerName` property added, which is how you know which host each finding came from:

```console
PS C:\> Invoke-Command -ComputerName (Get-Content C:\ops\servers.txt) -ScriptBlock {
>>   Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
>>     Where-Object { $_.StartMode -eq 'Auto' -and $_.State -eq 'Stopped' } |
>>     Select-Object Name, State, StartMode
>> } -ErrorAction Continue |
>>   Select-Object PSComputerName, Name, State, StartMode |
>>   Export-Csv C:\ops\stopped-services.csv -NoTypeInformation

PS C:\> Import-Csv C:\ops\stopped-services.csv | Format-Table

PSComputerName Name    State   StartMode
-------------- ----    -----   --------
dc02           W32Time Stopped Auto
fs01           Spooler Stopped Auto
```

If a host answers "WinRM cannot complete the operation", that host is not a clean row. Fix the connection, enable WinRM on the target with change approval, or mark the host unchecked. An unreachable server is not a healthy server, and `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` hides exactly that difference.

sections.h: Schedule it and keep the proof it ran
sections.body:
`Export-Csv` overwrites the file, so there are never two header rows, and one appended line records every run, including runs that found nothing:

```powershell
$servers = Get-Content 'C:\ops\servers.txt'
$rows = Invoke-Command -ComputerName $servers -ScriptBlock {
    Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
      Where-Object { $_.StartMode -eq 'Auto' -and $_.State -eq 'Stopped' } |
      Select-Object Name, State, StartMode
} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue -ErrorVariable connErr |
  Select-Object PSComputerName, Name, State, StartMode
$rows | Export-Csv 'C:\ops\stopped-services.csv' -NoTypeInformation
"$(Get-Date -Format s) rows=$($rows.Count) unreachable=$($connErr.Count)" |
  Add-Content 'C:\ops\check.log'
```

`-ErrorVariable` is what makes `SilentlyContinue` safe here: connection failures are not printed, but they are counted in the log line, so an unreachable host never disappears.

Register it once as SYSTEM, so a logged-off console does not matter:

```powershell
$action  = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'powershell.exe' -Argument '-NoProfile -File C:\ops\Check-Services.ps1'
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At 6:00AM
$principal = New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId 'NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM' -LogonType ServiceAccount -RunLevel Highest
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Ops-CheckServices' -Action $action -Trigger $trigger -Principal $principal -Settings (New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -StartWhenAvailable)
```

`LastTaskResult` is the field that matters, and it reports the task, not the servers:

```console
PS C:\> Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName 'Ops-CheckServices' | Select-Object LastRunTime, LastTaskResult

LastRunTime           LastTaskResult
-----------           -------------
11/24/2025 6:00:03 AM             0
```

Decision rule: result 0 with rows means the finding is real. Result 0 with an empty file means nothing matched. Any nonzero result means you say "the check did not run", never "the servers are fine".

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Your note is six lines: task name, run time, `LastTaskResult`, CSV path, row count, and the rows with host and service.

Closing note for this morning: "Ops-CheckServices ran 06:00, result 0, two rows in C:\ops\stopped-services.csv: fs01 Spooler (Auto/Stopped), dc02 W32Time (Auto/Stopped). Spooler restarted; W32Time left for investigation because it is a domain controller."

Escalation criterion: escalate to L2 when an Automatic service is stopped on a domain controller, a database host, or more than two hosts at once, or when it stops again within 24 hours of a restart. Restarting once is L1 work. A service that stops twice is a fault nobody has found yet.

diagram.title: From one console to a check that proves it ran
diagram.caption: Six steps, and the last one is the one that gets skipped. A check that cannot show LastTaskResult cannot be trusted on a morning call.

data.footer: A check that never proves it ran is a check nobody can trust.

video.title: Working with the PowerShell Pipeline
video.why: From the Where-Object chapter onward it filters live objects on screen, which is the part of the pipeline that reads badly in prose.

commands.cmd: Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.StartMode -eq 'Auto' -and $_.State -eq 'Stopped' } | Select-Object Name, State, StartMode
commands.what: the actual finding: automatic services that are not running
one query across the estate, with PSComputerName on every row
proof the scheduled check ran, and whether it finished
when the service manager recorded the stop, if the log still holds it

pitfalls: Filtering on Status -eq 'Stopped' alone: a healthy server has dozens of stopped Manual services, so the one real finding is buried and the shift stops reading the file.
Piping to Format-Table before Export-Csv: Format-Table hands on display objects, so the CSV holds formatting characters instead of properties.
Registering the task for the logged-on user without -RunLevel Highest: it silently never runs at 06:00 on a weekend, and the empty CSV reads as a clean estate.
takeaways: PowerShell returns objects; Get-Member is how you find the property worth filtering on.
Automatic and stopped is a finding, Manual and stopped is normal.
LastTaskResult tells you whether the check ran; the CSV tells you what it found. Never confuse the two.

drill.prompt: On your own Windows machine or lab VM, run the Win32_Service filter and export it to C:\ops\drill.csv. Then register a one-time task that runs the same script three minutes from now as your own account, check Get-ScheduledTaskInfo, and delete the task.
checklist: The Where-Object query returns only Automatic services that are Stopped
The CSV opens with one header row and one row per finding
Get-ScheduledTaskInfo shows a LastRunTime inside the last 15 minutes and LastTaskResult 0
You can state what a nonzero LastTaskResult would have meant for the call

l8-5.title: Logs, regex and indicators: re, pandas, hashlib
l8-5.subtitle: Extract the fields, count the sources, hash the file.
objectives: Pull named fields out of a log line with one compiled regular expression
Count events per source with Counter, then answer a two-key question with pandas
Hash an evidence file in chunks and cross-check the digest with a second tool
Decide which indicators are durable enough to hand to a blocklist

ticket.subject: Hundreds of failed logins on the web server overnight
ticket.body: The overnight report shows a large number of failed SSH logins on web01. We ran grep -c on auth.log and got 2,141 lines. A second host reported the same pattern this morning. We do not know whether it is one source or many, or whether any login succeeded.
ticket.impact: Two internet-facing hosts are being tried, and nobody can say whether the attempts are one actor or a hundred.

sections.h: Twelve thousand lines and nobody could say how many sources
sections.body:
At 09:20 a report arrived: web01 had hundreds of failed SSH logins overnight. The analyst ran `grep -c 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log`, got 2,141, wrote "brute force, single host" in the ticket, and closed it. At 11:05 a second host reported the same thing, then a third. The question nobody could answer was how many source addresses were involved and whether the set was the same on all three hosts.

`grep` answers "does this string appear". The question on the call was "group by source, count per source, across three files". That is a parsing job in three parts: pull the fields out, count them, and hash the file so the next person can prove they read the same bytes.

sections.h: Name the fields in the pattern, not the parentheses
sections.body:
Sample lines from `auth.log` look like this. The third one is a different message shape, which matters:

```text
2025-11-24T03:04:11.8821 sshd[41213]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.44 port 51422 ssh2
2025-11-24T03:04:12.1140 sshd[41213]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.44 port 51430 ssh2
2025-11-24T03:04:19.0032 sshd[41219]: Invalid user test from 198.51.100.23
```

One compiled pattern with **named groups** — `(?P<ip>...)` names the field, so you never count parentheses again:

```python
import re, sys, csv
from collections import Counter

PATTERN = re.compile(
    r'^(?P<ts>\S+) sshd\[(?P<pid>\d+)\]: '
    r'Failed password for (?:invalid user )?(?P<user>\S+) '
    r'from (?P<ip>\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3}) port (?P<port>\d+)'
)

fails, unmatched = Counter(), 0
with open(sys.argv[1], encoding='utf-8', errors='replace') as fh, \
     open('/evidence/fails.csv', 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as out:
    rows = csv.writer(out)
    for line in fh:
        m = PATTERN.match(line)
        if not m:
            unmatched += 1
            continue
        g = m.groupdict()
        fails[g['ip']] += 1
        rows.writerow([g['ts'], g['pid'], g['user'], g['ip'], g['port']])

for ip, n in fails.most_common(5):
    print(f'{ip:<16} {n}')
print('unmatched lines:', unmatched)
```

```console
$ python3 count_fails.py /evidence/auth.log
203.0.113.44     812
198.51.100.23    604
192.0.2.77       488
unmatched lines: 3
```

`(?:...)` is a non-capturing group, used for the optional `invalid user` prefix so it does not become a field. `match` anchors at the start of the line, so a line without a timestamp is counted as unmatched instead of half-parsed. Report that number: it tells the next analyst what was left out.

sections.h: Count with Counter, then ask a second question with pandas
sections.body:
`Counter` answers "how many per address". The next call asks "which account was tried", and that is a two-key group: source plus user. Write the rows to a CSV from the same loop, then let pandas do the grouping:

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('/evidence/fails.csv', header=None, names=['ts', 'pid', 'user', 'ip', 'port'])
print(df.groupby(['ip', 'user']).size().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5))
print(df['ip'].nunique(), 'sources between', df['ts'].min(), 'and', df['ts'].max())
```

```console
ip            user
203.0.113.44  root     402
203.0.113.44  admin    288
203.0.113.44  oracle   122
198.51.100.23 root     377
198.51.100.23 test     227
dtype: int64
4 sources between 2025-11-24T03:04:11.8821 and 2025-11-24T04:52:38.5560
```

`header=None, names=[...]` is not optional. The CSV has no header row, and without those arguments pandas takes the first event as the column names, so every count is short by one and nobody notices.

Decision rule: if the count per source is over 50 and spread across more than two sources, it is a distributed attempt and the ticket is not "one noisy client". If one source tried one account three times, it is a typo and it does not need a ticket.

sections.h: Hash the file before anyone believes the copy
sections.body:
An evidence file that moved between three hosts is not evidence until two people can hash it and get the same answer. `hashlib` reads in chunks, so a 4 GB log does not have to fit in memory:

```python
import hashlib, sys
h = hashlib.sha256()
with open(sys.argv[1], 'rb') as fh:
    for chunk in iter(lambda: fh.read(1024 * 1024), b''):
        h.update(chunk)
print(h.hexdigest(), sys.argv[1])
```

```console
$ python3 sha_file.py /evidence/auth.log
c29f78d2426f73f8d282049240e9eac066f27aca9fcc4cb5fa84aa3d7f3e2655  /evidence/auth.log
$ sha256sum /evidence/auth.log
c29f78d2426f73f8d282049240e9eac066f27aca9fcc4cb5fa84aa3d7f3e2655  /evidence/auth.log
```

Two tools, one digest. On Windows the cross-check is `Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 .\auth.log`. A hash proves the bytes are identical to another copy; it proves nothing about whether the content is malicious, so never write "hash confirms malware" in a ticket.

sections.h: Indicators are durable or they are decoration
sections.body:
An **indicator** is a value you can search for elsewhere: a file hash, a domain, a URI path, an IP address. Hash is the strongest, because it changes when one byte changes. An IP address is the weakest: hosting ranges, VPN exits and cloud addresses are reassigned constantly, and one is probably your own NAT egress.

Defang what you paste into a ticket — `203.0.113[.]44` — and deduplicate first. A list of 400 addresses that is really 60 repeated four times wastes an hour.

This work happens in the lab: sample logs on your own machine, no scanning of networks you do not own, and no live malware. Written authorization from the system owner is required before you collect logs from a host you do not administer or search for an indicator anywhere outside the lab.

Decision rule: a hash that matches the vendor's published value is a fact you can escalate on. An IP address that appears in the log is a fact about the log only. Check whether it is a scanner you pay for, a partner's egress, or your own address before it goes anywhere near a blocklist.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
One page: file path and SHA-256, time range, pattern used, counts per source, unmatched line count, and what you did not parse.

Closing note: "auth.log from web01, SHA-256 c29f78d2…2655, 03:04 to 04:52, 2,141 failed passwords from 4 sources. Top: 203.0.113.44 with 812 attempts across root, admin and oracle. Three lines did not match the pattern. No successful logon for those accounts in the window."

Escalation criterion: escalate when a source address has both failed and successful authentications for the same account, or when the same source appears on hosts in different subnets inside the window. One noisy client is not an incident. The same client succeeding is.

diagram.title: From a log file to a number you can defend
diagram.caption: Five steps. The unmatched count and the hash are what turn a count into evidence someone else can reproduce.

steps.label: Extract named fields
steps.detail: ts, user, ip from one pattern

data.footer: Unmatched lines are a number you report, not a detail you hide.

commands.what: the count that opened the ticket, and proof it is not the answer
extract and group by source address in one pass
hash the evidence before and after you copy it

commands.cmd: awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="from") print $(i+1)}' /var/log/auth.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
commands.what: the shell version of the same question, when Python is not installed

pitfalls: A greedy `.*` between fields: on a line with no "from" it swallows the rest of the record and the user field becomes a sentence.
Reading a 900 MB log with read() and splitlines(): the jump host runs out of memory halfway and leaves a partial CSV that looks complete.
pd.read_csv without header=None on a file your own script wrote: the first event becomes the column names and every count is short by one.
takeaways: One compiled pattern with named groups beats four greps and a spreadsheet.
The unmatched line count is part of the answer, not an embarrassment.
A hash proves two files are identical; it says nothing about whether either one is malicious.

checklist: The pattern has at least three named groups and the script prints them by name
The output shows a count per source address and an unmatched line count
The two digests are identical and the full 64 characters are recorded
The note names the time range covered by the file

l8-6.title: Detection, alerting and playbooks: the four capstones
l8-6.subtitle: YARA, alert routing, a written playbook, and the projects that prove it.
objectives: Write a YARA rule whose condition limits noise instead of matching a filename
Route an alert to an owned queue by severity with a dedupe window
Write a playbook whose first actions are commands, not adjectives
Tell a refused TCP connection from a filtered one on a monitoring call

ticket.subject: Suspicious binary found in Temp, escalated with no next step
ticket.body: An alert fired at 02:14 for a binary written to C:\Windows\Temp on fs01. The analyst on shift opened the path, found the file had already been removed, and escalated at 02:31 with 'possible malware, please advise'. No hash was recorded and no other host was checked. The queue has no written steps for this alert type.
ticket.impact: A possible execution on a file server is unresolved after six hours, and the same alert will be handled differently by whoever is on shift tonight.

sections.h: The alert fired at 02:14 and the queue had no next step
sections.body:
An alert came in for a binary written to `C:\Windows\Temp` on fs01. The analyst on shift opened the path, found the file gone, searched the file name on the web, and escalated at 02:31 with "possible malware, please advise". L2 spent an hour redoing work L1 could have done: hashing what was left, running the rules the team owned, and checking other hosts for the same hash.

None of that hour was analysis. It was the cost of an alert with no written next step and no owner. **Detection** is the rule that fires. **Response** is the ordered set of decisions that starts the moment it does. A detection without a playbook produces a ticket, not an outcome.

sections.h: A YARA rule is strings plus a condition that limits noise
sections.body:
**YARA** matches patterns in files. A rule has three blocks: `meta` (who wrote it, why), `strings` (what to look for), and `condition` (how many strings must appear, in what relation). The condition controls false positives.

```yara
rule win_psexec_service_binary
{
    meta:
        author = "l1-academy"
        description = "PsExec service binary names in any path"
        date = "2025-11-24"
    strings:
        $svc = "PSEXESVC" ascii wide
        $cli = "psexec" nocase ascii
    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and 2 of them
}
```

`uint16(0) == 0x5A4D` requires the file to start with `MZ`, so a text file containing the word is not a hit. `ascii wide` matches both encodings; `nocase` ignores case.

```console
$ yara -r -w rules/win_psexec_service_binary.yar /evidence/fs01/
win_psexec_service_binary /evidence/fs01/Windows/Temp/PSEXESVC.exe
win_psexec_service_binary /evidence/fs01/Tools/PSTools/psexec.exe
```

Two hits, one ticket worth writing. PsExec is a legitimate admin tool, so the rule found a tool, not an intruder. Path and parent process decide, which is why the playbook asks for both.

YARA is lab work without written authorization: scan copies in an isolated analysis VM, never a live share without the owner's approval, and never move a sample to a production host.

sections.h: Route by rule and severity, not by name
sections.body:
An alert addressed to a person waits for that person. One addressed to a queue with an owner and a backup gets worked by the next shift.

| Priority | Condition | Queue | Pages |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | confirmed execution, hash on the blocklist | IR on-call | yes, 24x7 |
| P2 | rule hit on a server, path outside Tools | Security queue | no |
| P3 | known admin tool, hash matches vendor build | Security queue, weekly | no |

**Dedupe** on rule, host and hash for 24 hours. Without it, a binary rescanned every hour becomes 24 tickets and the queue learns to ignore the rule name. An alert without a hash cannot be deduplicated or searched, which is why the 02:14 ticket stalled.

sections.h: A playbook is five decisions written before the call
sections.body:
A playbook is not a paragraph of advice. It is five decisions with an owner:

1. **Trigger** — the exact alert name and severity that starts it.
2. **Scope** — which hosts, accounts and time window are in play.
3. **First 15 minutes** — five numbered actions, each with a command.
4. **Containment** — the options, and who must approve each one.
5. **Closure and escalation** — the evidence that closes it, and the line that escalates it.

Step 3 is where most drafts fail: they say "investigate the binary". Write the commands — hash the file, search the hash across the fleet, list the parent, check scheduled tasks in the window. A playbook a tired analyst can follow at 03:00 without calling anyone is finished; one that needs interpretation is a wish.

The module ends with four capstones that each produce an artifact: the log parser and report, the scheduled Windows check with its CSV, a YARA rule with a written hunt result, and the playbook with a dated drill. A playbook nobody has walked through is a document, not a control.

sections.h: Probe the thing before you believe the graph
sections.body:
Many "host down" escalations at L1 are a monitoring gap, not an outage. A twenty-line probe tells you which one you have, and it runs from the jump host:

```python
import socket
for host, port in [('dc01', 445), ('fs01', 445), ('web01', 443), ('db01', 1433)]:
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=3):
            print(f'{host}:{port}  open')
    except socket.timeout:
        print(f'{host}:{port}  timeout')
    except OSError as e:
        print(f'{host}:{port}  error {e.errno}')
```

```console
$ python3 probe.py
dc01:445  open
fs01:445  open
web01:443  timeout
db01:1433  error 111
```

`error 111` is `ECONNREFUSED` on Linux (`10061` on Windows): the host answered TCP and nothing is listening on that port. `timeout` means the packets went nowhere — a firewall, a routing problem, or a dead host. Three different tickets, twelve seconds.

Decision rule: refused means the host is alive and the service is not. Timeout means you cannot tell, so the next check is `ping` and then the firewall rule, not a service restart.

sections.h: What you hand over
sections.body:
Two notes, because a detection and a response are handed over differently.

Detection note: rule name, the noise-limiting condition, where it ran, how many files matched, and the paths.

Response note: alert time, host, path, hash, what you ran, what you ruled out, and the escalation line. Closing note: "fs01 PSEXESVC.exe in Windows/Temp at 02:14, hash 221c2a27…c9eb, file removed before collection. Rule hit twice on the image, second hit is the admin copy in Tools/PSTools. No scheduled task created in the window. Playbook step 3 incomplete at 02:31; playbook updated."

Escalation criterion: escalate when the hash appears on a host outside the admin tool path and a scheduled task or service was created within the same hour. That is execution with persistence, and it is not an L1 close.

diagram.title: Where one detection becomes a ticket
diagram.caption: The P1 path skips the queue on purpose. Everything else needs an owner, a dedupe window and a hash before it can be worked.

video.title: Malware Analysis Bootcamp - Creating YARA Rules
video.why: Builds a rule from the metadata and strings blocks into the condition against a sample, which is the part of YARA that reads badly on paper.

commands.what: run the team rule set against a collected image, recursively
show which strings matched, which is what the ticket needs
hash the sample on Windows before it leaves the host
prove the service is listening before you blame the alert

pitfalls: A rule that matches the tool name only: PsExec is installed across the estate by the admin team, the rule fires weekly, someone mutes it, and the one real Temp execution goes with it.
Routing an alert to a named engineer: on the night that engineer is on leave the ticket sits unassigned until morning.
A playbook that says 'investigate the binary': no command, no path, no owner, so the next analyst copies the previous ticket's wording and the queue learns nothing.
takeaways: The YARA condition is the detection; the strings are only the search terms.
An alert needs a rule name, a host and a hash before it can be routed, deduplicated or escalated.
Refused means the service is down; timeout means you do not know yet. They are different tickets.

drill.prompt: In an isolated lab VM with no network, write one YARA rule for a benign file you choose, include a condition that limits matches, and run yara -r against a folder. Write the four-line detection note for the result, then list the three playbook steps you would need at 03:00. Do not scan any host you do not own.
checklist: The rule has meta, strings and a condition that is not a bare string list
The scan output names the rule and the matching file path
The detection note records the rule name, the condition, the match count and the path
Three playbook steps are written as commands with an owner

questions.q: A packet leaves a laptop and reaches a web server in another organization. In the TCP/IP model, which layer decides the next hop toward the destination network?
options: Application
Transport
Internet
Link
questions.explain: The Internet layer holds the destination IP address and the routing decision. Transport is the tempting answer, but it only separates conversations by port; it never chooses a path.

questions.q: An analyst reports that the link light is off and the cable is unplugged from the wall. Which OSI layer does that fault belong to?
options: Layer 1, Physical
Layer 2, Data Link
Layer 3, Network
Layer 4, Transport
questions.explain: Cabling, link lights and signaling are Layer 1. Layer 2 becomes the right answer only after the link is up and the question is about MAC addresses or VLAN tags.

questions.q: A host is being configured on the subnet 10.20.10.128/25. Which address may be assigned to that host?
questions.explain: A /25 covers .128 to .255, so .128 is the network address and .255 is broadcast, leaving .129 as the first usable address. .127 is the broadcast of the 10.20.10.0/25 half, one step to the left.

questions.q: Which service automatically supplies a client with an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers?
options: DNS
DHCP
ARP
NTP
questions.explain: DHCP hands out the lease and the options that go with it. DNS is tempting because both are name-related, but DNS resolves names to addresses and assigns nothing.

questions.q: Why does a normal DNS lookup travel over UDP rather than TCP?
options: UDP encrypts the query before it leaves the client
Recursive resolvers cannot speak TCP, so every query must use UDP
Port 53 is reserved for UDP, so TCP cannot be used for lookups
A query and answer fit in one datagram, so a retry is cheap
questions.explain: A typical exchange is one small request and one small response, so the three-way handshake costs more than the payload. Resolvers do speak TCP for large answers and zone transfers, which rules out the second option.

questions.q: A firewall rule denies inbound TCP port 3389. Which OSI layer does the rule act on?
options: Layer 2, by MAC address
Layer 3, by IP address
Layer 4, by port number
Layer 7, by application data
questions.explain: A rule written against a TCP port matches the transport header. A Layer 3 rule would stop at the IP address and could not tell 3389 from 443 on the same host.

questions.q: A user can ping the application server at 10.30.4.20, but the browser cannot open https://intranet.example. What do you check next?
options: The network cable and the switch port
The DNS servers on the laptop and the name's record
Free disk space on the application server
The default gateway configured on the application server
questions.explain: A successful ping to the IP proves the cable, port, gateway and route, so the first unproven step is turning the name into an address. The cable and switch port are already ruled out by that same ping.

questions.q: After a reboot, a laptop shows the address 169.254.18.7 with mask 255.255.0.0. What happened?
options: The laptop got no DHCP offer and used a link-local address
The laptop received a lease from DHCP, but the gateway is wrong
The laptop has a static address from the office range
The default gateway is blocking ICMP
questions.explain: 169.254.0.0/16 is the link-local range a host falls back to when no DHCP offer arrives, so it has no usable gateway or DNS. A wrong gateway is the tempting answer, but no lease arrived at all.

questions.q: A remote user connects the VPN and can reach 10.40.7.15 by IP, but every request to 10.40.8.20 times out. Their home internet still works. What is the best next check?
options: Ask the user to reboot the home router
Reinstall the VPN client so it picks up the latest profile from the gateway
Ask the user to clear the browser cache
Check whether the VPN pushes a route for 10.40.8.0/24
questions.explain: Reaching one internal subnet and not another usually means the tunnel carries only part of the address space. A reboot or a profile reinstall does not add a route that was never pushed.

questions.q: Host web01 (10.20.10.10/24) pings its own gateway 10.20.10.1 and gets replies. When it pings db01 at 10.20.11.10, web01 sends frames to the gateway's MAC and nothing comes back. Both switch ports are up in the correct VLANs. Where should you look?
options: The cable between web01 and the switch
DNS resolution for db01
The network card driver on web01
The routed path between the two VLANs
questions.explain: The frame reaches the gateway and stops, so the link, the port and the driver are already proven, and the test used an IP so no name was resolved. The failing hop is the Layer 3 path between the VLANs: an interface, a return route or an ACL on that hop.

q2.title: Linux for the desk — module test

questions.q: You are about to run a cleanup command with a relative path on a customer server. Which command tells you exactly which directory `./` resolves to?
options: `pwd`
`ls -la`
`whoami`
`history`
questions.explain: `pwd` prints the absolute working directory, so `./logs` cannot surprise you. `ls -la` shows what is inside the directory but never where the directory is, and that is the mistake that deletes the wrong tree.

questions.q: A user says the config file for their app is gone, but `ls /etc/payments` returns two entries and no error. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The file is owned by root, and plain `ls` hides files owned by other users
The filesystem is mounted read-only, so the file is not listed
The file name begins with a dot, and plain `ls` does not show dotfiles
Plain `ls` only lists files smaller than 1 MB
questions.explain: Plain `ls` hides names that begin with a dot, and application config and credential files are often dotfiles. Ownership and mount options do not change what `ls` lists, so `ls -a` settles it in one command.

questions.q: Which command shows the last 30 minutes of log lines for the sshd unit only?
options: `journalctl --since "30 min ago"`
`journalctl -u sshd --since "30 min ago"`
`journalctl -f -u sshd`
`grep -r sshd /var/log --since "30 min ago"`
questions.explain: `-u` narrows journalctl to one systemd unit and `--since` bounds the window. `-f` follows live output with no time bound, and `grep` has no `--since` option at all.

questions.q: You need to cite an exact line from a 4,000-line application log in a handover note. What does adding `-n` to grep give you?
options: Case-insensitive matching
A recursive search through subdirectories
Only the names of files that contain a match
The line number of each matching line
questions.explain: `-n` prefixes each match with its line number, which is what makes the citation checkable by the next engineer. `-i` ignores case and `-r` recurses; neither produces a line number.

questions.q: A file is set to `640` and owned by `deploy:appteam`. What can a member of the `appteam` group do with it?
options: Read and write it
Read it only
Neither read nor write it
Read and execute it
questions.explain: The digits are owner, group, other: 6 is read and write for `deploy`, 4 is read only for `appteam`, and 0 gives everyone else nothing. Reading the 6 as the group value is the common mistake, and it would wrongly grant write access.

questions.q: A server reaches some subnets but not 10.20.5.0/24. Which command shows the interface, source address and gateway that would be used for 10.20.5.11?
options: `ip addr`
`ss -lnt`
`ip route get 10.20.5.11`
`ip neigh`
questions.explain: `ip route get` answers for one destination and prints the interface, source address and gateway on that path. `ip addr` lists every address on the host but chooses nothing, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: A user gets `Permission denied` when writing to `/opt/app/logs/app.log`. `ls -l` shows `-rw-rw-rw- 1 app app` and the user is in group `app`. What do you check next?
options: The permissions on `/opt/app/logs` and its parent directories
Whether `chmod 777` on `app.log` is needed to allow the write
Whether the user account has expired
Whether the filesystem is mounted read-only
questions.explain: Writing a file needs write permission on the containing directory and execute permission on every directory in the path, so the file mode is not the blocker. `chmod 777` on the file changes nothing here, and a read-only mount returns a different error: `Read-only file system`.

questions.q: A service on `app01` answers `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health` locally. A user on 10.20.30.0/24 gets `Connection refused`. `ss -tulnp` shows `LISTEN 0 4096 127.0.0.1:8080` and the firewall already permits 8080 from that subnet. What is the finding?
options: The firewall is still blocking the subnet, so the network team must open 8080
The host has no route back to 10.20.30.0/24
The service has crashed and needs a restart
The service is bound to loopback only, so its listen address must change
questions.explain: A socket bound to 127.0.0.1 accepts only local connections, so a remote client is refused before any firewall rule is evaluated. The firewall answer would fit a socket on 0.0.0.0, and the listen-address change needs the app owner's approval.

questions.q: `systemctl restart nginx` returns `Job for nginx.service failed because the control process exited with error code`. Which command shows why it failed?
options: `ps aux | grep nginx`
`journalctl -u nginx -n 50 --no-pager`
`ss -tulnp | grep nginx`
`df -h`
questions.explain: The unit journal holds the config-test or bind error that ended the start, and `-n 50` keeps the output readable. `ps` proves the process is gone but never says why, which is the dead end most freshers hit.

questions.q: A checkout service returns 500 errors. `df -h /var` shows 100 percent used, but `du -xsh /var/*` totals 6 GB on a 20 GB volume. `journalctl -u checkout` ends with `no space left on device`. What is the most likely cause?
options: A deleted file is still open, so its blocks are not freed
The volume is genuinely full and must be grown
The disk is failing and will need replacement
The systemd journal has rotated incorrectly and must be vacuumed
questions.explain: df counts blocks that are still allocated, including a deleted file a process holds open, so df and du disagree exactly in that case and `lsof +L1` names the holder. Growing the volume would hide the cause for one more night, which is the expensive wrong answer.

questions.q: A user says their laptop cannot reach the file server. Before you change anything you need the address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, and whether the adapter uses DHCP, including for adapters that are disconnected. Which command returns all of that?
options: `ipconfig /all`
`whoami /all`
`netstat -ano`
`ping -n 4 <gateway>`
questions.explain: `ipconfig /all` prints every adapter with its DHCP state, lease times and DNS servers, and it still lists an adapter that is disconnected. `whoami /all` is the tempting near-miss because of the `/all` flag, but it lists your security groups, not the network.

questions.q: `ipconfig /all` shows `Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address: 169.254.37.12` and `DHCP Enabled: Yes`. What does that address prove?
options: A static address from the server team has not taken effect yet
The adapter is disabled, so Windows fell back to a default address
The DHCP server did not answer, so the host assigned itself a link-local address
DNS is misconfigured, so the host cannot resolve its own name
questions.explain: An address in 169.254.0.0/16 is self-assigned after the DHCP request goes unanswered, which puts the fault upstream of DNS and usually at the DHCP relay, scope or VLAN. A disabled adapter shows `Media disconnected` and no address at all, which is the answer most people reach for.

questions.q: A user insists they are in the local Backup Operators group, but a backup tool still returns access denied. Which command shows the account the console is actually running as, plus the groups in that process token?
options: `net user <username>`
`whoami /groups`
`Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Backup Operators'`
`hostname`
questions.explain: `whoami /groups` reads the token of the running process, and the token is what decides access. `net user` and `Get-LocalGroupMember` report configured membership, so they answer a different question than the one the access-denied error asks.

questions.q: A service must run under a dedicated account, and you need to prove which account it will use after the next reboot. `Get-Service` shows only `Status`, `Name` and `DisplayName`. Which command shows the logon account and the start mode?
options: `Get-Service <name> | Select-Object -Property *`
`tasklist /v`
`Get-Process <name>`
`Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='<name>'" | Select-Object Name, StartMode, StartName`
questions.explain: `Win32_Service` carries `StartMode` (Automatic, Manual, Disabled) and `StartName`, the account the service is configured to log on as. `Get-Process` shows the live process only, so a successful stop and start proves nothing about the account the service will use at the next boot.

questions.q: Before you unlock an account, you need two policy numbers: how many bad passwords trigger a lockout, and how long the lock lasts. Which command prints them on a member server?
options: `net accounts`
`net user <username>`
`net localgroup administrators`
`whoami /priv`
questions.explain: `net accounts` prints the lockout threshold, duration and observation window, and `/domain` reads the domain policy instead of the local one. `net user <username>` shows one account's active, expiry and last-logon fields but none of the policy numbers, which is why it leaves you guessing.

questions.q: A user is locked out at 09:14 and wants to know why. Which Security log record gives you the failed attempts behind the lockout, rather than just the fact that it happened?
options: Event 4624, a successful logon
Event 1102, the audit log was cleared
Event 4625, failed logon, in a burst before 09:14
Event 4720, a user account was created
questions.explain: 4625 records every failed attempt with its logon type and account, which is what separates a mistyped password from a stale service credential. Event 4740 records the lockout itself, so it proves the outcome and never the cause.

questions.q: At 08:40 you need every failed logon, event 4625, from the last 24 hours on a Windows Server 2016 host whose Security log holds about 900,000 events. Which command returns the answer in seconds?
options: `Get-EventLog -LogName Security -Newest 900000 | Where-Object { $_.EventID -eq 4625 }`
`Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-24)}`
`Get-WinEvent -LogName Security | Where-Object { $_.Id -eq 4625 }`
`wevtutil qe Security /c:20 /f:text`
questions.explain: `-FilterHashtable` is applied by the event log service before any event reaches PowerShell, so only matches travel down the pipe. Filtering after `Get-WinEvent -LogName Security` reads all 900,000 events into the pipeline, which is the version that locks up the console while the customer waits.

questions.q: Users cannot reach srv01 over RDP. `Test-NetConnection -ComputerName srv01 -Port 3389` returns `TcpTestSucceeded : False`. What have you proved?
options: The Remote Desktop service on srv01 is stopped
The user's password or RDP permission is wrong
srv01 is powered off
Something on the path or on srv01 refuses or filters TCP 3389, and the test does not say which
questions.explain: A failed TCP connect collapses three different faults, a missing listener, a firewall drop, and a path that goes nowhere, so it cannot separate them without the next check. Credentials are only validated after the TCP session exists, so a password problem would fail later, not at this test.

questions.q: The shift lead wants a plain list of service names, one per line, for services set to Automatic that are not running on a lab host. Which one-liner produces that list?
options: `Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.StartType -eq 'Automatic' -and $_.Status -ne 'Running' } | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name`
`Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.StartType -eq 'Automatic' -and $_.Status -ne 'Running' } | Format-Table Name`
`Get-Service | Select-String 'Automatic'`
`sc query type= service state= all`
questions.explain: `-ExpandProperty Name` returns the strings themselves, so the output pastes into a ticket as a clean column. `Format-Table` returns formatting objects built for the screen, which is why a pipeline that looks correct in the console produces nothing usable in a file.

questions.q: Every weekday at 02:00 the backup job fails and `svc-backup` is found locked out. The Security log shows 4625 for that account every four minutes from 02:00 to 02:20, then nothing. Unlocking clears the ticket until the next morning. What is the finding?
options: The lockout threshold is too low, so it should be raised until the backup job can finish
The account is disabled, so re-enabling it will let the job run
A user is mistyping the password at that hour, so a reset and a close will do
A scheduled task or service still holds an old password and retries, so each retry re-locks the account and the stored credential must be fixed at its source
questions.explain: A four-minute retry cycle that begins exactly at the job's start time points at stored credentials rather than a person, so unlocking without fixing the source guarantees the same ticket tomorrow. Raising the threshold is the tempting fix, and it leaves a real account exposed to whoever is trying the password.

questions.q: An account signs in with a valid password and an approved MFA prompt, then gets `Access denied` when opening the finance share on files01. Both facts are true at the same time. Which control is failing?
options: Authentication, because the user cannot reach the share
Authorization, because the account is identified but not permitted
Accounting, because no log entry was written for the share
Confidentiality, because finance data is exposed to this user
questions.explain: The password and the MFA prompt proved who the user is, so authentication worked; authorization decides what that identity may open, and the share permissions are where the denial came from. Authentication is the tempting answer because the error appears when the user connects, but a failed sign-in never gets as far as opening the share.

questions.q: A vendor publishes a 4 GB install image with a SHA-256 value. You hash the download on your laptop and the values match. What does that prove?
options: The file is free of malware, because malware would change the hash
The file was encrypted in transit and cannot be read by anyone else
The bytes you have are the bytes the vendor published
The file has not been modified since the vendor created it
questions.explain: A hash is a one-way fingerprint of the bytes, so a match proves your copy is identical to the copy the vendor described. It says nothing about malware, and it cannot prove the file was never altered before the vendor published that value.

questions.q: In a TLS connection to https://portal.example.com, what does the server certificate actually prove?
options: The server holds the private key for the name portal.example.com, and a trusted CA vouched for that binding
The web application behind the certificate is free of vulnerabilities
The tunnel keeps the data safe even if the server itself has been compromised
The certificate authority has verified that the owner is a legitimate business
questions.explain: The certificate binds a public key to a name and is signed by a CA the client trusts, and the handshake proves the server holds the matching private key. A padlock says nothing about whether the site is honest or patched, which is why the second option is the trap.

questions.q: A search page writes the query string straight into its results header, and a crafted link runs script in the victim's browser. Which change removes the flaw?
options: Validate the query string against a list of allowed words when it arrives
Switch the page from HTTP to HTTPS
Add a WAF rule that blocks the literal string `<script>`
Encode the value at the point where it is written into the page, and add a Content-Security-Policy
questions.explain: XSS is an output problem: the browser must receive the query as text, so encoding at the sink plus CSP stops execution. Blocking the literal `

questions.q: An application service account needs to read one folder on a file server, and nothing else. Which grant is the smallest one that meets the requirement?
options: Read on that folder only, granted to that account
Modify on the parent share, granted to the server administrators group
Domain Admin, so future permission problems do not block the application
Read on the whole volume, because the folder may move later
questions.explain: Least privilege grants the account only the access it needs, on the object it needs, so write access and broader scope are unnecessary risk. Domain Admin is the tempting shortcut that turns one compromised service account into a domain-wide incident.

questions.q: Workstations sit in VLAN 30 and servers in VLAN 40. A firewall rule allows only TCP 443 from VLAN 30 to one server and denies the rest. What does that rule buy you?
options: It encrypts workstation traffic to that server
It limits how far an infected workstation can spread and which services it can reach
It stops users from opening malicious email attachments
It removes the need to patch that server
questions.explain: Segmentation removes paths, so one infected laptop cannot reach every server on every port. It does not encrypt anything, and it cannot stop a user from opening an attachment on the machine they already control.

questions.q: At 02:10 a user receives 14 MFA push prompts in four minutes and approves the last one by mistake. The password was not reused on any other site. What is the correct first action?
options: Advise the user to deny any further prompts and carry on with the shift, then review the log later
Disable the user's MFA method and leave the account enabled
Wait for the identity team's morning report before changing anything
Revoke active sessions, reset the password, and escalate to identity with the prompt times
questions.explain: The attacker already has the password, and the approved prompt may have created a live session, so that session has to be killed and the credential replaced first. Telling the user to deny future prompts is the tempting answer, but it leaves the access the attacker already holds.

questions.q: A scanner reports a critical vulnerability on web01, which is internet-facing. The application owner says the fix has to wait for next month's change window. What does L1 do?
options: Record the exposure and evidence, check for a signed exception with an expiry, and escalate for a risk decision
Apply the patch tonight without a change record, because the host is internet-facing
Close the finding as accepted risk, because the owner has already decided
Escalate the finding to L3 and take no further action, because a critical finding on an internet-facing host is above L1
questions.explain: A deferral is only a decision when it is a signed exception with an approver and an expiry, and an internet-facing critical finding goes to the vulnerability and change owners with evidence attached. Deferring to L3 is the tempting habit, but the desk can assemble the evidence that forces the decision.

questions.q: At 02:14 every spreadsheet on the finance share is renamed to `.locked` inside the same second, and a `READ-ME.txt` appears one second after that. Which properties has this incident already broken?
options: Availability only, because the files cannot be opened
Integrity and availability, because the contents were replaced and the files cannot be opened by the finance team
Confidentiality, integrity, and availability, because the files were read, replaced, and left unusable
Integrity only, because the file names changed
questions.explain: The share is unusable (availability), the contents were replaced (integrity), and the process had to read each file before it could encrypt it (confidentiality). Availability is the tempting label because it is the only symptom the caller can see, but the restore decision depends on the other two.

questions.q: EDR flags WINWORD.EXE on ws-042 launching powershell.exe with `-enc` and a long base64 string, which then connects to 10.20.9.15:443. The user says the document was an invoice from a customer, and the alert is one hour old. What is the correct L1 action?
options: Close the alert as a false positive, because Word launches other programs during normal document use
Delete the document and run a full antivirus scan, then mark the alert resolved
Isolate the host, preserve the process tree and command line, and escalate to incident response
Ask the user to reboot and reopen the invoice, so the behavior can be reproduced
questions.explain: An Office process spawning encoded PowerShell and then reaching an internal host is the signature of a malicious document, so isolation stops spread while the evidence is captured intact. Deleting the file is the tempting quick clean, but it destroys the command line and the document the incident team needs.

questions.q: Your team is authorized to test a customer's new portal. The signed scope names `portal.example.com` and `10.30.4.15` only. During recon you find the customer's VPN gateway at `10.30.1.1`. What is the correct next move?
options: Scan 10.30.0.0/16 for completeness, then delete the out-of-scope hosts from the report
Scan the two in-scope targets and get a written scope change before touching 10.30.1.1
Scan the gateway but leave it out of the written report
Ask the customer on the call and proceed if they agree verbally
questions.explain: Authorization is the signed document, so the gateway stays untouched until the scope is amended in writing; a verbal yes leaves no record and a scan of an excluded host can end the engagement. Option A is the tempting one because it sounds thorough, but scope is set by the document, not by what you remove later.

questions.q: `nmap -sV 10.30.4.15` returns `443/tcp open https Apache httpd 2.4.49`. Which part of that line did `-sV` add?
options: The `open` state
The port number 443
The service and version, `https Apache httpd 2.4.49`
The host being up
questions.explain: `-sV` probes each open port after the connect scan and fingerprints what answered, which turns a bare port number into a name and a version. The `open` state already appears in a default scan, so the version string is the only new information on that line.

questions.q: Which task counts as passive reconnaissance?
options: Reading public DNS records and certificate transparency logs for the customer's domain
Running `nmap -sn` against the customer's office subnet
Replaying a captured login request through Burp Repeater
Running a credentialed vulnerability scan against the staging host
questions.explain: Passive collection reads records that already exist in public archives, so no packet reaches the customer's infrastructure and nothing appears in their logs. `nmap -sn` is the tempting choice because it is quiet, but it still sends probes to hosts you may not own.

questions.q: `nmap -Pn -p 443,3389 10.30.4.15` prints `443/tcp open` and `3389/tcp filtered`. What does `filtered` tell you?
options: The port is closed and the host answered with a reset
3389 was left out of the scan
The service on 443 is blocking 3389
A packet filter dropped the probes, so you cannot tell whether anything listens on 3389
questions.explain: No reply, or an ICMP administratively prohibited reply, is reported as `filtered`, and it proves only that something in the path drops the probes. `closed` is the different state where the host itself answers with a reset, which is the answer most people reach for.

questions.q: In Wireshark you want only the HTTP requests going to `10.30.4.15`. Which display filter does that?
options: `host 10.30.4.15 and port 80`
questions.explain: `ip.addr` matches either direction of the conversation and `&& http` narrows the view to the HTTP dissector. Option C is capture-filter syntax, so typing it into the display bar raises a syntax error, and `http.host` compares a Host header name rather than an address.

questions.q: A login POST is sitting in Burp, and you need to resend the same request with one parameter changed, ten times, without touching the browser. Which tool holds the request and resends your edits?
options: Proxy history
Repeater
Decoder
Scanner
questions.explain: Repeater keeps one request on the workbench so you can edit a parameter and resend it as often as needed. Proxy history only records traffic that already happened, and Scanner is a Pro feature you should not point at an unapproved target anyway.

questions.q: On a lab login form you enter `'` as the username and the page returns `You have an error in your SQL syntax`. What does that support?
options: The database is offline, so the application could not run the query
The quote character is rejected, so input validation is working
The input reached the SQL parser unescaped, which makes the parameter a candidate for injection
The account exists but the password is wrong
questions.explain: A database syntax error means your text became part of the statement instead of a value, which is the first evidence of injection. Option B is the tempting misread because an error message looks like a control working, but validation that works never reaches the database.

questions.q: A lab forum stores a comment containing `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>` and runs it every time another user opens the thread. Which class of issue is it, and what fixes it?
options: Reflected XSS; validate the query string parameter
SQL injection; use parameterized queries
CSRF; add an anti-CSRF token
Stored XSS; HTML-encode on output and add a Content-Security-Policy
questions.explain: The payload is saved on the server and executes in every viewer's browser, which is stored XSS. Reflected XSS is the tempting label, but there the payload only comes back in the response to the person who sent it.

questions.q: A scanner reports MS17-010 on `10.30.4.15:445`. The host is a lab VM you rebuilt last week with current patches. What should you do before writing the finding?
options: Report it as critical, because the scanner matched the signature
Confirm the patch level and the service banner with read-only checks, then record it as unconfirmed or a false positive
Run the Metasploit module to prove it works
Delete the row from the report and move on
questions.explain: Most scanner hits are inferred from a banner, so validation is the step that separates a finding from a guess, and the patch level is the evidence that settles it. Option C is the tempting shortcut, but exploiting a host outside an approved test window is unauthorized even when the finding is real.

questions.q: A capture on the client shows a SYN to `10.30.4.15:443`, then `RST, ACK` from the server, then nothing. The user reports that the app is down. What does the capture prove?
options: The path to the server is broken, so escalate to the network team
DNS is failing, so the client never found the server
The server received the SYN and refused it, so nothing is listening on 443 and the service or its listener is the fault
A firewall dropped the SYN, which is why the client timed out
questions.explain: A reset comes from the server's own stack, which proves the packet arrived and the port is not open, so the next check is the service and its listener. Option D is the tempting read, but a firewall drop produces silence or an ICMP error, not a reset.

q6.title: SOC, SIEM and detection — module test

questions.q: At 09:10 a customer reports an odd sign-in. The firewall logs `2026-11-24T14:02:11Z`; the domain controller logs `2026-11-24 19:32:11` with no zone. The SIEM shows the two events five and a half hours apart, in an order that cannot have happened. What is the most likely cause?
options: The DC clock has drifted five hours and needs a time service repair
The firewall is wrong because it stamps events in UTC instead of local time
The DC writes local time at UTC+05:30 and the SIEM applied no zone
The SIEM re-indexed both events at the wrong time after a restart
questions.explain: A gap of exactly five and a half hours is a zone offset, so one instant landed at 14:02:11Z and the other at 19:32:11 local; the parser has to carry that source's zone. NTP drift is the tempting answer, but drift lands on seconds or minutes and never on a half-hour boundary.

questions.q: Three sources describe the same failed sign-in. One calls the account `TargetUserName`, one calls it `user`, and one calls it `AccountName`. What does normalizing them onto one schema give you?
options: One field name and one query that work across every source
Smaller storage, because parsing compresses the raw event on disk
Encryption of the account field at rest, applied during parsing
Automatic removal of duplicate events before they reach the queue
questions.explain: Normalization maps vendor field names onto a common schema, which is what lets one correlation search and one rule span three vendors. Compression and de-duplication happen in other stages and neither makes a query portable.

questions.q: A search for `host=dc01 EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h` returns nothing today, though the same search returned 300 rows yesterday at the same hour. What do you check first to separate a data fault from a real drop in activity?
options: Whether the index retention window has rolled the data off
Whether the search string has a typo in the event code
Whether the account behind the failures was disabled or locked last week
Whether dc01 still forwards, by checking the age of its newest event
questions.explain: The age of the newest event in that sourcetype settles whether the data ever arrived, which is the first question when a working search suddenly returns zero. Retention is the tempting check, but yesterday's rows are still inside a normal 30-day window.

questions.q: You need the number of failed Windows sign-ins per account for the last 24 hours in Splunk. Which search does that?
options: `SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4625 | summarize count() by Account`
`index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h | stats count BY user`
`index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | table user count`
`index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h | dedup user`
questions.explain: `stats count BY user` counts the matching events per account and `earliest=-24h` bounds the window. The first option is the tempting one because it names the right event ID, but `where` and `summarize` are KQL and Splunk will not run that search.

questions.q: In Microsoft Sentinel you want one row per account with the number of failed sign-ins from `SecurityEvent`. Which line does the counting?
options: `| project TargetAccount, Failures = count()`
`| where ResultType == 50126 | project TargetAccount`
`| summarize Failures = count() by TargetAccount`
`| extend Failures = count() by TargetAccount`
questions.explain: The `summarize` line with `by TargetAccount` collapses the rows to one per account and names the count. `extend` is the tempting line because it creates the column you asked for, but it evaluates per row and cannot aggregate the table.

questions.q: A medium-severity rule fires on `srv-file02`, which holds the finance share. A critical-severity rule fires on `lab-vm-07`, which nobody uses. Which statement matches how priority is set?
options: Priority pairs rule severity with asset urgency, so finance can outrank the lab VM
Priority is the rule's severity alone, so the critical alert on the unused lab VM must come first
Priority follows the order the alerts arrived in the queue
Priority is set by whichever user calls the service desk first
questions.explain: The rule fixes severity and the asset fixes urgency; priority needs both, which is why a medium rule on a finance server can outrank a critical rule on a throwaway VM. The second option is the tempting one because the severity label is printed on the alert, but the label says nothing about what the asset is worth.

questions.q: An alert shows 12 failed sign-ins for `svc_backup` from 10.20.4.55 in six minutes on dc01. The analyst plans to close it as a password issue. The paired search returns a successful 4624 for the same account from the same address four minutes later, and 10.20.4.55 has no entry in the asset inventory. What is the right call?
options: Close as benign, because service accounts retry after a credential change
Close it and raise a password reset with the identity team
Wait for more failures before deciding anything
Escalate with the paired 4625 and 4624 events and the unknown source
questions.explain: A success that follows a burst of failures, from an address the asset inventory cannot account for, is valid-account use rather than a forgotten password, and L2 needs it now with both events. The first option is the tempting close because service accounts do retry, but a retry from a known host would not end in one success from an unknown one.

questions.q: An EDR alert shows `powershell.exe -enc` with `WINWORD.EXE` as its parent on `ws-042`, user `rpatel`. The decoded command opens a test harness, change `CHG00418` covers the deployment, and no other alert names that host in 24 hours. Your queue holds 20 alerts. What is the best action?
options: Escalate at critical severity because encoded PowerShell is a known ATT&CK technique used by ransomware crews
Close as benign true positive with the change number, the decoded command and a tuning request
Disable the PowerShell rule so the queue clears
Ask the user to rebuild the laptop before the rule fires again
questions.explain: The parent, the decoded command and the change number all point at authorized work, so the alert closes with evidence and the rule gets a tuning request instead of a ticket. The first option is the over-escalation this module exists to stop: a technique name describes behavior, not intent.

questions.q: An alert fires on `WINWORD.EXE` spawning `powershell.exe -enc`. Which ATT&CK technique should the rule be tagged with?
options: T1566 Phishing
T1078 Valid Accounts
T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact
questions.explain: The telemetry observed a scripting interpreter running an encoded command, which is T1059.001. T1566 is the tempting tag because Word is the parent, but phishing is a delivery hypothesis the alert itself cannot prove.

questions.q: A rule for five failed sign-ins in ten minutes on one account has not fired in three weeks. Last month's tuning added the filter `NOT user=svc_*`. A manual search returns 4,800 sign-in failures in that period, including 12 against `svc_backup` from 10.20.4.55 in six minutes. What is the cause?
options: The wildcard matched svc_backup, so those events never counted
The events stopped arriving after the tuning change
The threshold of five is too high for a ten-minute window
The rule's severity was lowered, so it no longer generates an alert
questions.explain: The wildcard matches `svc_backup`, so the exclusion removed the 12 failures before the threshold was ever evaluated. The threshold is the tempting answer because thresholds do cause misses, but twelve events are well above five.

q7.title: Incident response and forensics — module test

questions.q: At 08:40 your monitoring tool raises an alert: CPU on `app02` held at 91 percent for six minutes, then returned to 30 percent. No user has called and the application is responding. How do you classify this?
options: An incident, because the monitoring tool labeled it an incident and the tool label sets the ticket type
A capacity ticket for the infrastructure team, because a CPU spike is always a sizing problem
An event and a note: a threshold breach alone is not an incident until there is confirmed or suspected harm
A false positive to close with no note, because the value returned to normal on its own
questions.explain: A threshold breach is an event; it becomes an incident when it is tied to confirmed or suspected harm, and a six-minute spike that cleared with no user impact fails that test. Option A is tempting because the tool stamps the word incident on the alert, but the tool's label is not your classification.

questions.q: A colleague takes a suspicious USB stick from a user's laptop, plugs it into her own workstation to look at the filenames, then writes the serial number on a sticky note. Which step damaged the evidence most?
options: Plugging it into her workstation, which writes to the device and adds artifacts from a second host
Writing the serial number on a sticky note instead of in the case log, so the log cannot show who held the stick
Taking the stick without photographing the port it came from
Not telling the user why the stick was taken
questions.explain: Attaching the device changed it, so the timestamps and host records no longer show only what the attacker left. The sticky note is a documentation weakness and has to be fixed, but it does not alter the exhibit itself.

questions.q: A server is suspected of running a miner. It is still powered on and reachable, and the business wants it back in service within the hour. What do you collect first?
options: A full disk image, because the disk holds the largest amount of evidence and the image can be examined later without the host
The application log files, because they are the easiest to export
The disk image and the memory dump at the same time, to save the hour
Memory, because the running process list and connections exist only in RAM and are lost at reboot
questions.explain: RAM holds the process list and live connections that no disk image can recover, so it is the evidence that expires. Imaging the disk first is tempting because disk evidence feels more permanent, but a running process disappears the moment the host restarts.

questions.q: At 14:10 a user reports that files on the shared drive are renamed with a `.locked` extension. The file server is still serving the share and her laptop is still on the network. Your lead says contain it now. Which action stops the spread and keeps the evidence you will need?
options: Delete the renamed files on the share so the encryption cannot continue and the users get their folders back
Disconnect the laptop from the network, disable her account, and leave both machines powered on
Run a full antivirus scan on the file server and let it quarantine whatever it finds
Pull the power cable from the file server so nothing else can be written, then restart it once the share stops changing
questions.explain: Cutting the network stops the spread while the memory and running processes stay intact for collection. Pulling the power is tempting as the fastest stop, but it destroys the volatile evidence the next step needs, and deleting the files destroys the exhibit.

questions.q: A ticket carries an attachment named `invoice_2411.docm` and the user asks whether it is safe. You have a corporate laptop and no isolated lab available today. What do you do?
options: Open it in Word with macros disabled and look for anything unusual
Upload it to a public multi-engine scanner and read the report, since a hash alone cannot tell you whether the macro is bad
Hash the file, check the hash against the approved source, and send the file to the malware team unopened
Rename it to `.txt` and open it in Notepad to read the macro code
questions.explain: A hash lookup answers whether the file is known without executing it, and an unopened file is still clean evidence. Opening it with macros off feels harmless, but a malformed document can still exploit the parser, and the attachment stops being evidence once it has run on a corporate host.

questions.q: You image a 500 GB disk with `dd` and hand the image to another team. Which record makes that copy defensible when they open it next week?
options: Matching SHA-256 hashes of the original and of the image, with the tool and the UTC time recorded in the case log
The byte size of the image file
A screenshot of the imaging tool at the 50 percent mark
The name and employee number of the technician who ran the command, recorded when the image is handed over
questions.explain: Identical hashes are the claim that the copy is bit-for-bit the same, which is what another examiner relies on. The technician's identity belongs in the custody record, but on its own it says who made the copy, not that the copy is intact.

questions.q: On one host inside 20 minutes you see six 4625 failures for `svc_backup`, a 4688 record for `powershell.exe -enc <base64>`, and an antivirus detection that was quarantined. Which finding moves this from suspicious to an incident you escalate now?
options: The six 4625 failures, because repeated failures in a short window are brute force and brute force means someone is trying to get in
The antivirus detection, because any detection is an incident by definition
All three signals together, because three signals on one host is correlation
The encoded PowerShell launch, because code executed on the host instead of merely being attempted against it
questions.explain: Escalation rests on execution: a process ran with an encoded command, which is behavior on the host. The failures are the tempting signal because brute force sounds severe, but they prove attempts, and the detection was already stopped by quarantine.

questions.q: Your draft report says the outage happened because a user fell for a phishing email. The client's security manager sends it back, saying that is not a root cause. What is missing?
options: A severity rating for the phishing email itself
The control that failed and let one click become an outbreak, such as missing sandboxing or an over-privileged account
The full name and address of the person who sent the email, so the sender can be blocked at the mail gateway and named in the report
The exact second the email arrived, so the timeline can be reconstructed precisely
questions.explain: Root cause names the failed control that turned one click into an incident, which is the only part the client can fix. Adding a severity rating is tempting because it looks like rigor, but rating the email still does not explain why the click mattered.

questions.q: You are L1 on a confirmed incident: one laptop, malware detected and quarantined, the user's account still active. When do you stop and escalate?
options: Immediately, because L1 does not handle security incidents at all
After you wipe and rebuild the laptop, so L2 receives a clean machine and starts from a known state
