When the scope is unknown or growing, compromise is confirmed on a shared system, or the next step needs authority you do not have
After you have taken the memory and disk images yourself, so the case arrives complete and nobody has to go back to the user a second time
questions.explain: L1 can identify, classify, preserve and contain within policy; unknown or widening scope, confirmed compromise of a shared system, or a decision above your authority are the triggers to hand over. Imaging it yourself is tempting because it sounds thorough, but it delays containment and forensics collection is not an L1 task in most organizations.

questions.q: A user forwards a suspicious email and asks whether it is real. The mail client already downloaded the attachment. What gives the investigation the most to work with?
options: Ask the user to delete the message so nobody else opens it, then tell the service desk it is handled
Have the user forward it again as an attachment, and export the original with full internet headers
Reply to the sender to ask whether the message is legitimate
Screenshot the email body and attach the image to the ticket, because the ticket is the record that gets archived and audited
questions.explain: Full headers carry the received chain, the true sender and the message ID that let the team find every other copy. A screenshot is tempting because it is fast and safe, but it throws away the routing data and cannot be matched against other recipients.

questions.q: Your per-hour CSV sums to 41,208 requests. `wc -l access.log access.log.1` prints 20,604 and 21,004, and the app team insists the figure is 41,608. What is the right next move?
options: Send 41,208, because the CSV was built from the log itself and `wc -l` counted both files twice
Re-run the script after deleting the CSV, because a partial write explains a round 400-row gap
Count the lines with no parsable timestamp, read a few of them, and fix the pattern before re-sending
Use 41,608 and subtract the 400 from the 5xx column, because a line the parser skipped cannot be an error
questions.explain: A 400-row gap means the regex did not match 400 lines, and an unparsed line can be exactly the 5xx line the question is about, so subtracting it assumes the answer. Count the lines with no timestamp, read three of them, and fix the pattern; a reconciliation you cannot explain is a second wrong number.

questions.q: A host check prints `FAIL dc02 /var over 90%` and then ends with `echo done`, so the job exits 0. Cron runs it as `check.sh >> /var/log/check.log 2>&1`. What happens to the full disk?
options: Nothing; exit 0 tells cron the run succeeded, so the full disk waits until someone reads the log
Cron mails the log, because cron reports any non-zero exit code from a pipeline
Cron retries the job, because the FAIL text on stderr is treated as a retry signal
Cron raises an alert on the FAIL line, because cron counts failure words in the output
questions.explain: Cron reads the exit code and not the words in the log, so `echo done` erases the only signal it uses; the fix is to end the script on the test, `(( fail == 0 ))`. Option B is the common belief, but there is no non-zero code for cron to report.

questions.q: A ticket pull returns status 200, and `r.json()` raises `JSONDecodeError`. `r.headers["Content-Type"]` is `text/html`. What happened, and what do you do?
options: The token is missing or expired, so re-send the request with a valid `Authorization` header and expect JSON back
The API is failing, so retry once after 30 seconds and escalate with the request id
The result set is empty, so check the `state` parameter and run it again
A login or proxy page came back; escalate with the endpoint, status and request id
questions.explain: A 200 with `text/html` means something in front of the API answered, often an expired session or a proxy error page, so the parser is telling you the data never arrived. Retrying (option B) assumes a server error, but a 200 is not a 5xx and the same expired session will serve the same page.

questions.q: A script starts with `set -euo pipefail` and runs `df -P /var | awk 'NR==2 && $5+0 > 90 {exit 1}'`. On one host `df` fails with `No such file or directory`. Without `pipefail`, what would happen?
options: The script would stop anyway, because `-e` applies to every command inside a pipeline, not only to simple ones
The pipeline would report the exit code of `awk`, so the check would pass and the failure would be lost
The script would print the `df` error and skip to the next host in the list
`-u` would abort the script when `$5` expands to an empty string
questions.explain: Without `pipefail` a pipeline reports the status of its last command, so a failed `df` is hidden by a successful `awk` and the host looks healthy. `-e` does not save that case, because the pipeline as a whole returned 0.

questions.q: A cleanup script runs `rm -rf "$TARGET"/*`. A variable file sets `TARGET` to an empty string. Which change actually stops the deletion?
options: Quote the variable, so `rm` receives one argument instead of a glob that expands to every file
Add `set -e`, because an empty variable is an error under `-e`
Use `rm -rf "${TARGET:?}"/*`, which aborts when the variable is unset or empty
Add `-i` to `rm`, so it asks before removing each file
questions.explain: `${TARGET:?}` aborts the script when the variable is unset or empty, before `rm` is reached, and an empty `TARGET` would otherwise expand to `/*`. Quoting changes word splitting and not the empty value, and `set -e` does not treat an empty variable as an error; `-u` covers the unset case, not the empty one.

questions.q: You request 100 open tickets and get exactly 100 back, with no `Link` header. The queue badge shows 137. What is the correct next request?
options: Page 2 with the same `per_page`, because a page that comes back full means there may be more
Page 1 with `per_page=200`, because the API caps the page size at the badge count
No further request; 100 is the answer, because the badge also counts tickets that were closed overnight
Page 1 again, because the first response may have come from a cache
questions.explain: A page that comes back exactly full is the signal to ask for the next one, and 137 rows is 100 plus 37 more. Option C is how the overnight reopened tickets stay missing while the report still looks complete.

questions.q: `Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq "Stopped" | Measure-Object` counts 4. A colleague pipes `Get-Service | Format-Table -AutoSize` into the same `Where-Object` and gets errors. Why?
options: `Format-Table` shows only the first 10 services, so the filter has nothing to match
`Format-Table` emits formatting records, so the next filter reads display rows, not services
`Where-Object` cannot compare a string status, only a boolean property
`Get-Service` returns text on the console and only becomes objects when you assign it to a variable
questions.explain: `Format-*` cmdlets consume objects and emit formatting records, so anything piped after them filters the display instead of the services. Filter first and format last, and the count after `Where-Object` is the one you can defend.

questions.q: A working `C:\ops\service-check.ps1` writes a timestamped CSV. Your lead wants it to run every 15 minutes on a lab Windows host, unattended, with the CSV still written when nobody is signed in. Which setup does that?
options: Leave a PowerShell window open running `while ($true) { .\service-check.ps1; Start-Sleep 900 }`
Add a call to the script in `$PROFILE` so it starts with every session
Copy the script into the Startup folder of the account that administers the host
Register a scheduled task with action `powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\ops\service-check.ps1`, set to run whether or not the user is signed in
questions.explain: A registered task runs without an open console and survives logoff, and the explicit arguments make the run repeatable on a host whose policy blocks unsigned scripts. The loop in option A dies at logoff or reboot, which is exactly when the CSV gap appears.

questions.q: You must record a SHA-256 for a 3 GB evidence file on an 8 GB laptop, with two other files also open. Which method gives a correct digest without exhausting memory?
options: Read the file in chunks such as 1 MiB and call `update()` on one hash object
Read the whole file with `.read()` and hash it in one call, because hashing a stream changes the digest
Hash the first and last 10 MB and combine the two digests
Use MD5 instead, because it is computed in a single pass
questions.explain: A hash object accumulates across `update()` calls and produces the digest of the whole file, so chunking changes memory use and not the value. Hashing only the ends of the file (option C) cannot show the middle is intact, which is the one claim the digest exists to support.

questions.q: A check you inherited prints `CRITICAL: 3 services stopped` for `dc01` every morning. The app owner says the service has been fine for months. The three are Spooler, RemoteRegistry and WSearch, all set to Manual or Disabled. What is your finding?
options: A real service failure; escalate to L2 with the three names and the count, because three stopped services on a domain controller is above L1 scope
A monitoring gap; restart the three services and confirm they are still running after an hour
A false positive: it filters status alone, so Manual and Disabled services count; filter StartMode Auto with State Stopped
An acceptable alert; close it as informational and stop running the check
questions.explain: A stopped service is normal when its start mode is Manual or Disabled, so a status-only filter produces noise and hides the one Automatic service that matters. Sending the three names to L2 (option A) is the over-escalation this module removes: the filter is what needs fixing.

assignments.title: Map one failed request to a layer, not a guess
assignments.scenario: A user says the portal will not load and has already restarted the laptop twice. Your mentor wants the failure named by layer before anyone touches a firewall rule, and you have ten minutes of the user's time. You also have a terminal and your own laptop.
assignments.task:
1. Make a working folder and a notes file:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/m1/day1 && cd ~/m1/day1
touch triage.md
```

On Windows PowerShell: `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$HOME\m1\day1"` then `New-Item "$HOME\m1\day1\triage.md"`.

2. Prove layers 1 and 2 are up. Run `ipconfig /all` on Windows, or `ip -br link` and `ip -br addr` on Linux. Note the interface state and the MAC address.

3. Prove layer 3 by address, not by name:

```bash
ping -c 4 1.1.1.1      # macOS/Linux
ping -n 4 1.1.1.1      # Windows
```

4. Prove the name step fails for a name that cannot exist. `.example` is reserved for documentation, so this never touches a real zone:

```bash
nslookup intranet.example
```

5. Prove layer 7 with the status code only:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com
```

6. Fill in `triage.md` with one row per command, using this header:

| Command | Layer tested | Healthy output | Failing output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

7. Add one decision rule of the form "If X works and Y fails, the fault is at layer Z". Write it as a sentence you could read out loud on a call.

Do this on your own laptop. Do not point these commands at a customer network, and replace your own hostname and public address with placeholders before you save the note.
assignments.deliverable: triage.md with a four-row table (command, layer, healthy output, failing output) and one decision-rule sentence.

rubric.lookFor: each of the four commands is mapped to the right OSI layer and the row shows the layer number as well as the name

rubric.criterion: Evidence comes from the actual run
rubric.lookFor: the table quotes the real reply line, the NXDOMAIN line and the HTTP status code instead of describing them

rubric.criterion: Decision rule is usable on a call
rubric.lookFor: one sentence of the form if X works and Y fails then the fault is at layer Z, with no hedging or 'might be'

hints: Use a name in the reserved .example domain for the failure case. It always returns NXDOMAIN, so you never touch a real customer zone.
If curl prints nothing at all, ask for the exit code: `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}' https://example.com` separates a name failure from a connection failure.
A successful ping to 1.1.1.1 while a name fails is not a network outage. Read the Server line from nslookup before you name the layer.

assignments.title: Audit an address plan before you approve it
assignments.scenario: A customer sends the address plan for a new site and wants approval today. Office is 10.20.10.0/24 with gateway 10.20.10.1, voice is 10.20.10.128/25 with gateway 10.20.10.129, servers are 10.20.11.0/24, and the new camera VLAN is requested as 10.20.10.64/26. Nobody on their side has run the overlap check.
assignments.task:
1. In a scratch folder, print the facts for each submitted range instead of doing the math in your head:

```bash
python3 - <<'EOF'
import ipaddress
for cidr in ["10.20.10.0/24", "10.20.10.128/25", "10.20.11.0/24", "10.20.10.64/26"]:
    n = ipaddress.ip_network(cidr)
    print(cidr, n.network_address, n.broadcast_address, n.num_addresses - 2)
EOF
```

2. Test every pair for overlap and print the answer:

```bash
python3 - <<'EOF'
import ipaddress, itertools
nets = [ipaddress.ip_network(c) for c in ["10.20.10.0/24", "10.20.10.128/25", "10.20.11.0/24", "10.20.10.64/26"]]
for a, b in itertools.combinations(nets, 2):
    if a.overlaps(b):
        print("OVERLAP", a, b)
EOF
```

3. Confirm the mask arithmetic by hand on one range. In PowerShell:

```powershell
$mask = '255.255.255.192'
$bin = (([ipaddress]$mask).GetAddressBytes() | ForEach-Object { [Convert]::ToString($_,2).PadLeft(8,'0') }) -join ''
($bin.ToCharArray() | Where-Object { $_ -eq '1' }).Count
```

That prints `26`. On Linux, `ipcalc 10.20.10.64/26` prints the same facts.

4. Write `address-plan.md` with a table of the four submitted ranges: name, network address, first usable, last usable, broadcast, usable hosts.

5. List every overlapping pair and say which range contains which.

6. Design a corrected plan for the same four roles with no overlap, keep every range inside 10.20.8.0/21, and re-run the script from step 2 with your new ranges. Every pair must print nothing.

7. Add one sentence saying why the submitted plan cannot be routed as written.

Work from the ranges in this brief only. Do not paste a real customer's address plan, and do not scan any of these ranges from a network you do not own.
assignments.deliverable: address-plan.md listing every overlapping pair and a corrected plan whose re-run overlap check prints nothing.

rubric.lookFor: names both colliding pairs, voice against office and cameras against office, and states that 10.20.10.0/24 contains each of them
network address, broadcast address and usable host count are right for the /24, /25 and /26 ranges in the table

rubric.criterion: Corrected plan is addressable and justified
rubric.lookFor: new ranges do not overlap each other or the server range, stay inside 10.20.8.0/21, and one sentence explains the rejection

hints: A child subnet cannot sit inside a subnet that is already routed at the same site: 10.20.10.128/25 is entirely inside 10.20.10.0/24.
`python3 -c "import ipaddress; print(ipaddress.ip_network('10.20.10.0/24').overlaps('10.20.10.128/25'))"` answers one pair. Loop over the pairs you care about.
Keep the corrected plan inside 10.20.8.0/21, from 10.20.8.0 to 10.20.15.255, so the site still summarizes to one route at the firewall.

assignments.title: Prove the resolver, then the lease
assignments.scenario: Three tickets in one morning all say the internet is down. One user can reach 10.30.4.20 by IP but not by name, one has the address 169.254.4.9, and one resolves everything but slowly. Your lead wants one check order that separates these three before anyone restarts a service.
assignments.task:
1. Capture the address facts from your own machine:

```bash
ipconfig /all                        # Windows
ip -c addr && cat /etc/resolv.conf   # Linux
ipconfig getpacket en0               # macOS, lease detail
```

2. In `dns-dhcp-notes.md`, record the IPv4 address, the DHCP server, the lease obtained and lease expires timestamps, and every DNS server in the order listed.

3. Ask the system resolver for a name that exists and one that cannot exist:

```bash
nslookup example.com
nslookup intranet.example
```

4. Ask a specific resolver and compare. A different answer means the resolver is the variable:

```bash
nslookup example.com 1.1.1.1
Resolve-DnsName example.com -Server 1.1.1.1 -Type A   # Windows PowerShell
```

5. Copy the failure text exactly. `Non-existent domain`, `SERVFAIL` and a timeout are three different findings, and the ticket text changes with them.

6. Build a three-row table for the symptoms in the scenario: name fails while IP works, address starts with 169.254, and everything resolves but slowly. For each row give the proving command, the exact output line that proves it, and the team that owns the fix.

7. Only if you need the renewal step, run `ipconfig /renew` on your own laptop, never during a call, and note that the address can change.

Use your own laptop. Redact your public address and hostname before you save or share the note, and never run a release against a machine someone is working on.
assignments.deliverable: dns-dhcp-notes.md with the resolver address and lease expiry from the machine, plus a three-row table mapping each symptom to a proving command and an owner.

rubric.lookFor: the note quotes the DNS server addresses and the lease obtained and expires timestamps taken from real command output
each row pairs the symptom with the right command and the 169.254 case is sent to the DHCP owner, not to DNS
each row ends with a system or team, such as the DHCP scope, the resolver or a zone record, rather than a bare 'L2'

hints: nslookup prints the server that answered on the Server line. If that address is not in ipconfig /all, you are looking at the wrong resolver.
NXDOMAIN means a resolver answered and the name does not exist. A timeout means nothing answered. Those are different tickets with different owners.
A 169.254 address is link-local. The proof is the missing DHCP server line in ipconfig /all, not the failed ping.

assignments.title: Prove the port, not the ping
assignments.scenario: The application team says their service is running on web01. The user cannot load it. Ping to web01 answers in 2 ms, which is why the last three tickets were closed as 'network fine'. You have your own laptop, which is not on the customer network, and forty minutes.
assignments.task:
1. Build the table first: 443, 8443, 3389, 25, 53, 445. For each one, the service name and the layer a filter would act on.

2. Prove the web port from your laptop:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' https://example.com
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443   # Windows PowerShell
nc -vz example.com 443                     # macOS/Linux
```

3. Prove that a successful ping says nothing about a filtered port. Ping the same host, then test a port most home ISPs filter:

```powershell
Test-Connection example.com -Count 4
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 25
```

4. Show a refused connection and a working one side by side, on your own machine. In one terminal:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000
```

In a second terminal:

```bash
curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8000   # connects, HTTP 200
curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8001   # connection refused, in under a second
```

5. Find the local side of a live conversation:

```bash
netstat -ano | findstr :443        # Windows
ss -tnp | grep :443                # Linux
lsof -iTCP:443 -sTCP:ESTABLISHED   # macOS
```

6. Write `port-proof.md` with the six-port table, the two step 3 results quoted verbatim, and one line each for connection refused, timed out, and no route to host, matched to the command that produced it.

7. Add the sentence you would say to the user whose application is down while ping answers.

Only test hosts you own or public documentation targets such as example.com. Do not scan a customer range, an employer network, or anyone else's host.
assignments.deliverable: port-proof.md with the six-port table, verbatim results for 443 and 25, and three failure signatures each matched to a command you ran.

rubric.lookFor: each of the six ports has the right service name and the layer the filter acts on

rubric.criterion: Blocked port distinguished from a down host
rubric.lookFor: quotes a successful ICMP reply and a failed TCP test to the same host, and states that ping does not test the port
refused, timed out and no route to host are each tied to real output from a command, not to definitions

hints: Run the local server in one terminal and curl it from another. A closed port on your own machine refuses in under a second, which is the signature you want to recognize.
On macOS use `nc -vz host port`, on Windows use `Test-NetConnection host -Port N`. Both print one success or failure line you can paste into a ticket.
Refused means a host answered with a reset. Timed out means nothing answered, which points at a filter or the wrong destination. Do not write 'refused' for a hang.

assignments.title: Close or escalate: a full triage with evidence
assignments.scenario: Ticket 4471: a remote user on the VPN cannot open the internal app at 10.40.7.15:8443. They can ping 10.40.7.15 by IP, and a colleague in the office opens the same app without trouble. The user's home internet works, and this is their second report this week. Your shift ends in an hour.
assignments.task:
Part A - reproduce a port block with equipment you own, a laptop and a phone on the same Wi-Fi.

1. Start a listener on the laptop:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8443 --bind 0.0.0.0
```

2. Get the laptop's local address with `ipconfig` or `ip -4 addr`, then open `http://<laptop-ip>:8443` from the phone. It should load. Note how long it took.

3. Block only that port inbound and repeat the phone request:

```powershell
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Block 8443 test" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 8443 -Action Block
```

On macOS, enable the application firewall and set it to block all incoming connections for the test. On Linux, `sudo ufw deny 8443/tcp`.

4. From the phone the page now hangs until it times out, while `ping <phone-ip>` from the laptop still works. Write down both results and the layer the block acted on.

5. Remove the test rule:

```powershell
Remove-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Block 8443 test"
```

Part B - triage ticket 4471.

6. List five hypotheses, each tagged with the layer it would fail at and the command that would prove or kill it: name resolution over the VPN, a missing route for the app subnet, a filter on TCP 8443 for the VPN pool, no listener on the server, and a client proxy or browser setting.

7. Put the checks in the order you would run them on the call, and for each one state what the colleague's working session already rules out.

8. Use these commands exactly: `nslookup app.internal.example`, `Test-NetConnection 10.40.7.15 -Port 8443`, `tracert 10.40.7.15`, `ipconfig /all` on the VPN adapter, and `netstat -ano | findstr 8443`.

9. Write the handover note in five lines: Symptom, Scope, Evidence, Ruled out, Ask. Keep it under 120 words.

10. Make the close-or-escalate call and write the one condition that would flip it.

Keep the listener on your own laptop and your own Wi-Fi, and remove the firewall rule when you finish. Do not open a listener on a corporate network, do not scan 10.40.7.0/24, and put placeholders in the note instead of the user's real name or address.
assignments.deliverable: triage-4471.md with the firewall proof (two timings), an ordered check table built on five hypotheses, and a five-line handover note with one escalation criterion.

rubric.lookFor: five hypotheses, each tagged with a layer and a command, ordered so the cheapest cause is proven or killed first
records the before and after result of the 8443 block and states that a Layer 4 port block leaves ping working
the five-line note has all five labels filled in and the close-or-escalate call names the evidence that would flip it

hints: Start with what the colleague already proves: the office-to-app path and the listener are healthy, so the difference sits in the VPN path or on the client, not on the server.
Ping answers because ICMP is a different protocol from TCP on 8443. A filter on one says nothing about the other, and the note should say so in one line.
If Test-NetConnection fails on 8443 from the VPN but succeeds from the office subnet, the finding is the firewall rule for the VPN pool. Escalate with that comparison, not with 'app is slow'.

assignments.title: Find the file that changed before the outage
assignments.scenario: web01 runs the checkout API for a retail customer on 10.20.4.0/24. At 09:52 the API starts returning errors, and the 08:00 handover note says only "config touched on web01". The application owner is unavailable until 11:00, and any change under /etc needs a ticket. You rebuild the same tree in the lab at ~/lab/web01.
assignments.task:
1. Confirm the host and your starting directory before you use a relative path. Every later step uses an absolute path or an explicit `~/` path.

```
hostname
pwd
whoami
```

2. Build the lab tree that mimics `web01`. This is your playground, not a customer host.

```
mkdir -p ~/lab/web01/etc ~/lab/web01/opt ~/lab/web01/var/log
echo 'listen 0.0.0.0:8080' > ~/lab/web01/etc/app.conf
echo 'upstream 10.20.4.11:5432' > ~/lab/web01/etc/app.conf.bak
echo 'started worker 4' > ~/lab/web01/var/log/app.log
touch -d '45 minutes ago' ~/lab/web01/etc/app.conf
touch -d '5 minutes ago' ~/lab/web01/var/log/app.log
touch -d '2 days ago' ~/lab/web01/etc/app.conf.bak
```

3. List the tree in long format, including dotfiles.

```
ls -la ~/lab/web01/etc
ls -laR ~/lab/web01 | head -n 30
```

4. Ask the question that matters on this call: which files changed inside the incident window. Two files will match, and one of them is a log.

```
find ~/lab/web01 -type f -mmin -90 -ls
```

`-mtime -1` answers the last 24 hours; a 90-minute incident window needs `-mmin -90`.

5. Narrow to configuration, then read the candidate.

```
find ~/lab/web01 -name '*.conf' -mmin -90 -ls
cat ~/lab/web01/etc/app.conf
```

6. Prove the path has no symlink or surprise component in front of it.

```
ls -ld ~/lab/web01/etc
readlink -f ~/lab/web01/etc/app.conf
```

7. Run the same read-only check against the real system directories of your lab VM. This is the version you would run on a host you do not own.

```
sudo find /etc -xdev -type f -mmin -240 -ls | head -n 20
```

8. Write the handover line: absolute path, the time the file changed, and one sentence on what the change did. Name the application owner as the next team if the change has no ticket.

Safety: every command here is read-only. Do not edit, move, or delete a file under `/etc` or `/opt`; a configuration change needs an approved ticket and a backup copy.
assignments.deliverable: One line naming the absolute path and modification time of the only changed `.conf` file, quoting the `find` line it came from.

rubric.lookFor: the answer names a path starting with `/home/` or `~/lab/`, and every command uses a path starting with `/` or `~/` or follows a checked `pwd`; a bare `app.conf` does not score

rubric.criterion: Timestamp from the tool, not from the story
rubric.lookFor: quotes a `find` line whose date and time are about 45 minutes before the run, and identifies `var/log/app.log` as the newer file that is not the config
states the path and time in one sentence and names the application owner as the next team when the change has no ticket

hints: `-mmin -90` means modified within the last 90 minutes; `-mtime -1` means within the last day, which will return far more than you want.
The path comes before the tests in a find expression: `find ~/lab/web01 -name '*.conf' -mmin -90` lists matches, while the reverse order tests the wrong tree.
`readlink -f` prints the path the kernel actually uses, so a symlinked directory shows up before the path goes into a ticket.

assignments.title: Read the journal before you restart anything
assignments.scenario: Since 07:15 the payments API on app01 has returned 502 through the load balancer. payments.service restarts about every 90 seconds, and the on-call has already restarted it twice. The application connects to PostgreSQL on db01 at 10.30.4.12:5432. You have the host console and no permission to change the database.
assignments.task:
1. Build the failing unit in your lab. Run this on an Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 host with systemd, as a free VirtualBox or UTM VM or WSL2 with systemd enabled. The unit is a stand-in for `payments.service` and reproduces the symptom: the process starts, cannot reach the database, and exits. It restarts every 5 seconds so the loop is visible inside the drill; production restarts every 90 seconds.

```
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/payments.service >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Payments API (training fixture)
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/payments-start.sh
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF
```

2. Add the start script and load the unit. The error string is the one from the incident, and the application writes it to its own log as well as to stderr.

```
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/payments
sudo tee /usr/local/bin/payments-start.sh >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo 'dial tcp 10.30.4.12:5432: connect: connection refused' >&2
echo 'payments start failed: dial tcp 10.30.4.12:5432: connect: connection refused' >> /var/log/payments/app.log
sleep 2
exit 1
EOF
sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/payments-start.sh
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now payments
```

3. Read the state and the restart count before you change anything.

```
systemctl status payments --no-pager
systemctl show payments -p NRestarts
```

4. Pull the incident window and read the last lines of the unit journal.

```
journalctl -u payments --since '10 min ago' --no-pager | tail -n 40
```

5. Filter to errors for this boot, and count the start attempts.

```
journalctl -u payments -p err -b --no-pager | tail -n 20
journalctl -u payments --since '10 min ago' --no-pager | grep -c 'Starting'
```

6. Find the line that names a dependency rather than a symptom, in both sources the lesson names.

```
journalctl -u payments --since '10 min ago' --no-pager | grep -iE 'refused|timeout|dial|panic'
grep -n 'refused' /var/log/payments/app.log | tail -n 5
```

The journal records what the unit did; the application log records what the app saw. Quote the line with the timestamp and, from the file, the line number.

7. Prove the database port is closed, and prove your test method works against a port that is open.

```
timeout 3 bash -c '</dev/tcp/10.30.4.12/5432' && echo '5432 open' || echo '5432 closed or filtered'
timeout 3 bash -c '</dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/22' && echo '22 open' || echo '22 closed'
```

8. Show what a healthy listener looks like, so the note can state what is missing.

```
python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1 &
HTTP_PID=$!
sleep 1
ss -tulnp | grep ':8080'
kill "$HTTP_PID"
```

9. Write one line for the ticket: the quoted journal error, the port result, and the team that owns port 5432 on 10.30.4.12.

Safety: do not restart `payments` again while you investigate; each restart overwrites the journal lines that explain the exit. Stop the fixture with `sudo systemctl disable --now payments` when you are done.
assignments.deliverable: One line with the unit name, the quoted `connection refused` string, the port test result from step 7, and the team the ticket routes to.

rubric.lookFor: cites `payments.service` with `-u payments` and a bounded window such as `--since '10 min ago'` or `-b`
quotes the line containing `connect: connection refused` for 10.30.4.12:5432 with its timestamp, and gives the closed-port result as supporting evidence
routes to the database team, states that no further restart was performed, and does not claim the Linux host is faulty

hints: `-p err` keeps error priority and above, so the steady `Starting` and `Stopped` lines stop hiding the failure.
A 502 from the load balancer means the proxy reached nothing on the backend, so the backend journal is the first place to read, not the proxy access log.
If step 7 prints closed, the listener is missing or the path is filtered; the journal line already names the address, so the note needs no port scan.

assignments.title: Fix access with the smallest change, not 777
assignments.scenario: The deploy account on app01 cannot read files that the intake process drops into /srv/uploads, so the 02:00 import fails and 340 orders stay unprocessed. A colleague on the shift suggests `chmod -R 777 /srv/uploads`. The directory holds customer uploads from the last 30 days and is covered by the data-handling policy.
assignments.task:
1. Create the account the ticket names and reproduce the denial. The file is owned by `root` and readable only by its owner, which matches the production condition.

```
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash deploy 2>/dev/null || true
mkdir -p /tmp/m2perm/uploads
echo 'id,name' | sudo tee /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv >/dev/null
sudo chown root:root /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv
sudo chmod 600 /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv
sudo -u deploy cat /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv; echo "exit=$?"
```

2. Read the mode in a form you can quote in the ticket, and check every directory in the path.

```
ls -ld /tmp/m2perm /tmp/m2perm/uploads
ls -l /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv
```

3. Decide who needs what before you type a mode. The intake process writes new files into the directory, the deploy account reads them, and no other account needs either.

4. Create the group and apply the smallest sufficient change. The setgid bit is what makes new files inherit `appteam`.

```
sudo groupadd -f appteam
sudo usermod -aG appteam deploy
sudo chgrp appteam /tmp/m2perm/uploads /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv
sudo chmod 640 /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv
sudo chmod 2750 /tmp/m2perm/uploads
```

5. Prove it with an account that should succeed, one that should fail, and one write that must still be refused.

```
sudo -u deploy cat /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv
sudo -u nobody cat /tmp/m2perm/uploads/report.csv; echo "exit=$?"
sudo -u deploy touch /tmp/m2perm/uploads/deploy-was-here; echo "exit=$?"
```

6. Show what 777 would have allowed. In a world-writable directory, any local account can delete a file it does not own.

```
mkdir -p /tmp/m2perm/open && chmod 777 /tmp/m2perm/open
echo 'customer row' | sudo tee /tmp/m2perm/open/export.csv >/dev/null
sudo chown deploy:appteam /tmp/m2perm/open/export.csv
sudo -u nobody rm -f /tmp/m2perm/open/export.csv && echo 'deleted by nobody: yes'
```

7. Write the change line for the ticket: old mode, new mode, who gained what, and what 777 would have exposed.

Safety: use the lab tree only. On the real host, `chmod -R 777 /srv/uploads` would let any local account read and delete 30 days of customer files; a mode change on customer data needs the change ticket, the data owner's approval, and the old mode recorded.
assignments.deliverable: One line with the before and after `ls -l` line for `report.csv` and the mode that changed between them.

rubric.lookFor: shows the `Permission denied` output from `sudo -u deploy cat` and the `ls -l` line from before the fix, with `-rw-------` and owner `root`
sets group `appteam`, gives the directory 2750 and the file 640, and no step applies 777 or a recursive 777
explains that intake needs write on the directory while deploy needs read on the file, and names what 777 would have exposed to every local account

hints: The three digits are owner, group, other: 640 is read and write for the owner, read for the group, and nothing for anyone else.
If `cat` fails even though the file looks readable, run `ls -ld` on each parent directory and check for the execute bit before you touch the file mode.
`chmod 2750` sets the setgid bit on the directory, so new files inherit the `appteam` group instead of the creating user primary group.

assignments.title: Find the process before someone reboots the host
assignments.scenario: At 10:20 the checkout page on web01 slowed from 300 ms to 6 s per request. `top` shows one process pinning a core, and a senior colleague messages "just reboot it". The host also runs a nightly report rebuild that normally takes 40 minutes, and the business report is due at 12:00.
assignments.task:
1. Start a stand-in for the nightly report job as a transient systemd unit. It burns one core, so you have a real process to investigate.

```
sudo systemd-run --unit=report-rebuild --working-directory=/tmp /usr/bin/python3 -c 'while True: pass'
uptime
```

2. Find the top CPU consumer and note the difference between elapsed time and CPU time.

```
ps -eo pid,ppid,pcpu,pmem,etime,args --sort=-pcpu | head -n 8
top -b -n1 | head -n 15
```

3. Take the PID of `python3` and get its full story.

```
ps -o pid,ppid,user,etime,time,pcpu,cmd -p <PID>
```

4. Find which unit owns the process.

```
cat /proc/<PID>/cgroup
systemctl status report-rebuild --no-pager
```

5. Check whether a scheduled job explains it.

```
systemctl list-timers --all --no-pager | head -n 15
ls -l /etc/cron.d
```

6. Check what is listening and how many sessions are open, because CPU alone does not explain slow responses.

```
sudo ss -tulnp | grep -E ':(80|8080|5432)'
sudo ss -Htan state established | wc -l
```

7. Decide between throttle and stop. Lowering priority is reversible and keeps the job alive; stopping it needs approval and a note of what work is lost.

```
sudo renice 10 -p <PID>
ps -o pid,ni,pcpu,args -p <PID>
```

8. Record the decision and what a reboot would have discarded: the running job progress and the process state that explains the slowdown.

Safety: `renice` and `kill` change a running host. Capture the `ps` and `ss` output before either, and get approval before any `kill` or `systemctl restart`; a reboot erases the state that explains the slowdown. Stop the fixture with `sudo systemctl stop report-rebuild`.
assignments.deliverable: One line with the PID, its unit, its elapsed time, and the decision (renice, stop with approval, or escalate) with the reason.

rubric.criterion: Process identified by PID and unit
rubric.lookFor: gives a PID that matches the `ps` output and names `report-rebuild.service` from `/proc/<PID>/cgroup` or `systemctl status`
compares `etime` with `time` and says whether the job is busy or stuck, instead of calling any high-CPU process a leak
rejects the reboot with a reason tied to the running job, and names the exact next action plus who approves it

hints: `etime` is wall-clock time since start and `time` is CPU time used. A job with 20 minutes of `etime` and 19 minutes of `time` is spinning; one with 7 hours of `etime` and 12 minutes of `time` is mostly waiting.
`ps -eo ... --sort=-pcpu` sorts descending; drop the minus sign and the idle processes come first.
`systemd-run --unit=NAME` creates a transient unit, so `systemctl status` and `/proc/<PID>/cgroup` both name it; stop it with `sudo systemctl stop report-rebuild`.

assignments.title: Run the four-check triage on an unknown fault
assignments.scenario: It is 08:45 on app02, the checkout host. Two users report timeouts and one reports an error page, but no dashboard panel is red. The customer call is at 09:30 and the L2 engineer is on another bridge. You own the lab host and the next 45 minutes.
assignments.task:
1. Build a healthy baseline first, so later evidence has something to compare against.

```
sudo mkdir -p /srv/checkout
echo 'checkout ok' | sudo tee /srv/checkout/index.html >/dev/null
sudo chmod 644 /srv/checkout/index.html
sudo systemd-run --unit=checkout --working-directory=/srv/checkout /usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:8080/; echo
```

2. Record the baseline. These are the values a healthy host returns, and the note will quote them later.

```
date
ip -br addr
ip route
df -h / /var
df -i /var
sudo ss -tulnp | grep ':8080'
systemctl status checkout --no-pager | head -n 5
```

3. Inject exactly one fault and write down the time. Pick one and do not read the others.

Fault A, service stopped:

```
sudo systemctl stop checkout
```

Fault B, service bound to loopback only:

```
sudo systemctl stop checkout
sudo systemctl reset-failed checkout 2>/dev/null || true
sudo systemd-run --unit=checkout --working-directory=/srv/checkout /usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1
```

Fault C, port 8080 already owned by another process:

```
sudo systemctl stop checkout
sudo systemctl reset-failed checkout 2>/dev/null || true
sudo systemd-run --unit=stray-web /usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0
sudo systemd-run --unit=checkout --working-directory=/srv/checkout /usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0
```

4. Leave the host for 10 minutes. When you return, do not read your note of which fault you chose. Run the checks in the order you choose and state why that order.

5. Run the four-check runbook plus the network checks.

```
df -h /var
df -i /var
sudo lsof +L1 | head -n 5
systemctl --failed --no-pager
systemctl status checkout --no-pager | tail -n 15
journalctl -u checkout --since '20 min ago' -p warning --no-pager | tail -n 20
sudo ss -tulnp | grep ':8080'
namei -l /srv/checkout/index.html
stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' /srv/checkout/index.html
ip -br addr
ip route
getent hosts "$(hostname)"
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:8080/; echo
```

If `lsof` is not installed, add it once with `sudo apt install -y lsof`; the package is in the standard Ubuntu repository.

6. Write the note: symptom, start time, the check that failed with one line of its output, at least two checks that passed, and the close-or-escalate line naming the team.

7. Revert the fault and confirm the baseline returns.

```
sudo systemctl stop checkout stray-web 2>/dev/null || true
sudo systemctl reset-failed checkout stray-web 2>/dev/null || true
sudo chmod 644 /srv/checkout/index.html
sudo systemd-run --unit=checkout --working-directory=/srv/checkout /usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:8080/; echo
```

8. Write the five-line runbook a colleague can follow without you: one command per check, in the order you would run them, plus the condition that turns the ticket into an escalation.

Safety: break only the lab host, and record every command with its revert line in the ticket. On a production host, `chmod` on customer files and any change to a running service need the change ticket before you type the command.
assignments.deliverable: One triage note with the failing check and its output, at least two checks named as passed, the close-or-escalate line with the team, and the five-command runbook.

rubric.lookFor: runs the disk, service, port and permission checks plus address and route, and gives one sentence on why the order is cheapest-first
quotes one output line per check, names the failing check, and names at least two checks that passed instead of reporting only the failure
closes with the fix when the fault is inside L1 scope, or escalates with the failing check, the evidence, and the named team; never a bare request for L2 to look at the server

hints: Negative evidence is evidence: 'disk at 41 percent, no failed units, 8080 listening on 0.0.0.0' is what stops an unnecessary escalation.
Use `journalctl -u checkout --since '20 min ago'` rather than the whole journal; the incident window is the only part the note needs.

Read the socket before you guess: `ss` showing 127.0.0.1:8080 means the listen address, nothing on 8080 means the process is gone, and 8080 held by a process you did not start means something else owns the port.

assignments.title: Identity, address and reachability in one guided pass
assignments.scenario: At 10:05 a user on the third floor reports that the network is down on laptop WS-0412. Nothing has been changed yet, and the ticket carries no IP address, no error text and no screenshot. You have the machine in front of you, a local account, and 25 minutes before the next call. The last three tickets like this were closed with one `ipconfig /all` and one ping.
assignments.task:
1. Open PowerShell and record who you are before you record anything else. The account matters, because half of the later commands behave differently for a standard user.

```
whoami
hostname
Get-Date
```

2. Capture the full addressing block. Plain `ipconfig` is not enough: it hides the DNS servers and the DHCP state that the note needs.

```
ipconfig /all
```

3. Read four fields off the output for the active adapter and write them down exactly: the adapter description, the IPv4 address with its subnet mask, the default gateway, and the DNS servers. Note whether `DHCP Enabled` is Yes or No.

4. Check the address against the decision rule. If the IPv4 address starts with 169.254, DHCP went unanswered and every later ping will fail for that reason alone. Record that and skip to step 7.

5. Test three things in this order: the gateway, then a public address, then a name.

```
ping -n 4 <gateway-from-step-3>
ping -n 4 8.8.8.8
Resolve-DnsName www.microsoft.com
```

6. Mark each of the three tests as pass or fail with the reply text, not with an impression. `Request timed out` and `Destination host unreachable` are different failures and different tickets.

7. Write the handover. Three lines are enough: identity, address, reachability, then one line naming the next team.

Safety: every command here is read-only. Do not run `ipconfig /release` or `ipconfig /renew` before the output is captured: release drops the address, ends the user's session, and destroys the evidence you came for.
assignments.deliverable: One handover block containing the account, the adapter, the IPv4 address, the gateway, the DNS server, the pass or fail result of the three tests, and the single next team.

rubric.lookFor: quotes the `ipconfig /all` lines for the active adapter showing the IPv4 address with mask, the default gateway, the DNS servers and `DHCP Enabled`, and no step runs release, renew or flushdns before that output appears
labels each of the three tests as pass or fail with its reply text, distinguishes timed out from unreachable, and does not call the network down when only the name test failed

names exactly one next team with the evidence that supports it, for example the network team with the adapter name and gateway result, or the resolver address for a name fault, instead of escalating the laptop

hints: `ipconfig` on its own prints address, mask and gateway; the DNS servers and lease details only appear with `/all`.
A 169.254 address means the DHCP request was never answered, so a failed ping after it proves nothing about the cable; record the address first and say why the later tests are inconclusive.
If the gateway answers and 8.8.8.8 does not, the local link and the VLAN are fine and the path out is not; that is a different team than a dead adapter.

assignments.title: Name the service behind the PID before anyone reboots
assignments.scenario: WS-0412 has run at 100 percent CPU since 09:20 and the fan has not stopped. Task Manager shows a `svchost.exe` at 38 percent under SYSTEM, which tells the user nothing and the ticket less. The user has a deadline at 14:00 and a colleague has already posted "just reboot it" in the ticket. The machine has been up for 41 days.
assignments.task:
1. Start from the process list and note the PID. Sort by memory first and by CPU second, because the slow-PC call is more often memory or a leak than a busy core.

```
Get-Process | Sort-Object WS -Descending | Select-Object -First 8 Name, Id, WS, CPU
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 8 Name, Id, CPU, StartTime
```

2. Ask Windows which services live inside that PID. `svchost.exe` is a container, so the service name is the only thing the ticket can act on.

```
tasklist /svc /fi "PID eq <pid>"
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "ProcessId=<pid>" | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, State, StartMode, StartName
```

3. Pull the full record for the service you found: state, start mode, logon account and binary path.

```
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='<service>'" | Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName
Get-Service <service> | Select-Object Status, StartType
```

4. Answer the reboot question from configuration, not from opinion. A service set to Automatic returns after a reboot; one set to Manual or Disabled does not.

```
Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object LastBootUpTime, FreePhysicalMemory, TotalVisibleMemorySize, CSName
```

5. List what else starts at boot, so the note can say what a reboot would restart besides the problem.

```
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select-Object Name, Location, User, Command
Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.StartType -eq 'Automatic' -and $_.Status -ne 'Running' } | Select-Object Name, Status
```

6. Write the note: PID, service name, start mode, logon account, uptime in days, and a yes or no to "would a reboot have fixed this".

Safety: the commands are read-only. Do not stop a service or restart the machine to test a theory: a restart ends the user's session and erases the process state that explains the 41 days of uptime. Any stop needs the service owner and an approved change.
assignments.deliverable: One line with the PID, the service inside it, its StartMode and StartName, the uptime in days, and the yes or no answer to whether a reboot would have fixed it.

rubric.lookFor: gives a PID that matches the `Get-Process` output and the same PID's service name from `tasklist /svc` or `Win32_Service`, rather than leaving the answer at `svchost.exe`
answers with the `StartMode` value and explains what Automatic versus Manual or Disabled means for the next boot, and quotes a `LastBootUpTime` or an uptime figure instead of a guess
states that no restart or service stop was performed, names the `StartName` account as the owner, and routes to that service's team rather than asking L2 to look at the PC

hints: `tasklist /svc` prints the service names on the same line as the PID, which is one command instead of a cross-reference exercise.
`WS` is working set in bytes. Divide by 1073741824 for GB, or the 4 GB leak reads as 4294967296 and looks like a different problem.
`Get-Process` describes the live process; `Win32_Service` describes the configured start mode and account, and only the second one can answer a question about the next boot.

assignments.title: Unlock the account, then find what keeps locking it
assignments.scenario: At 08:55 a.reyes calls: the account is locked and she has a client call at 09:30. Her manager says nobody changed her password. The service desk has unlocked her twice already this week, and both tickets were closed with "account unlocked, user confirmed working". You have a lab virtual machine and a throwaway account to reproduce the pattern without touching hers.
assignments.task:
1. Read the policy before you touch the account. The threshold and the window explain the timing you are about to see.

```
net accounts
net accounts /domain
```

The second command works on a domain-joined host and fails or returns the local policy on a workgroup machine; note which one you got.

2. Read the account and notice what `net user` does and does not show.

```
net user a.reyes
```

3. Build the reproduction on the lab VM only. Create a throwaway account, then set a lockout policy low enough to trigger in three attempts.

```
net user lab.lockout * /add
net accounts /lockoutthreshold:3 /lockoutduration:15 /lockoutwindow:15
```

4. Generate failed logons against the throwaway account and confirm each one is recorded.

```
net use \\localhost\IPC$ /user:lab.lockout WrongPass1
net use \\localhost\IPC$ /user:lab.lockout WrongPass2
net use \\localhost\IPC$ /user:lab.lockout WrongPass3
```

If no 4625 appears afterwards, the loopback connection reused your session; use this variant instead and run it three times.

```
$c = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('lab.lockout', (ConvertTo-SecureString 'WrongPass1' -AsPlainText -Force))
Start-Process cmd.exe -Credential $c
```

5. Read the two records the lesson named, and quote their timestamps.

```
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-15)} -MaxEvents 5 | Format-List TimeCreated, Id, Message
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4740} -MaxEvents 3 | Format-List TimeCreated, Message
```

6. Read the logon type on the 4625 events. Type 2 is a console logon, 3 is network, 5 is a service, 10 is RDP. The number is what separates a person from a device with a saved password.

7. Check for the local admin problem while you are there, because an over-privileged account is an escalation on its own.

```
net localgroup administrators
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' | Select-Object Name, ObjectClass, PrincipalSource
```

8. Decide: is this a person or a stored credential? If the failures repeat on a fixed interval and at hours when nobody is at a keyboard, the source is a phone with an old password, a mapped drive, or a scheduled task. Name the source and the team that owns it.

Safety and privacy: the reproduction runs on the lab VM only. Locking a real account is a denial of service and a reportable change; never test against a colleague's account or a production service account. Usernames, computer names and source addresses in event output are personal data, so redact them before anything goes into the ticket.
assignments.deliverable: One line with the 4740 timestamp, the number of 4625 events before it with their logon type, and the source of the retries that you identified.

rubric.lookFor: quotes the lockout threshold, duration and observation window from `net accounts`, and uses those numbers to explain why the attempts locked the account when they did
cites a 4740 time and at least two 4625 events before it for the same account, names the logon type, and argues from the interval between failures whether the source is a person or a device

does not close on unlock alone; names the concrete source to fix (cached credential on a phone, mapped drive, scheduled task) or routes to the team that owns it, and states that the real account was not used for testing

hints: `net user <name>` shows `Account active`, password expiry and last logon, but it never shows lockout state; that fact comes from event 4740 or from the directory tool for the domain.
Failures every four minutes at 02:00 are a device, not a person. Failures spread through the working day with type 2 logons are a person at a keyboard.
Unlocking a third time without naming the source is the exact ticket the manager complained about, so the note has to end with something other than "unlocked".

assignments.title: Turn three logs into a timeline you can defend
assignments.scenario: At 07:10 on Monday the lab host shows an unexpected reboot overnight and a local account nobody recognizes. The night shift note reads "server rebooted, checking in the morning". You have until the 08:00 call to produce a timeline with timestamps, and the word of a colleague is not evidence.
assignments.task:
1. Check which logs you actually have before you query them, and their sizes.

```
Get-WinEvent -ListLog Security, System, Application | Select-Object LogName, RecordCount, MaximumSizeInBytes, IsEnabled
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion
```

2. Establish the boot and shutdown times from the System log. 6005 and 6006 are the event log starting and stopping, 6008 is an unexpected shutdown, 1074 is a shutdown or restart requested by a process, and 41 is a boot with no clean shutdown before it.

```
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=6005,6006,6008,1074,41; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-3)} | Sort-Object TimeCreated | Format-Table TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName -AutoSize
```

3. Query the account events in one pass. 4720 is an account created, 4726 an account deleted, 4740 a lockout.

```
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4720,4726,4740; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-3)} | Sort-Object TimeCreated | Format-List TimeCreated, Id, Message
```

4. Check whether anyone cleared a log. 1102 is the Security log cleared, 104 is another log cleared and is recorded in the System log, and 1102 on a production host is treated as hostile until proven otherwise.

```
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=1102} -MaxEvents 5
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=104} -MaxEvents 5
```

5. When a query returns nothing, check whether the audit policy records that category at all. An empty result and an unconfigured audit policy look identical in the console.

```
auditpol /get /category:"Account Management"
auditpol /get /category:"Logon/Logoff"
```

6. Confirm the version behavior the lesson warned about: `Get-EventLog` exists in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and is gone in PowerShell 7.

```
Get-EventLog -LogName System -Newest 3 -EntryType Error
```

Run it once in `powershell.exe` and once in `pwsh.exe` if both are installed, and record the difference.

7. Export what you found so the next engineer can check it, and keep the bounded filter on the export.

```
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=6005,6006,6008,1074,41; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-3)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, Message | Export-Csv "$HOME\Desktop\m3-timeline.csv" -NoTypeInformation
```

8. Write four lines: last clean boot, first event after it, any account change, and any log clearing. Where a query returned nothing, write the query and the reason it returned nothing.

Safety and privacy: the Security log holds usernames, computer names and source addresses, so redact them before the export leaves the machine. Never clear a log to tidy a timeline: event 1102 is itself an investigation item, and destroying a log is a reportable act.
assignments.deliverable: A four-line timeline with a timestamp on each line, plus one line listing the event IDs you queried and found nothing for, with the audit policy value that explains each empty result.

rubric.lookFor: every event query is limited by `-FilterHashtable` with a `StartTime`, or by a `-MaxEvents` value, and no query reads a whole log unbounded

lists a boot or shutdown event from 6005, 6008, 1074 or 41 and an account event from 4720 or 4726 with timestamps taken from the output, in chronological order, and keeps what was found separate from what returned nothing
when 4720 or 1102 returns no rows, checks `auditpol` for the category or states that the audit policy may not record it, instead of writing that the event did not happen

hints: `-FilterHashtable` takes an array for `Id`, so `Id=4720,4726,4740` is one query rather than three passes over a log with hundreds of thousands of records.
`Get-EventLog` is a Windows PowerShell 5.1 cmdlet and does not exist in PowerShell 7; check `$PSVersionTable.PSVersion` before you report a command that appears to be missing.
A quiet log and a log that records nothing are different findings, and the second one is a finding about the audit policy, not about the incident.

assignments.title: One runbook, three calls, one decision to defend
assignments.scenario: It is 08:45 on the lab host and three tickets are open. One user says the PC is slow, one cannot connect over RDP, one has been locked out twice this week. No dashboard panel is red and L2 is on another bridge until 10:00. You have 50 minutes, the lab VM, and no production system in scope. Nobody will tell you which ticket to take first.
assignments.task:
1. Choose your order and write it down before you run anything, with one sentence per ticket on why that order: cheapest check, most likely cause, or least disruptive.

2. Reproduce at least two of the three symptoms on the lab host so the evidence is real.

Slow PC: a process pinning a core, or a service holding memory.

```
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, Id, CPU, WS
Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object FreePhysicalMemory, TotalVisibleMemorySize, LastBootUpTime
```

No RDP: check the listener, the rule, and the logon separately, because a failed connect does not say which one broke.

```
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <host> -Port 3389
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3389 -State Listen
Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup "Remote Desktop" | Select-Object DisplayName, Enabled, Direction, Action
quser
```

Locked account: the policy, the account, and the failed attempts behind it.

```
net accounts
net user <username>
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625,4740; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-12)} -MaxEvents 20 | Format-Table TimeCreated, Id -AutoSize
```

3. For each ticket record four things in the same order every time: the symptom in the user's words, the check that proved the cause, the check that ruled out the nearest alternative, and the fix or the route.

4. Write the reusable runbook: no more than twelve commands, in the order you would run them on a fresh call, one line each, with the evidence that command produces. Include the command that tells you to stop checking, for example a listener on the right address or a rule that is enabled.

5. Write the close-or-escalate rule for each ticket: what L1 closes outright, what goes to L2 or to the network team, and the exact sentence the ticket needs, naming the team and the evidence.

6. Find at least one check you ran that produced nothing and remove it from the runbook. Say what it cost in minutes on this call.

7. Pick the one decision where the tempting escalation was wrong, and defend it with the negative evidence that closed it.

Safety and privacy: lab host only, and never against a customer machine. Do not stop services, change firewall rules or reset passwords to create a symptom, because the fix becomes the new incident. Redact usernames and addresses from anything you paste into the ticket.
assignments.deliverable: A runbook of twelve commands or fewer with one evidence line each, plus a three-row table giving the decision, the team, and the single sentence of evidence for each of the three calls.

rubric.lookFor: numbers twelve or fewer checks, gives the command and the evidence line it produces for each, and states an order that puts read-only and cheap checks before anything disruptive

for at least two of the three calls, names the check that ruled out the nearest alternative, for example a listener on 0.0.0.0 with the Remote Desktop rule enabled, or a 4625 interval that matches a device; restating the symptom does not score
decides close or escalate for all three calls with a named team and a one-sentence evidence line each, and identifies at least one escalation in the set that L1 should have closed itself

hints: Write the runbook after the three calls, not before. A first draft always contains one check that answered nothing, and the edit is part of the exercise.
A negative result belongs in the ticket: "3389 listening, Remote Desktop rule enabled, logon still refused" is what makes a handoff legitimate instead of a handoff by exhaustion.
If you cannot name the team that owns the next action, the diagnosis is not finished, and that is the moment the ticket should have gone back to the checks rather than to L2.

assignments.title: Prove what changed before you call it a breach
assignments.scenario: It is 08:10 on Monday and three tickets are open. The HR share on files01 now lets all staff read salary files. The customer portal has been down since 07:40. The nightly invoice file no longer matches the copy finance approved on Friday. The shift lead wants all three marked security incident and sent to L3. Your job is to separate evidence from noise before that happens.
assignments.task:
1. Build a synthetic invoice on your own laptop. Nothing here is customer data.

```
mkdir -p ~/m4/day16 && cd ~/m4/day16
printf 'invoice,amount\nINV-1001,240.00\nINV-1002,118.50\n' > invoice-mon.csv
cp invoice-mon.csv invoice-mon.orig
date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ
sha256sum invoice-mon.csv
```

On macOS use `shasum -a 256 invoice-mon.csv`. On Windows use `certutil -hashfile invoice-mon.csv SHA256`.

2. Change the file the way an unapproved edit would, and hash again.

```
printf 'INV-1003,9100.00\n' >> invoice-mon.csv
sha256sum invoice-mon.csv
```

3. Restore the approved copy and hash a third time. A digest that returns to the baseline value proves the bytes are back; it does not prove who changed them or when.

```
cp invoice-mon.orig invoice-mon.csv
sha256sum invoice-mon.csv
```

4. Read the metadata that answers the who and when question.

```
ls -l invoice-mon.csv
stat -c '%U %G %a %y' invoice-mon.csv
```

On macOS use `stat -f '%Su %Sg %Lp %Sm' invoice-mon.csv`. On Windows use `icacls invoice-mon.csv`.

5. Classify each of the three tickets as confidentiality, integrity, or availability, and write one line of business impact for each. The portal outage is availability until you have evidence of a cause.

6. Decide for each ticket: close at L1 with the check you performed, or escalate to a named team. Sending all three to L3 is the behavior this drill is designed to stop. If a change looks malicious, capture the ACL and the timestamps before anyone repairs it; a repair destroys the evidence the incident team needs.

7. Write the triage note. It needs the UTC time, the two digests that differ, the digest that matches the baseline again, the CIA label per ticket, and one escalation criterion per ticket.

Safety: use only the synthetic file you create. Never hash, copy, or upload a real customer file to a personal machine or a public site; a hash of a small, guessable file can be brute-forced.
assignments.deliverable: One note that gives each of the three tickets a CIA label, a one-line impact, the measured hash evidence for the invoice file, and a close-or-escalate decision with a named team.

rubric.criterion: Integrity evidence is measured, not described
rubric.lookFor: quotes two SHA-256 values that differ after the edit and shows the digest returning to the original value after the restore; a paragraph explaining what hashing is does not score
each ticket is labeled confidentiality, integrity, or availability with one sentence naming who is blocked or exposed, and the portal outage is not defaulted to a security incident
each ticket states close at L1 or escalate, and every escalation names a team and the evidence that travels with it; 'send all three to L3' scores nothing

hints: `printf` writes exactly the bytes you give it. Use it instead of a text editor so a stray trailing newline does not change the digest for a reason you cannot explain.
A matching digest proves the bytes are identical. Attribution needs a log or a filesystem timestamp, so the note must name the second source for the who and when.

Availability is one leg of the triad. A portal outage is an availability incident; it becomes a security incident only when you can point to a cause such as tampering, ransomware, or an account compromise.

assignments.title: Take the extra privilege away, on paper first
assignments.scenario: app01 runs the payments API for a customer on 10.20.4.0/24. The vendor support account svc-vendor is in the local administrators group. Three shift engineers share the password for the local account helpdesk2. A contractor's VPN account is active and has no MFA. The quarterly access review is due Friday and L2 has asked you to prepare the evidence.
assignments.task:
1. Enumerate privilege read-only on your own lab VM. Do not run this against app01.

```
hostname; id
getent group sudo
getent group adm
getent passwd | awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1, $3, $7}'
sudo -l -U "$USER"
```

On Windows use:

```
net localgroup administrators
Get-LocalUser | Select-Object Name,Enabled,LastLogon
whoami /priv
```

2. Build a synthetic sign-in export and find the accounts that succeeded without MFA.

```
printf 'user,mfa,result,src_ip\nana,true,success,10.20.30.11\nraj,false,success,10.20.30.12\nsvc-vendor,false,success,10.20.9.15\nhelpdesk2,false,success,10.20.30.13\nlee,true,success,10.20.30.14\n' > signins.csv
awk -F, 'NR>1 && $2 ~ /false/ && $3 ~ /success/ {print $1, $4}' signins.csv
wc -l signins.csv
```

On Windows use `Import-Csv signins.csv | Where-Object { $_.mfa -eq 'false' -and $_.result -eq 'success' }`.

3. Check the password and lockout policy that applies to those accounts.

```
sudo grep -E '^(PASS_MAX_DAYS|PASS_MIN_LEN)' /etc/login.defs
sudo grep -E 'pam_pwquality|pam_unix' /etc/pam.d/common-password
```

On Windows use `net accounts`.

4. Find out whether the privileged account ever logs in interactively.

```
last -n 5 svc-vendor
sudo lastlog -u svc-vendor
```

5. Rank three findings by exposure times impact, and state the number you used for each. A vendor account that can log in interactively with local admin rights is a different finding from a stale account that has never logged in.

6. Write the change request for the top finding. It needs the exact command, the rollback, the approver role, and the window. Do not execute it on a shared host.

```
sudo deluser svc-vendor sudo
sudo usermod -L helpdesk2
```

`deluser` is the Debian and Ubuntu command; on RHEL and Rocky use `sudo gpasswd -d svc-vendor sudo`.

7. Separate what L1 closes (the evidence pack, the MFA gap count, the report) from what the identity team must do (enforce MFA, replace the shared account, remove the vendor access). State that a group change only reaches an application when a new token is issued, so the user signs out and back in.

Safety: enumeration only. Do not remove a vendor account, lock a shared account, or change a group on a host you do not own; the change request is the deliverable, not an executed change.
assignments.deliverable: A three-row finding table with account, privilege, exposure, and owner, plus one exact removal command with its rollback and the approver who must sign it.

rubric.lookFor: names the account and the group or privilege exactly as the output shows it, for example the sudo line from `getent group sudo` or the Administrators row from `net localgroup`, and quotes that line
uses the CSV numbers, such as 3 of 5 successful sign-ins with mfa=false, and names helpdesk2 as a shared account whose actions cannot be attributed to one person

rubric.criterion: Change request is safe and approvable
rubric.lookFor: gives the exact command, a rollback command that restores the access, the approver role, and an explicit statement that L1 does not execute the change without that approval

hints: `getent group sudo` reads the same source the system uses, so it catches group memberships from LDAP that `cat /etc/group` will miss.
`awk -F,` splits on commas, and the header line will match a loose filter. Keep `NR>1` so the export header is not counted as a finding.
A shared account cannot be attributed to one engineer, so removing it needs a named replacement account per person, not just a password change that everyone learns again.

assignments.title: Read the certificate before you blame the VPN
assignments.scenario: Since 09:00, users on the VPN get a browser warning on portal.example.com, while users in the office do not. The service desk has opened a network ticket, and the portal team says nothing changed on the server. You cannot reach the portal host from your laptop, so you rebuild the case with a lab certificate and 40 minutes before the 10:00 bridge.
assignments.task:
1. Check your OpenSSL build before you start. The date options below need OpenSSL 3.x, and the system binary on macOS is LibreSSL.

```
openssl version
openssl req -help 2>&1 | grep -E 'not_before|not_after'
```

If those two lines are missing, run the drill in a Linux VM or install OpenSSL with Homebrew.

2. Build a lab certificate that expired in February 2024 and carries no SAN. This is the certificate a portal team can still serve after a migration that never finished.

```
mkdir -p ~/m4/day18 && cd ~/m4/day18
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -not_before 20240101000000Z -not_after 20240201000000Z -subj '/CN=portal.example.com' 2>/dev/null
```

3. Read the same fields the browser reads.

```
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
```

Expect subject and issuer to be identical because the certificate signs itself, a notAfter date in the past, and `No extensions in certificate` on stderr because there is no SAN at all.

4. Serve the certificate locally and connect to it the way a client would.

```
openssl s_server -accept 8443 -cert cert.pem -key key.pem -www >/dev/null 2>&1 &
SERVER_PID=$!
sleep 1
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername portal.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'verify error|Verify return code|notAfter'
kill $SERVER_PID
```

Two verify errors appear: 18 for the self-signed issuer and 10 for the expired date. `Verify return code` reports the one that ends the session, and that is the one the browser shows.

5. Repeat against a live certificate that is valid and has a SAN, to see what good looks like. If you are offline, skip this step and say so in the note.

```
openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -servername github.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates -ext subjectAltName | head -n 5
```

Compare the SAN line with the name you typed. A name that is not in that list is a mismatch, even when the certificate is valid and trusted.

6. Check the clock on the machine that sees the warning, because a wrong clock produces the same browser warning as an expired certificate.

```
date -u
```

On Windows use `w32tm /query /status`.

7. Check HSTS on a site that sends it, because the header decides whether the browser ever tries HTTP again after a warning.

```
curl -sI https://github.com | grep -i strict-transport-security
```

8. Map each failure to the field that proves it: expired (`notAfter` in the past), missing or non-matching SAN (the SAN line does not contain the host), untrusted chain (`verify error:num=18`, 20, or 21). Name which handshake fact failed: the private key, the trust chain, or the name. Then answer the ticket question. A genuinely expired certificate warns every user, so it cannot explain a VPN-only split on its own; a TLS-inspecting proxy, or an internal CA that only domain machines trust, can.

9. Write the handover with the failing field and its value, the failure mode, the mechanism that explains the VPN-only split, the team, and one line on what L1 closes without the portal host.

Safety: every certificate here is generated on your laptop and `s_server` binds to 127.0.0.1 only. Do not bind it to a shared network, and do not test hosts you are not authorized to test.
assignments.deliverable: One line naming the failing field and its value, the failure mode, the most likely cause of the VPN-only split with the check that would confirm it, and the team that owns the fix.

rubric.criterion: Certificate fields quoted from the run
rubric.lookFor: quotes the actual subject, issuer, and notAfter values plus the missing-SAN or SAN line from the output; describing what a certificate contains does not score

rubric.criterion: Failure mode named from the verify code
rubric.lookFor: names expired and untrusted chain from verify error 18 and 10 or from the notAfter date, and states which code stops the handshake; 'bad certificate' with no code does not score
reports the client clock result and names the mechanism that affects only VPN users, either a TLS-inspecting proxy or a CA trusted only on domain machines, then names the portal or PKI team

hints: `-servername` sends SNI. Without it a shared listener may return a different certificate and you will diagnose the wrong host.
Pipe `s_client` into `openssl x509` only with stderr discarded, or the handshake text is parsed as a certificate and the command fails.
Two verify errors appear here: 18 for the self-signed issuer and 10 for the date. `Verify return code` reports the one that ends the session, and that is the one a browser shows.

assignments.title: Find the open port and the missing patch
assignments.scenario: The EDR console shows ws-042 in VLAN 30 opening SMB connections to 40 hosts in four minutes. Two other workstations in the same VLAN accept port 445 from each other, and the server team says patching is 90 days behind. The asset owner is on leave and the VLAN has no rule between workstations.
assignments.task:
1. List what the host is listening on and which process owns each socket. Run this on your own lab VM.

```
sudo ss -tulnp
```

On Windows use:

```
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Sort-Object LocalPort | Select-Object LocalPort,OwningProcess
```

2. Check whether the host firewall is actually enabled, not just installed.

```
sudo ufw status verbose
```

On Windows use `Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name,Enabled`. If ufw is inactive, use `sudo nft list ruleset | head -n 40`.

3. Measure patch age instead of accepting the story.

```
sudo apt list --upgradable 2>/dev/null | head -n 20
```

On Windows use:

```
Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 HotFixID,InstalledOn
```

Then check whether the host has restarted since the update. Installed, loaded, and rebooted are three different facts, and only the last one makes a kernel or library patch effective.

```
sudo needs-restarting -r; echo "exit=$?"
[ -f /var/run/reboot-required ] && cat /var/run/reboot-required
```

The first command is for RHEL and Rocky, the second for Ubuntu. On Windows, compare `Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object LastBootUpTime` with the newest InstalledOn date.

4. Check endpoint protection state and the signature date.

```
Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMServiceEnabled,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated
```

On Linux, `systemctl status clamav-freshclam --no-pager` if the agent is installed; otherwise record that no agent is present, which is a finding.

5. Test 445 from a second host you own. One port against a customer range is still an unauthorized scan.

```
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 10.20.30.21 -Port 445
```

On Linux use `nc -vz -w 3 10.20.30.21 445`.

6. Write the segmentation rule that would have contained the spread: source VLAN 30, destination VLAN 30, TCP 445, deny, with one exception for the file server. Give it as a paste-ready line, not a paragraph.

7. Decide what L1 closes (an agent that is stopped, a stale signature, a firewall profile that is off) and what escalates (the patch campaign, the VLAN ACL, host isolation). Name the team for each.

8. List the evidence you would preserve first if this were real: the EDR process tree and the connection list, captured before anyone cleans the host.

Safety: test only hosts you own. A single-port `Test-NetConnection` against a customer range is still an unauthorized scan.
assignments.deliverable: A three-row table covering listener, patch age, and protection state with quoted output, plus one deny rule for TCP 445 and the team that implements it.

rubric.criterion: Listener evidence with the owning process
